Bitcoin’s real test is happening here Young Kenyans in urban centers are rapidly embracing Bitcoin as a form of payment /RT/ Kenya is touted as Africa’s hub for technology and innovation. Across the East African nation, mobile money has become the most common and widely used form of payment and banking, both in the formal and informal sectors of the economy. But even as mobile money dominates Kenya’s economy, a new wave of cryptocurrency payment is taking root in urban areas across the country. A 2022 UN report listed Kenya as the largest market of crypto users in Africa, with four million crypto owners. Kenya’s crypto sector is estimated to register 4% growth by the end of 2025. ’It saves me time and money’ Since 2022, Brian Omondi has operated an electronics and gaming shop in Kibera, Kenya’s largest urban slum, 10km south of the Capital, Nairobi. The 26-year-old business management graduate has embraced Bitcoin as a form of payment, which he says is “more effective.” “I have clients from across the country, and online marketing is central to my business. Bitcoin payments are fast and secure because once the funds are in my wallet, they can’t be reversed, unlike mobile money,” Omondi told RT. He says most of his customers are tech-savvy young Kenyans and college students who are increasingly turning to cryptocurrency. “With Bitcoin, there’s no need to visit an agent to deposit or withdraw money. All I need is a smartphone and internet access. There is no bureaucracy, no transaction charges,” he said. Omondi, who gets his electronics supplies from China, says using Bitcoin has also made it easier to restock his shop by transacting directly with suppliers who accept cryptocurrency. “With Bitcoin, I can place orders and make payments instantly, bypassing currency conversions or international banking procedures,” he explains. “It saves me time and money, and my goods arrive faster.” Young Kenyans in urban centers are rapidly embracing Bitcoin as a form of payment, with many turning to the cryptocurrency as a flexible, borderless alternative amid limited access to traditional banking due to a lack of formal employment. Increased Bitcoin usage is also driven by the digital lifestyles of Kenyan youth, widespread smartphone usage, and enhanced internet connectivity. ’Bitcoin guarantees financial freedom to users’ In 2022, AfriBit Africa, a Kenyan fintech company, introduced the use of Bitcoin in Kibera. Ronnie Mdawida, AfriBit Africa co-founder, told RT that “Bitcoin guarantees financial freedom to users since it does not require the same documentation as traditional banking.” Small-scale traders and motorcycle taxi riders are among those accepting bitcoin payments in Kenyan towns. AfriBit Africa claims to have invested approximately $10,000 worth of bitcoin in Kibera since 2022. Mohammed Rajab, a taxi operator in the tourist city of Mombasa, says he began accepting Bitcoin in 2023 because many of his foreign clients prefer to pay using cryptocurrency. “Bitcoin is safe because I own and control my funds without relying on a third party,” Rajab told RT. Rajab says most of his foreign clients find it easier to pay in crypto rather than converting currency or using cards. “Bitcoin comes with the flexibility of saving and converting when rates are favorable,” he said. With the rise of remote freelance work, Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies have become essential for many young Kenyans earning a living through digital platforms. Sarah Thuo, based in Kisumu City, Western Kenya, has been a content writer for the past six years and has been accustomed to crypto payments. “All my clients are from the international market, and having a Bitcoin wallet enables faster payments, unlike bank transfers, which are prone to delays and restrictions,” she told RT. For Sarah, Bitcoin also shields her earnings from currency fluctuations and high bank transfer fees. Flip side of the Bitcoin In 2024, the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) collected approximately $77.3 million (Ksh 10 billion) from virtual asset service providers (VASPs). In 2023, under the Finance Act 2023, the Kenyan government introduced the Digital Assets Tax (DAT). Under the provision, crypto incomes are taxed. The law introduced a 3% tax on the transfer or exchange of digital assets. But experts warn that even as Bitcoin use gains momentum across Kenya, legal loopholes could expose many to the risk of fraud. Ali Hussein Kassim, chair of the FinTech Alliance in Kenya, told RT that many Kenyans are oblivious of the risks associated with bitcoin. “The investors are more interested in making profits and do not educate the users about the potential risks of bitcoin; no one takes to evaluate the risks involved,” Kassim warns. Kassim notes that the population being exposed to cryptocurrency is vulnerable. According to him, Bitcoin lacks the same protections as other financial services due to a lack of strong regulations. However, Mdawida told RT that, to cushion Kenyans against crypto risks, they have invested in financial literacy training and crypto courses for those using Bitcoin. Cases of cryptocurrency-related fraud have previously been reported in Kenya. In February 2025, two Kenyans were arrested for defrauding a Chinese national in a crypto scam. Will fines work? In January 2025, the IMF, in a Technical Assistance Report for Kenya has called for the enhancement of the country’s safety and regulation of the crypto sector. According to the IMF report, Kenya currently lacks a clear regulatory framework to oversee crypto-related activities. This loophole, the IMF said, has exposed cryptocurrencies to unlawful purposes. To address the challenges and guard cryptocurrencies against misuse, the IMF advised Kenya to implement robust anti-money laundering laws and counter-terrorism financing measures. In 2022, the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) explored the possibility of introducing a digital shilling dubbed the Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC), but the plan was abandoned due to the clear effectiveness of the already existing Kenya’s leading mobile money infrastructure, M-Pesa. Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin are not illegal in Kenya, and the law allows owning and trading of crypto. They are, however, not recognized as legal tender, nor accepted for official transactions like paying taxes, bank transactions or paying fees charged for government services. The growing adoption of crypto, especially among the young and tech-savvy population, has prompted the government to draft legislation that aims to regulate digital asset services and related activities. Kenya’s Finance Ministry introduced the Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASP) Bill, 2025, which outlines the licensing requirements for crypto service providers. The proposed law, which is currently before parliament, requires virtual asset service providers to register as formal businesses and obtain a government-issued license. The law proposes fines of up to KES 20 million ($150,000) for companies and KES 10 million and/or up to ten years in prison for individuals found in violation of the regulations. To enhance consumer protection and financial integrity, the law proposes fines of up to KES 30 million or imprisonment for up to a decade for offences related to scams, pump-and-dump schemes, or market manipulation. At the same time, the Kenyan government also requires crypto companies to implement strict Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) policies to enhance accountability and combat financial crime. And just like banks and traditional financial institutions, crypto companies are required to report any suspicious activities to the Financial Reporting Centre (FRC). Kassim argues, however, that the global nature of cryptocurrency makes it difficult for Kenya to regulate users who access international platforms outside its jurisdiction. “Most cases of the fraud being reported have a foreign link, and many of those defrauded never recover their money,” he told RT. Just as with the AI, Kenya cannot run away from the cryptocurrency reality and all it needs are strong and implementable policies that will cushion the public from exploitation. “The world is headed the cryptocurrency way and Kenya must not be left out. We must however get it right even as we join the bandwagon,” Kassim concluded. ***** While Wall Street has embraced Bitcoin through ETFs and institutional investments, the real proving ground seems to be places like Kenya, where young entrepreneurs and freelancers are using Bitcoin for everyday transactions. Here’s what’s happening: In urban centers like Nairobi and Mombasa, Bitcoin is being used to pay for groceries, electronics, and even taxi rides. Many Kenyans lack access to traditional banking, so Bitcoin offers a borderless, low-cost alternative. Freelancers and small business owners are using it to transact with international clients, bypassing delays and fees from banks. Local fintechs like AfriBit Africa are investing in crypto education and infrastructure to support adoption. But it’s not all smooth sailing: Kenya introduced a 3% Digital Assets Tax and is drafting legislation to regulate crypto service providers. The IMF has urged Kenya to tighten its crypto regulations to prevent misuse and fraud. Experts warn that without strong consumer protections, users could be vulnerable to scams. So while Wall Street may be validating Bitcoin’s value, Kenya is testing its utility—as a tool for financial freedom, not just speculation. This is a breakdown of what BOB is about in the picture below I'll give a detailed explanation of what this picture means What is a Hybrid ZK Rollup? A Hybrid ZK Rollup is a type of Layer 2 scaling solution that combines different technologies to improve speed, scalability, and security while holding back to Bitcoin for trust and finality. In BOB’s case, the hybrid design blends: ZK Proofs (Zero-Knowledge Proofs): These are cryptographic proofs that verify a transaction's validity without revealing the actual data. This helps scale efficiently while keeping transactions private and secure. OP Stack: This is the software framework from Optimism (used in Ethereum’s L2 solutions) that handles execution and coordination of smart contracts. Bitcoin Anchoring: The rollup’s state is periodically committed to Bitcoin, using Bitcoin’s security to ensure data cannot be tampered with. Staking Mechanism: Validators or participants can stake assets to help finalize states and secure the network. Why it matters: The hybrid approach gives BOB the flexibility of Ethereum (smart contracts, DeFi tools) and the security of Bitcoin (robust, time-tested finality). It’s like having the best of both chains. What are Ethereum Blobs? Ethereum blobs are a feature introduced with EIP-4844as part of Ethereum’s scaling upgrades. In simple terms: A blob is a large chunk of off-chain data that can be posted to Ethereum cheaply. It’s not permanently stored on-chain, but it’s available long enough for rollups or other Layer 2 networks to verify their state and generate proofs. Blobs reduce congestion and cost by separating raw data from the core Ethereum transaction data. In BOB’s case: Ethereum blobs are used as the primary data availability layer meaning the rollup posts transaction data to Ethereum (via blobs) so that anyone can later verify the state if needed. Bitcoin acts as a fallback DA layer for added security or redundancy. In summary of I've explained The Hybrid ZK Rollup ensures fast, secure, and scalable execution by merging Ethereum and Bitcoin tech. Ethereum blobs help store rollup data efficiently without burdening the main Ethereum chain, keeping gas costs low and performance high.

Understandng about What is the Timewarp Attack? The timewarp attack exploits Bitcoin’s rules around block timestamps and difficulty retargeting. (which occurs every 2016 blocks) In vulnerable networks like testnets, miners with sufficient hash power can manipulate timestamps to artificially lower difficulty: • Miners set timestamps progressively backward (but within the 2-hour future limit enforced by consensus). • At the end of a difficulty period, they advance the timestamp to the present, triggering the 20-minute rule (allowing minimum difficulty if a block’s timestamp is >20 minutes after the previous one). • This resets difficulty to 1, enabling rapid “block storms” where thousands of blocks are mined quickly, disrupting the network and amplifying attacks. This has historically caused issues on Testnet3, such as mining three years’ worth of blocks in weeks, leading to instability and usability problems. “The BIP-94 Timewarp Rule” To prevent this, BIP-94 adds a consensus rule for Testnet4: • For the first block of each difficulty period (where block height modulo 2016 == 0), the block’s timestamp (nTime) must be ≥ the previous block’s nTime minus 600 seconds. • The block must still comply with existing Median Time Past (MTP) rules, which require the timestamp to be greater than the median of the previous 11 blocks’ timestamps. This 600-second “grace period” allows minor adjustments for clock drift or network latency but blocks the large backward jumps needed for a timewarp attack. The rule originates from “The Great Consensus Cleanup” proposal and is enforced from Testnet4’s genesis. While BIP-94 primarily targets Testnet4, Bitcoin Core version 29.0 (released around April 2025) extends consideration of this timewarp fix to all networks (mainnet, testnet, signet, and regtest) in the getblocktemplate RPC. This RPC is used by miners to generate block templates and now adjusts: • curtime (from BIP-22): The suggested current timestamp for the new block. • mintime (from BIP-23): The minimum allowable timestamp for the block. Even on networks where the rule isn’t actively enforced as a consensus change (e.g., mainnet), the template logic now respects the -600 second limit when calculating these fields. This was implemented to unify behavior across networks and prepare the codebase for potential future deployments. Why This Makes Future Soft Fork Activations Safer??? Soft forks (e.g., via BIP-9 version bits) often rely on activation mechanisms tied to block heights, difficulty periods, or timestamps, with defined start/timeout windows. A timewarp attack could allow malicious miners to, • Manipulate chain progression by forcing rapid block production at low difficulty. • Warp timestamps to prematurely hit activation thresholds or extend/avoid timeouts. • Disrupt signaling periods, potentially blocking or forcing activations against community consensus. By accounting for the BIP-94 rule in mining templates across all networks, Bitcoin Core reduces the risk of such exploits during testing or live activations. This ensures more predictable timestamp behavior, prevents amplification of attacks on test networks (where soft forks are often trialed), and lays groundwork for safer mainnet deployments. For instance, it mitigates scenarios where attackers use timewarp to grief activations on testnet/signet, which could otherwise spill over to mainnet confidence. Overall, this proactive change enhances protocol robustness without altering existing consensus on mainnet.

PortaltoBitcoin (formerly Portal DeFi) is a trust-minimized, non-custodial protocol enabling atomic swaps between Bitcoin and other blockchain assets without bridges, wrapped tokens, or intermediaries. Why BitScaler is a Game-Changer Unlike traditional bridges that require locking assets in smart contracts (risking hacks like Wormhole or Multichain), BitScaler enables direct peer-to-peer (P2P) atomic swaps via: Federated liquidity pools (no single point of failure) Threshold Signature Schemes (TSS) for secure key management Layer-2 execution for fast, low-cost trades This means users can swap BTC for STX, ETH, or other assets natively without giving up custody. Use Cases & Advantages DeFi on Bitcoin No Counterparty Risk Cross-Chain Interoperability Backed by Industry Leaders Portal is supported by Coinbase Ventures, OKX Ventures, and Arrington Capital, signaling strong confidence in its infrastructure for Bitcoin’s DeFi future. With integrations like Stacking DAO’s stSTXbtc, Portal is unlocking Bitcoin liquidity for DeFi while staying true to self-sovereign finance.

Welcome to August. Since this month started, I’ve seen everything and its opposite on CT, and every bear woke up from their nap. July brought solid performances, but August has historically been quite bearish, for ETH, and by extension for altcoins as well. That’s why I don’t think we’re looking at the "end of the cycle" or an "I missed the window" moment. This feels more like a pause and it's not something bad. Let’s rewind for a second Yes, BTC is growing and bringing new money into crypto. But the truth is that in terms of capitalization, the altcoin market hasn’t grown at all since 2021. TOTAL3 was around $1T in November 2021 and still sits near $1T in July 2025. On paper it looks like we’re holding the line, but in reality, we lost liquidity in altcoins because TOTAL3 includes stablecoin supply, and that has exploded since 2021. As of March 2025, stablecoins reached about $232B, up nearly 45x since 2019. By May 2025, supply hit $247B, a 54% year‑over‑year increase, now close to 10% of all U.S. currency in circulation. So while the chart suggests stability, most of that "growth" is just stablecoins piling up. We’ve basically been playing with the same stack of money for four years, rotating it around like kids, while a chunk of it is parked in USDT and USDC rather than fueling alts. So the real question: are altcoins just short‑term bets to eventually rotate into BTC? Right now, yes, and here’s what the data shows. BTC dominance rose from ~40% in mid‑2021 to 62% today. A 20‑point gain while TOTAL3 stayed flat shows exactly where liquidity went: out of alts, back into Bitcoin. History proves that most alts can’t hold value once hype fades, even DeFi leaders and metaverse tokens from the last cycle still trade 60–90% below their 2021 peaks. This market runs on attention, with narratives rotating and few winners surviving more than a cycle. That’s why most people play alts as short‑term bets, rotating gains into BTC. BTC crushed 2024 and 2025 so far, becoming a digital reserve for both institutions and governments. That, of course, fueled ETH and the altcoin market, but BTC has outperformed throughout. In my view, the Fed remains the only true catalyst that can reignite full‑blown mania in the market. When the Fed cut rates near zero in March 2020, BTC went from ~$5k to ~$69k and ETH from ~$110 to ~$4.8k within 18 months. Liquidity rushed into risk assets because the risk‑free yield collapsed, forcing investors out the curve. Even a shift from 5% to 3% on T‑bills makes a DeFi pool yielding 7% far more attractive and lowers leverage costs across exchanges, giving traders room to scale up. Are we in a Bull Market right now? For BTC, yes, of course. For Altcoins, doesn't look like one. Can we top without having a true Bull Run for Alts, maybe. For now, retail still hasn’t returned. And the Liquidity is still in BTC. It’s mostly institutions, traders, and a handful of degens, all focused on pumping their bags. Fundamentals barely matter to anyone, they just hodl to get back to their entry, just to avoid losses. We also need fresh blood. Making crypto more accessible, but more importantly through making it genuinely interesting, something that draws people in and makes them want to understand it. I'm not sure we'll have again the kind of "degen" mass adoption we got with memecoins & NFTs, it's hard to predict, but we could have more adoption through DeFi, RWA, and other projects with realy utility. And that’s where real on‑chain traction matters more than Google Trends. If you want to know whether real liquidity is coming, a few things you can watch: • Stablecoin issuance versus on‑chain usage • DeFi TVL and unique active wallets • L2 transactions and fees • ETH burn and issuance dynamics • ETF inflows into BTC and ETH If the Fed signals a rate cut into year‑end, the setup mirrors 2020: cheaper leverage, stronger risk premiums, and the spark retail needs to come back. September will be a turning point. With a dovish Fed, this pause won’t be the end of the cycle, it could be the real beginning of the next one. ----------- Anyway, all that yapping to say I don't think we've hit the market top yet, but there is always stuff to monitor and the situation can change quickly. And we’re still seeing a strong BTC with high dominance, and almost no real trust in altcoins. That’s why I don’t invest long-term in tokens, except for a few that are truly undervalued and likely can’t go much lower, since their valuations are already below what their fundamentals justify. What's proof mining in zk? Proof mining is how ZK systems reward people for doing the hard work of generating proofs. As well all know that generating a ZK proof takes time and compute power but verifying it is cheap and fast. So instead of everyone doing that heavy lifting themselves, they outsource it to provers,individuals or networks that generate the proof for them. This opens up a market: If you have the hardware (like GPUs or ASICs) and know-how, you can earn by selling proofs. It works like mining in Bitcoin, but instead of hashing, you're proving statements. Real-world examples: ZK rollups: Provers generate proofs to confirm all L2 transactions are valid before sending a summary to Ethereum. ZKML: Proofs are used to verify that an AI model ran correctly, without revealing the input or the model itself. ZK identity: You prove something about your identity (like being over 18) without revealing who you are. Where Cysic fits in: cysic_xyz builds custom hardware (ASICs) to make proof generation faster and cheaper. That means more efficient mining, more scale, and lower costs for users. This is how ZK compute becomes its own economy.

For the cryptocurrency market, especially BTC, these factors may lead to price fragmentation and frequent corrections, increasing investor risk. Some nads might not know what BFT means,in which monad testnet-1 is going to be upgraded to on Tuesday. Imagine you and a group of friends are trying to decide where to eat, but some friends might lie or try to trick the group (like suggesting a terrible restaurant just to mess with you).BFT is like a rule system that helps the group agree on a decision even if some friends are being dishonest or unreliable. Simple Example of BFT in Blockchain: Let’s say 4 friends (nodes) are voting on what to order for dinner: 1.Proposal: One friend (the leader) suggests,"Let’s order pizza!" 2. Voting: The other friends check if pizza is a good idea: - If at least 3 out of 4 friends (more than 2/3) agree, pizza is finalized. - If 1 friend lies (e.g., says "no" just to cause chaos), the honest majority still wins. 3. Final Decision: Once agreed, the order is placed no takebacks! (This is called finality in blockchain.) What If Bad Friends Try to Trick the System? - If 1 friend is lying, the other 3 can still outvote them. - But if 2 friends lie, the system fails (since you need 3 honest votes). - BFT ensures the group can tolerate up to 1/3 liars before things break. How This Applies to Monad - Instead of friends, you have validator nodes voting on transactions. - The blockchain keeps working even if some validators are hacked or act maliciously, as long as most are honest - Unlike Bitcoin/Ethereum (where you wait for multiple confirmations), BFT blockchains finalize decisions instantly, like your pizza order being unchangeable once agreed upon. BFT is like a trust system where the majority’s honesty keeps everything secure, even if a few bad actors try to mess things up.

Why is BOB the first to use it? Let’s unpack it⬇ What is a ZK Rollup? A ZK Rollup (Zero-Knowledge Rollup) is a blockchain scaling solution that processes transactions off-chain, then submits a cryptographic proof back to the main chain. This proof verifies that all transactions are valid without revealing every single detail. The benefits are clear: -- Scalability: Handles thousands of transactions at once -- Lower fees: Costs are spread across many users -- Security: Inherits the trust and stability of the underlying blockchain. So, what makes BOB different? BOB is the first Hybrid ZK Rollup, meaning it doesn’t rely on just one chain. It’s anchored to Bitcoin for settlement and ultimate security, while using Ethereum’s EVM for execution and smart contracts. This design gives BOB the best of both worlds: -- The immutability and security of Bitcoin -- The flexibility and programmability of Ethereum -- Direct access to BTC and ETH liquidity without wrapping or centralized custodians Why this matters For years, Bitcoin has been the most valuable crypto asset, but it’s been underutilized in DeFi. BOB changes that by activating BTC in a scalable, secure, and fully programmable environment — enabling it to be used in DeFi, NFTs, gaming, and more. The takeaway is simple: Not all rollups are the same. The future of blockchain is not just about choosing one network, it’s about combining strengths. That’s what build_on_bob's Hybrid ZK Rollup delivers. And that’s why it’s worth paying attention to.

ANOMA - An Introduction to Intents and Intent-centric Architectures The Current Problem Most decentralized applications today are built on blockchain-centric architectures—systems where everything revolves around the blockchain itself. This focus limits what can be built, because applications must fit the blockchain’s rules, structure, and capabilities. While different dApps exist, no architecture currently exists that can handle any kind of user goal (“intent”) in a general, scalable way. Complex apps often rely on centralized Web2 components for certain steps, creating bottlenecks and losing full decentralization. �� The Core Idea: Intents An intent is simply a statement of what a user wants to achieve—an end goal. Examples: “I want to buy a pizza with BTC” or “I want to vote in a quadratic funding round.” Intents can be simple (single action) or highly complex (multi-party, multi-step processes). Historically, humans have always acted on intents, but mechanisms to fulfill them—barter, money, traditional finance, crypto—have changed over time. Observation: Simple intents have many fulfillment mechanisms; complex intents have very few today. From Blockchain-Centric to Intent-Centric Blockchain-centric architectures (like Bitcoin, Ethereum): Excel at settlement (recording final outcomes on-chain). Can work for simple or moderately complex apps (tokens, DAOs, AMM DEXes). Struggle with complex, multi-party apps without relying on centralized components. Intent-centric architectures start with the intent as the core primitive—not the blockchain. They are generalized: can process any intent, not just those tied to one specific app. Provide all the properties dApps need natively: Generalized intents – any type of desired end state. Counterparty discovery – finding others whose intents match yours. Solving – combining intents into valid, executable solutions. Settlement – finalizing results on-chain.

Zama is developing technology that allows you to use cryptocurrencies while keeping your data encrypted, even during transactions. Currently, blockchains like Bitcoin and Ethereum are completely transparent. This means anyone can see balances, transfers, and other activity. While this is great for transparency, it's a major problem for privacy. .zama_fhe aims to solve this with a technology called Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE). Often referred to as the "holy grail" of cryptography, FHE lets computers perform operations on your data without ever having to decrypt it. A good way to think about this is like solving a puzzle inside a locked box. The puzzle pieces are your data. FHE lets the computer solve the puzzle without ever opening the box, ensuring your information remains private while still being usable.

The more I explore build_on_bob and tenprotocol, the more I realize they’re solving two completely different but equally critical problems for blockchain adoption, and they’re doing it in ways most people aren’t paying attention to yet. Let’s start with BOB. Everyone’s heard the “Bitcoin is the most secure blockchain” line, but security alone doesn’t give you DeFi, dApps, or complex smart contracts. That’s where BOB’s hybrid architecture changes the game. BOB connects Bitcoin’s unmatched security with Ethereum’s rich smart contract ecosystem through a dual settlement, modular rollup system. This means developers and users aren’t locked into one chain, they can settle on Bitcoin when they want the strongest security, or on Ethereum when they need speed and flexibility. For BTC holders, this is huge. It’s no longer about wrapping BTC into risky bridges; it’s about plugging Bitcoin directly into DeFi, NFTs, and any onchain innovation, without losing its original security model. Imagine a future where your BTC is just as active in DeFi as ETH, but safer. Now, TEN. TEN is tackling something most users ignore until it bites them, privacy and synchronization. And I don’t mean privacy for the sake of hiding illegal activity. I mean protecting your wallet data, your trades, and your strategies while they’re happening. Right now, every transaction on Ethereum is public the moment you send it. Bots can see it, copy it, and profit from it before you, this is called MEV extraction. TEN’s privacy layer encrypts transactions end-to-end, so even while they’re being processed, no one can frontrun or copy you. But TEN doesn’t stop there. It’s also a coordination layer, a kind of “control tower” for Ethereum Layer 2, keeping tasks, updates, and cross-dApp dependencies perfectly in sync. No bottlenecks, no messy manual workarounds. The bigger picture. BOB is about unlocking Bitcoin’s dormant potential. TEN is about protecting Ethereum’s active economy. One builds the bridge for value to flow freely across ecosystems, the other shields that value from being exploited. In the next bull run, both problems will explode in importance: Billions in BTC will want safe access to DeFi. Billions in ETH transactions will need privacy and reliability. So here’s the debate: When the pressure is on, will the market reward the platform that gives Bitcoin users new powers… or the one that safeguards Ethereum users’ existing powers? Or maybe, just maybe, these two will become the invisible backbone of the multi-chain world, where security, privacy, and flexibility finally coexist without compromise. BOB TEN COOKIES

Here’s why it matters: traditional swaps often require either a centralized platform or wrapped assets, which introduces counterparty risk. Understanding atomic swaps in this context is key: it’s a contract that ensures either both sides execute successfully, or the swap doesn’t happen at all, removing the possibility of loss due to counterparty failure. In short, PortaltoBitcoin makes cross-chain trading safe, transparent, and decentralized, letting Bitcoin holders participate in multi-chain DeFi without compromising security.

BitVM Summary BitVM is a way to expand the range of what is possible to do on Bitcoin It does this by performing computation off-chain that is held accountable by an on-chain fraud proving mechanism Since bitcoin script is very limited in what it can do, running more advanced programs on bitcoin requires a way to verify that the results of off-chain calculations are correct Existing bridges typically rely on centralized entities, such as Wrapped Bitcoin (WBTC) and Coinbase Wrapped Bitcoin (cbBTC) or semi-trusted networks like tBTC, where security depends on the honesty of the majority of participants In contrast, BitVM bridges introduce a superior security model, BTC deposits cannot be stolen as long as there is a single honest and online node in the network and this node can be the depositor themself BitVM verifies off-chain computation similarly to optimistic rollups 1- An operator performs a computation off-chain 2- Then makes an on-chain claim about the results of that computation 3- If the claim is incorrect, a verifier will invalidate it directly on the Bitcoin blockchain In practice, this would look like a collection of operators depositing their collateral and committing to manage a pool of BTC according to the rules of a specific, pre-defined computer program (a bridge, for example)

The history of Bitcoin and its forks (BTC and BCH) can be seen as the ultimate intelligence test of the century. A test so subtle and so profound that even some of the most financially savvy and technologically brilliant minds fell for the wrong narrative. Bitcoin’s original vision was crystal clear: a trustless, global-scale digital ledger that allowed people to transact in the digital world with the same finality, simplicity, and freedom as handing over cash in the physical world. No middlemen. No arbitrary restrictions. Just scalable, peer-to-peer money and data exchange. Yet along the way, the vision was fractured. BTC chose artificial scarcity through block size limits, turning the system into a speculative asset rather than a functional network. BCH kept closer to the original design but still fell into ideological and governance pitfalls. Only Bitcoin SV (BSV) has stayed true to that founding vision—unbounded scaling, ultra-low fees, and the ability to process not just payments but enterprise-level data transactions on a single, immutable ledger. The irony? Because the market value of BSV is currently low, many dismiss it without realizing that the very essence of Bitcoin’s design is alive and functioning today on BSV. History will show that this was not just about price charts—it was about understanding the true purpose of Bitcoin. And those who can see past the noise will recognize that the original Bitcoin protocol has been restored and is quietly building the digital economy of the future.

HOW YOU ARE ABLE TO USE SAME WALLET ADDRESS ACROSS EVM CHAINS I already spoke on my previous post on the process of wallet address creation/generation through your selected wallet provider. So you already know that your wallet address was gotten from the public key derived from your private key. Now do you know you can use a single wallet address on different EVM chains such as Ethereum, Arbitrum, Polygon, Base etc but not on a chain like Solana or Cardano? The reason is simply because EVM chains all use the same cryptography, so when you import the same private key into any EVM chain, you’ll get same wallet address, but each EVM chain node tracks the balance separately, so — ETH on Ethereum is tracked by Ethereum nodes — ETH on Arbitrum is tracked by Arbitrum nodes DIFFERENT CHAINS CRYPTOGRAPHY AND ADDRESS FORMAT — EVM chains: Uses secp256k1 and keccak-256 encoding — Bitcoin: Uses secp256k1 and format address using Base58Check encoding — Solana: Uses ed25519 curve and Base58 encoding — Cosmos: Uses secp256k1 with Bech32 encoding — Cardano: Uses ed25519 with Bech32-like encoding GM!

It fails because the denominator is dying. Gold was slow enough to be modeled as an asset. Bitcoin is fast enough to reveal itself as the new monetary foundation. The failure of power-law models isn’t a bug in Bitcoin’s trajectory…..it’s the proof that we’ve crossed a monetary event horizon.

Blockchain 101 – Basics Part 2 – Blocks and Transactions As a quick reminder, in the previous article we explored the ledger what it is and why blockchain can’t exist without it. Now, let’s focus on transactions and how they get grouped into blocks to build a secure network. Think of the blockchain ledger like a shared notebook that me, Odin, Vahid, Filsoof, and Emad all keep together. Every transaction we make has to be recorded so no one can change or erase it. For example: I send 0.01 BTC to Vahid, Filsoof sends me 0.05 BTC for a joint project, and Vahid sends 0.02 BTC to Emad. Each of these is a valid transaction that nodes check for balance and authenticity. Once approved, they go into a block. A block is like a page in our shared notebook that bundles multiple transactions together. When the page fills up, a unique number called a hash is generated, and the next page links to it. This forms a chain of blocks that is tamper-proof and secure. For example, my transaction, Vahid’s, and Filsoof’s are collected in Block 1, and Vahid’s 0.02 BTC to Emad goes into Block 2, linking back to Block 1. If anyone tried to alter a transaction, the hash would break and the network would immediately notice. Some history: Bitcoin was introduced in 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto to create decentralized digital money. It was the first practical system of blocks and transactions that everyone could trust. Later, Ethereum introduced smart contracts, allowing the blockchain to handle complex tasks automatically. Imagine me setting up the ledger while Vahid and Filsoof add features, keeping the network safe together. Limitations exist too. Transactions can take time to confirm, especially larger ones. Block sizes grow, and Proof-of-Work consumes a lot of energy like powering our shared ledger. TL;DR Blocks are pages of the ledger linking transactions together to secure the network. This is the foundation for nodes, networks, smart contracts, and advanced protocols. Next up: Nodes and Network. We’ll see how nodes work, communicate, and maintain decentralization.

News Bitcoin Mining Bitcoin mining is the process by which new bitcoins are created and transactions are verified on the Bitcoin network. Miners use specialized hardware to solve complex mathematical puzzles, which secures the network and earns them rewards in the form of newly minted bitcoins and transaction fees. Key Points: Purpose: Validates transactions and prevents double-spending by adding them to the blockchain, a decentralized ledger. Process: Miners compete to solve cryptographic puzzles (Proof of Work) to create a new block. The first to solve it broadcasts the block to the network for verification. Hardware: Modern mining uses Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) for efficiency, as GPUs and CPUs are no longer competitive. Rewards: As of August 2025, the block reward is 3.125 BTC (halved from 6.25 BTC in April 2024). Rewards halve every 210,000 blocks (roughly every 4 years). Energy Use: Mining is energy-intensive, often requiring significant electricity, leading to debates about environmental impact. Difficulty: Adjusts every 2,016 blocks (about every two weeks) to maintain a 10-minute block time, increasing as more miners join. Profitability: Depends on electricity costs, hardware efficiency, Bitcoin price, and network difficulty. Many miners join pools to share rewards and reduce variance. Geographic Trends: Miners often locate in areas with cheap electricity, like parts of the U.S., China, or regions with renewable energy. Current Context (August 2025): Market Dynamics: Recent X posts suggest mining remains profitable for some, with firms like Marathon Digital expanding operations (e.g., acquiring a 200 MW data center). However, smaller miners face challenges due to rising difficulty and energy costs. Energy Debate: There's ongoing discussion about Bitcoin mining's environmental impact, with some miners adopting renewables or flared gas to mitigate criticism. Halving Impact: The 2024 halving reduced rewards, pushing less efficient miners out and increasing competition among larger players. It means that a system, through time, is dispersed, redundant, adaptive, and also resistant to coercion and subversion. Specifically for bitcoin, it means these three things: 1. Decentralization of Mining Bitcoin must maintain credible neutrality of its global ledger: tick tock, next block. History shows that governments take control of economic blocs, especially during wartime. At these times, bitcoin runs the risk of fracture at the consensus level. 2. Decentralization of Custody and Control Custody should be dispersed, redundant, and accessible to many. We need multisig, multi-institutional, multi-jurisdictional, and multi-form-factor security—every layer matters. No single entity should ever hold or control more than 1% of bitcoin. 2. Decentralization of Payments Bitcoin should function as peer-to-peer electronic cash and everyday money. Payments capabilities augment bitcoin's digital gold properties. But it will take a huge effort to improve the privacy, UI, UX, and scale of payments. There it is: decentralization of mining, custody, and payments. If no single entity can co-opt any of the three, bitcoin has won!

So i will take _ALCPB as example but its universal to use. Warning, geeks only Let’s break this down into simpler steps to calculate the dilution and future Bitcoin (BTC) stack for a company like Capital B, without needing to know the future stock price or BTC price. What you need as input: Current BTC holdings: 2,201 BTC Current fully diluted share count: 331,000,000 shares Forward avarage mNAV: 3 End of year target: 3,000 BTC Months remaining: 4 months Step-by-Step Calculation: Step 1: Calculate the Needed Dilution Rate We need to figure out how much the BTC stack needs to grow and spread that growth over the 4 months. Formula: Dilution Rate = (POWER(End of Year Stack / Current Stack; 1 / Future Months) - 1) / mNAV In Excel: =(POWER(C9/C6;1/C8)-1)/C10 C9 = End of Year Stack (3,000 BTC) C6 = Current Stack (2,201 BTC) C8 = Future Months (4) C10 = mNAV (3) This tells us the monthly dilutuin rate at which new shares need to be issued to reach the target. Step 2: Calculate Added Shares New total shares = Current shares × (1 + Dilution Rate) Added shares = New total shares - Current shares This shows how many new shares will be created due to dilution. Step 3: Calculate Bitcoin Added Bitcoin added = Added shares × mNAV × Current BTC holdings / Current shares This estimates how much BTC the company can buy with the new shares, based on the mNAV and current holdings. Step 4: Update the BTC Stack New BTC balance = Current BTC holdings + Bitcoin added This gives the total BTC after adding the new amount, reaching the 3,000 BTC target. Why Stock Price and BTC Price don’t matter here: The mNAV assumption (set at 3) lets us work with the relationship between shares and BTC without needing actual prices. The calculation focuses on share growth and BTC accumulation, making future prices irrelevant for these steps. Ofcourse after these calculations we could calculate sats/share and fiat pricing per share. Step 5: Sats per share Stats per share = BTC holdings / Shares * 100,000,000 Step 6 (Optional): Calculate Future Stock PriceIf you want to estimate a stock price, use: Stock Price = New BTC holdings × BTC Price (assumption) × mNAV / New Total shares This step 6 requires a BTC price assumption, but it’s optional and comes after the dilution plan. Summary: By using forward mNAV and the target BTC stack by a period end, you can plan dilution and BTC growth without knowing future prices. Union Build solves this by: •Using zero-knowledge proofs so one chain can mathematically verify another chain’s state, without trusting intermediaries. •Creating a modular system where developers can write apps once and make them work across chains. •Making cross-chain actions (like sending assets or governance votes) trustless, faster, and cheaper. You’re holding crypto but want more exposure. Maybe your capital is tied up in retirement accounts, qualified funds, or stocks with your wealth manager. You’re looking for digital asset access but aren’t sure of the best route. Here’s what most people don't know about the differences between ETFs and treasury companies. Bitcoin ETFs launched in January 2024 after years of waiting. ETH ETFs followed shortly after. Both trade on traditional stock exchanges and fit perfectly in retirement accounts like IRAs and 401ks. But here's the catch - you can't contribute your actual crypto to get shares. So why consider ETFs at all? Simple...you can margin them more easily. ETF shares can typically be borrowed against at roughly 50% loan-to-value, often with better interest rates than borrowing against crypto directly. On top of that, they usually trade nearly 1:1 with the net asset value of the underlying asset. ETFs come with fees. For example, the iShares Bitcoin ETF charges around 25 basis points a year, while some others push close to 1%. What you’re paying for is convenience and smooth integration into a traditional portfolio. The tradeoff? ETFs strip away the DeFi benefits. You can’t stake, provide liquidity, or earn yield—they only give you exposure to price movement. No extra cash flows, no dividends...just tracking the asset’s price, minus fees. Enter Digital Asset Treasury (DAT) companies, these are companies essentially following MicroStrategy’s general model but extending it beyond Bitcoin. Some are building treasuries concentrated in a single asset, while others are structuring diversified baskets that function more like crypto indexes.. Here's where it gets interesting - as a retail investor, you CAN contribute crypto in-kind to treasury companies if you're a seed investor. If the company fails, you often get your assets back. Why do this? Treasury companies can generate value you can't get holding assets directly. They pay dividends to shareholders. They often trade at 1.5x to 2x the net asset value of their holdings. Borrowing against treasury company shares is also more favorable. Instead of 60% LTV on raw Bitcoin at high rates, you get better rates on stock. If the stock trades at 2x NAV, your 50% margin equals 100% of your original crypto investment value. These companies also face dilution from debt issuance, governance issues, and the risk of trading below net asset value during bear markets. When sentiment flips, stocks can trade at discounts to their crypto holdings. For in-kind investing, treasury companies win hands down. Retail investors get zero access to ETF in-kind contributions. But early treasury company investors can seed with actual crypto and potentially get assets back if things go south. My personal take? I wouldn't put more than 20-30% of my crypto portfolio into treasury companies. There's significant upside potential but also amplified risk. The rewards could be massive if managed properly, but the downside cuts both ways. ETFs track underlying assets almost perfectly - usually 1:1 after fees. They hold crypto in institutional custody and can't do much with it. Treasury companies have flexibility to generate yields, pay dividends, and potentially stake assets for additional returns. Upside potential differs dramatically. ETFs give you clean asset exposure with minimal additional returns beyond price movement. Treasury companies offer leverage multiples, dividend payments, and the potential for significant premiums above net asset value. Risk profiles are opposites. ETFs provide stable, low-risk exposure perfect for retirement accounts and conservative investors. Treasury companies amplify both gains and losses through leverage, management risk, and market sentiment swings. If crypto continues up and right due to increasing utility, treasury companies could be incredible wealth multipliers. But sharp downturns or extended bear markets create serious problems. For clean, stable exposure, ETFs are the safe choice. They fit perfectly in qualified accounts and give your traditional advisor something they understand. No management risk, no leverage concerns, just pure asset tracking. For the potential of amplified upside, treasury companies offer compelling opportunities - if you can stomach the risk. In-kind investments, dividend payments, premium trading, and better margin access create multiple return vectors beyond just crypto price appreciation. Smart investors probably want both as a small portion alongisde their direct crypto exposure. A diversified approach means ETFs for stability and qualified account exposure, plus treasury companies for amplified returns on risk capital. Don't put all eggs in one basket, but don't miss the opportunities either.

Just wrapped my first conference in Tokyo WebX_Asia. A few takeaways: * Japan is a sleeping giant in crypto. GDP close to Germany/India, population more than 2x larger than Korea, but relatively low retail trading volume today, and few world-stage crypto companies. Only ~5% of Japanese retail trades crypto vs ~25% in Korea. Why? * The main culprit is taxes. Crypto gains are taxed as income (55%) vs cap gains (20%). Crazily enough, until recently, they taxed unrealized gains (!!), making domestic TGEs impossible, as you'd owe a boatload of taxes immediately. This was recently repealed, but still need to fix the punitive tax rate. * This tax arbitrage is a big part of why MetaPlanet trades at a premium to NAV—buying a corporate shell of BTC is tax-advantaged vs trading BTC directly. * The Japanese Prime Minister and Finance Minister both spoke at WebX about crypto. (Bitcoin Las Vegas 2024 vibes?) Clear political vibe shift, probably following the US's lead. They promised to fix crypto tax treatment soon, but probably takes over a year? * Corporates drive a lot of the energy here, which is pretty unique. Most countries, grassroots retail leads and corporates follow late. But in Japan, you see SBI (major Ripple stake), Sony, Sega, Nomura, all moving fast and making big moves. * Lots of focus on NFTs/IP tokenization—Japan knows IP is one of its biggest global exports and are always looking for new ways to monetize it. * Like everyone else, they also see the finance angle. Recently approved a yen stablecoin (JYPC), but not much distribution yet. * Retail loves XRP and ADA here. They’re cult assets, with their own communities separate from the rest of the scene. * Once Japan fixes its tax laws, I expect crypto adoption to accelerate here. For founders looking to expand to the Japanese market, localization + ground game + strong local partners are critical. Can't treat Japan as an afterthought, culture is very different. Edifying trip! What adds to their credibility is that they identified years ago that Texas would be the best place to built them due to extremely low energy prices. So to recap these guys had to vision 5-7 years ago that this would happen and they correctly predicted the hottest place in the world to built datacenters, which is Texas. This is further validated by OpenAI & Oracle, which are building the industry's flagship AI site Stargate relatively nearby in Texas. That's not a coincedence! So now they are sitting on a land plus power portfolio of 3GW, which is triple A in today's world real estate acquired for pennies on the dollar. The purpose of BitCoin was never to cloak transactions in shadows or to build a system of anonymity detached from accountability. The design was deliberate: a ledger, public and traceable, where every transaction is etched into history. Privacy comes not from hiding in the dark but from the ordinary use of small notes, everyday payments, casual exchanges that blend into the sheer scale of activity. The ledger ensures that nothing is erased, nothing is denied. That is what makes it honest. What is being built now with Taproot and these other contrivances abandons this. They twist the idea into something it was never meant to be. By trying to force anonymity into the protocol, they strip away the very strength of the system: the transparency of a blockchain that can be verified by anyone. They imagine they are making things stronger, but in reality they weaken it, removing the assurance that every payment is accounted for, that fraud cannot hide. It was not meant to be a playground for those who wish to vanish. It was a system of digital cash—cash that could be traced through the ledger, the same way coins pass through hands but still leave an audit in the accounts of those who use them. That is how law and order coexist with freedom of exchange. To discard this, to try to replace it with shadows, is to betray the entire purpose. A system without traceability is not a blockchain. A system without verification is not secure. And a system that confuses anonymity with privacy will collapse, because what gives it value is not concealment but the certainty that every transaction is real, permanent, and unfalsifiable.

Fiat vs. Bitcoin: Why Collateral and Leverage Are the Real Challenges At its core, the fiat system isn’t as bad as Bitcoiners often portray it—at least not in the way it’s typically framed. Even though central banks create money out of thin air through complex processes, the primary creation of new monetary units is actually relatively “decentralized” and, in essence, not inherently inflationary. Let me explain why these two aspects can be viewed this way. Decentralization vs. Collateral New monetary units are fundamentally created only when individuals, companies, or governments need fresh capital in the form of debt, which typically requires collateral. Through loans, bonds, or other forms of credit issued by the banking sector, new money is created—essentially in a decentralized manner. However, the real issue lies with collateral, which leads to two major problems. First, collateral must be valued by humans, and either through valuation errors or corruption-driven misvaluations, low-quality collateral can overburden the system. Second, newly created money backed by collateral—especially in the context of an inflated real estate market—tends to be more accessible to those who already hold significant assets, while those with fewer resources are severely disadvantaged (Cantillon effect). Inflation vs. Leverage When examining bank-issued debt over the repayment period, money is created at the outset and gradually repaid or “destroyed” over time (I’ll address the interest component in a separate post). Inflation, or more accurately, the continuous expansion of the money supply, doesn’t primarily stem from newly issued debt itself but from the ever-increasing excessive leverage in the system. Examples include vacant, credit-financed properties where value appreciation outpaces interest rates due to politically motivated, inefficient market conditions, or excessive government spending, which is essentially a form of leverage relative to GDP. In short, it’s a kind of Ponzi scheme. Thus, the main problems with the fiat standard are not centralization or inflation but collateral and leverage. I’m not saying centralization and inflation aren’t issues—they can be—but collateral and leverage are far more critical, especially when considering the future and how it’s likely to unfold. The 16 Oracles Digital Assets??? Real-World Limits??? Here Goes... Alright, let’s break this down in a way that hits both how digital assets work and where the real-world limits come in when they exist on a blockchain. What are Digital Assets? Digital assets are items of value represented on a blockchain. They can be: Currencies: e.g., Bitcoin, Solana, Ethereum. Tokens: representing ownership, utility, or governance. NFTs: unique digital collectibles, artwork, real estate deeds, tickets. Stablecoins: digital assets tied to real-world currencies (USD, EUR, etc.). The blockchain ensures: Scarcity → Supply limits (BTC max 21M, THE16 token capped at 16). Authenticity → Provenance is public, recorded, and unchangeable. Transferability → Anyone with a wallet can send or trade assets. Programmability → Smart contracts define behaviors (royalties, staking, access). Real-World Limits on Blockchain Even though blockchain creates digital “infinite reproducibility,” real-world rules add boundaries: Supply Caps Many digital assets enforce scarcity through code (e.g., Bitcoin’s hard cap). NFT collections may be permanently capped at 10,000. Once minted, no more can be created without community consensus. Physical Asset Representation A blockchain token may represent a real-world asset (e.g., a house, gold, or stocks). The blockchain can track ownership digitally, but physical enforcement relies on real-world law and custodians. Example: If you own a token tied to gold in a vault, you’re trusting the vault’s integrity. Energy & Performance Blockchains like Bitcoin or Ethereum are bound by energy costs and throughput limits. The digital world is infinite, but computation and storage aren’t. This forces efficiency (layer-2 networks, sidechains, compression). Legal & Regulatory Constraints Governments can regulate what digital assets represent. A tokenized share of Tesla stock must comply with securities law. Digital ID systems must comply with privacy laws. Economic Ties Stablecoins are “digitally limitless” in movement but limited by reserves. If USDC claims $1 backing per token, real-world dollars must exist in a bank. Without those reserves, the blockchain record is meaningless. Human Factors Wallets get lost. Keys get forgotten. Assets may become permanently inaccessible. This creates an unintended hard limit on circulating supply. Why Limits Matter Without limits, digital assets lose meaning: If NFTs could be copied infinitely, they’d lose value. If stablecoins had no reserve limits, they’d collapse like hyperinflated currency. If Bitcoin had no hard cap, it would be just another inflationary currency. So blockchain combines digital abundance with code-enforced scarcity, giving us assets that are valuable because they are both programmable and limited. Is anyone else still reeling from the hype of BitcoinAsia2025 last week? 'Cause we sure are! While some of the highlights of our Day 2 include watching both cz_binance and EricTrump on stage, the focus of the conference is of course still to draw meaningful attention to Bitcoin - its ecosystem, the crypto community, and how far the space has come. As mentioned earlier, BitcoinMagazine was livestreaming the conference, but if you missed out, here are a few key points from the sessions we attended that we'd love to share with you all. 1 ⃣ In the session 'What's the End Game of a Bitcoin Treasury Company', the panelists Jesse Myers (The Smarter Web Company), Siddarth Bharwani (Jetking) and Alexander Laizet (Capital B) dived into why a Bitcoin Treasury is a solid strategy for companies to adopt to strengthen their balance sheet, including some details of how a Bitcoin Treasury works. It seemed to be an unanimous thought that we are still new in the Bitcoin space, and that we're set to be in a 3-decade long bull run. 2 ⃣ Yat Siu from AnimocaBrands mentioned during his panel session that he believes Bitcoin is a culture and a movement, not just a 'digital currency'. There are many millionaires out there in the world, but not that much BTC - having one whole coin feels like it almost puts you in a "club". But if Bitcoin reigns supreme, is there a need for other ecosystems and altcoins? Yat Siu believes that while BTC is still the ultimate store of value - akin to 'digital gold', altcoins represent innovation and how the community / developers can expand on their ideas. 3 ⃣ In an interesting session conducted in Chinese - Bitcoin's Rise in Asia's Institutional Circles, panelists Jack Kong (Nanolabs, CyberportHK) and Jademont Zheng (Waterdrip Capital) spoke about the amazing potential for the rise of crypto in Asia especially in regions like Singapore and HongKong. However, they spoke about how the community shouldn't be too focused on the 'location' aspect of which markets are embracing digitalassets, as Bitcoin is decentralized, and it's a win for the crypto community regardless of which countries choose to be supportive of it. They both also agreed that crypto ETFs and DATs are positive for investors as it provides an easier way for traders to get their skin in the game, as buying and storing Bitcoin is not simple for the average user that's new to the space. 4 ⃣ Last but not least, Eric Trump's session definitely gained much enthusiasm from the crowd, as he came on stage with a pretty positive outlook on Bitcoin in general. He's mentioned that 90% of his time is spent in the crypto space now, believing we're still super early and companies/countries have not even scratched the surface of what digital assets will be in the future. In our last post, we've posted about him saying 'Bitcoin will hit 1 million dollars'. According to Eric Trump, lots of institutions and family offices are interested in the growth of Bitcoin, which is a bullish sign. As for how it'll pan out, we're certainly optimistic, but we will have to see how it pans out over the next couple of years and decades. The result is a streamlined system where every component shines in its role: Bitcoin handles secure settlement, the EVM drives fast execution, Babylon provides BTC backed security, and Celestia ensures efficient data management. This modular approach links Bitcoin seamlessly to the wider DeFi ecosystem, all without altering its fundamentals. Ultimately, it's what enables BOB to drive the future of decentralized apps. TL;DR: BOB's modular design scales Bitcoin for DeFi by separating execution (EVM), settlement (Bitcoin ledger), security (Babylon restaking), and data availability (Celestia/EigenDA). What is on kris's reading list? I have always been interested in "backdrop bookshelves" in interviews. Figuring out what is on the bookshelf behind him was a bit difficult, as the background is blurry, but here are some of the books I know (some I have also read) in no particular order. First, there are two classics from Nassim Nichals Taleb Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder and Skin in the Game. Why is reth such a big deal ? Reth is a high performance, modular ehtereum client, written in rust, by virtue of it being built on rust, speed is assured, it's less resource intensive and able to achieve maximum efficiency with a much more cleaner code base. When processing millions of usdt transactions daily, that performance difference factor is definitely the difference between success and failure, this is why Reth/Rust is such a big deal and hence the reason plasma built it's execution environment on it. 3 - Bitcoin Anchoring Plasma integrates a native trust minimized bitcoin bridge that periodically post state differences to bitcoin i.e., they often write permanent record of all transactions to bitcoins ledger, in other words, if a person/group of bad actors decide to hack plasma, they would have to hack bitcoin. Fed , Crypto Assets, and the Anticipated Great Bull Run: Toward 2026 The long-anticipated “great bull run” in the cryptocurrency markets has been a subject of speculation among many investors and analysts. However, considering the current economic conditions and global financial dynamics, it is evident that this major rally has not yet materialized. In my view, the strong upward movement the market is waiting for will only emerge at the intersection of specific economic and political developments. Fed Policies and Short-Term Expectations The recent decline in U.S. non-farm payroll data has increased expectations of interest rate cuts. In response, the Fed may cut rates twice by 50 basis points, potentially lowering them to 3.50%. Such a move could trigger a short-term movement—what might be called a “mini rally.” However, this is unlikely to mark the beginning of a true bull run. For a strong and sustainable rally, a much lower interest rate policy is necessary. The estimated 3.50% interest rate is still high for the markets. Households in particular require lower rates to borrow more effectively. A Strong Bull Run Scenario After 2026 I believe the real bull run could begin after May 2026. This view rests on two main arguments: Regulatory steps in the U.S.: The implementation of the Genius Act and the involvement of certain insurance funds in cryptocurrency processes will provide institutional investors with new security and regulatory frameworks. This, in turn, could bring a far stronger inflow of liquidity into the markets. Change in Fed leadership: The change of Fed Chair in 2026 could introduce a new approach to monetary policy. A more flexible or market-supportive stance would serve as a critical catalyst for the cryptocurrency markets. The convergence of these two developments has the potential to drive a massive flow of capital into the crypto space. The China Factor and Global Dynamics In addition to the U.S., China’s moves will also play a decisive role in shaping the process. The lifting of mining bans and the development of a stable digital asset pegged to its own currency could give the market a new direction. This would be significant not only for the global hash power but also for integrating the Asia-centered financial system with cryptocurrency markets. Conclusion: The Expected Date for the Real Bull Run I expect that after cutting rates twice, the Fed could maintain a stable monetary policy until May 2026. However, the real bull run will not be triggered by interest rate cuts alone; it will require the alignment of U.S. regulatory clarity, a change in Fed leadership, and China’s renewed approach to cryptocurrencies. Taken together, these factors point to 2026 as a historic turning point for crypto markets. While short-term rallies should certainly be monitored, I believe the true opportunity lies in the post-2026 period. Guess what? JoeCarlasare is wrong again! You can store a JPEG (or any arbitrary data) on Bitcoin, but Bitcoin was not designed for general file storage, so it’s inefficient and potentially expensive. Here’s the breakdown: 1. How It’s Done There are a few main ways to embed data (like a JPEG) in Bitcoin: Method How It Works Pros Cons OP_RETURN Puts up to 80 bytes of arbitrary data in a Bitcoin transaction output. Simple, standard, widely supported. Extremely small — not enough for a full JPEG (you’d only store a hash or tiny chunk). Multi-part Transactions Break file into chunks and store across many transactions. Technically possible to store entire file. Very expensive; clogs blockchain; frowned upon by many node operators. Ordinals / Inscriptions (popular since 2023) Use Taproot witness data to “inscribe” arbitrary data (images, text, etc.) directly into the blockchain. Actively used for NFTs and images; permanent; decentralized. Still costly (depends on file size + network fees). Hash Commitment Just store a cryptographic hash of your JPEG in Bitcoin. Cheap, efficient, proof-of-existence. Doesn’t actually store the file — you must host the JPEG elsewhere. 2. Practicality A JPEG file can be stored, but the bigger the file, the higher the cost. Typical on-chain storage prices (via Ordinals) can be several dollars or even hundreds of dollars for large files, depending on network fees. Bitcoin Core developers generally discourage using the blockchain for arbitrary data because it increases chain bloat (all nodes must store your file forever). 3. Best Practice Instead of uploading the entire JPEG, most projects: Store the file off-chain (on IPFS, Arweave, or a normal web server). Store the hash of the file on Bitcoin for immutability and timestamping. This approach is much cheaper but still gives you cryptographic proof that your JPEG existed at a certain time and has not been altered. TL;DR You can store a JPEG on Bitcoin — the most common way today is using Ordinals inscriptions. But it’s expensive and not the most efficient use of Bitcoin. For most use cases, just store the hash on-chain and the file off-chain. (for the next years) 1 - USD macro trend shift? 2 - Bitcoin effect? 3 - How I'm playing it The dollar has been range-bound since 1986, basically trading from one extreme to the other, deviating above or below, and then moving to the other side of the range. Simple range facts: > When an asset is ranging, the highest probability is for more ranging > A deviation and return inside the range increases the probability of moving to the other side > Acceptance inside (lower low after a top deviation, or higher high after a bottom deviation) makes it even more probable As you can see in the chart above, a down or uptrend historically took 5-10 years. Bitcoin was born at the bottom deviation and grew from $0 to $120,000 during the dollar’s 10-year uptrend. In this environment, the 4-year cycles took shape with the familiar bull and bear markets. We formed our bull markets when the dollar paused its uptrend and went for a higher low. Once the dollar pushed higher again, it triggered our bear markets. But what if the dollar now heads into a 5-to 10-year-long downtrend? I genuinely believe that, based on this chart, my higher time frame bias for the dollar is down towards the lows because: > The dollar has been range-bound, so I expect more ranging, and we’re currently at the highs. > A deviation has formed. > Bearish market structure is showing back inside (acceptance) The tricky part is that this is a higher time frame range. But if we forget the time frame for a second, perfectly normal range price action could be: > An instant drop > Or, like at the bottom (when Bitcoin was born), extended ranging, which, on this time frame, could feel like forever. We even revisited the lows again at the bottom. If that happens in this case before breaking down, it could keep us in our familiar 4-year structure a little longer. For me, the macro outlook on the dollar suggests we may enter (on the macro) a new paradigm where the 4-year Bitcoin cycle changes. The 4-year cycle was formed in an environment where: > The dollar was trending up on higher time frames > Bull and bear periods were shaped by the short breaks the dollar took in its uptrend If the dollar starts trending down on the macro, it would mean: > A weaker dollar and a broader downtrend > Dollar longer downtrends vs the other way around, longer uptrends. > More aggressive up periods we’ve known Before, when the dollar had strong up periods, it meant deep bear markets for us. When the dollar had short consolidation periods, it meant bull markets for us. Now it changes: we’ll still see those same consolidation periods, but instead of a strong dollar up move sending us deep into a bear, we could get a strong dollar down move fueling us higher. If that happens, it only makes sense that the 4-year cycle changes into: > Longer and more aggressive bull markets > Shorter and more tempered bear markets Bitcoin has never experienced a macro dollar downtrend, but gold has. The last time the dollar deviated at the top of the range and trended down to the low, it sent gold into a 3,800-day supercycle, moving from $250 to $1,800. Pretty poetic that at the dollar deviation we had: USD > Debt explosion > Historic money printing (40% of supply created at the deviation). The Founding Team In early 2014, Vitalik brought together a group of co-founders who played key roles: Gavin Wood → Wrote the Ethereum Yellow Paper (formal technical specs) and created Solidity, Ethereum’s programming language. Later founded Polkadot. Joseph Lubin → Provided funding and later founded ConsenSys, a company that builds Ethereum-based tools and infrastructure. Anthony Di Iorio → Early investor and financier of the project. Charles Hoskinson → Helped establish the Ethereum Foundation’s early structure. Later founded Cardano (ADA). Mihai Alisie → Co-founder who worked on community building and helped set up the Ethereum Foundation in Switzerland. Amir Chetrit → Involved in the early stages but stepped away from active development. Launch 2014 → Ethereum held its public crowd sale (ICO), raising over 31,000 BTC (~$18M at the time). 2015 → The Ethereum mainnet launched, marking the beginning of smart contract–powered blockchain applications. Legacy While Vitalik Buterin is recognized as the visionary behind Ethereum, the project was truly collaborative with multiple co-founders shaping it into what it is today.

Imua’s plug-and-play architecture makes it versatile across industries. From feeding real-world data into smart contracts, to safeguarding financial protocols, to powering secure AI-driven services, Imua ensures reliability at scale. In essence, IMUA introduces a shared security model for the off-chain world, bridging the gap between blockchain infrastructure and real-world applications. By making trust both accessible and scalable, Imua accelerates the path toward more reliable decentralized systems and unlocks the next wave of blockchain adoption.

imagine running a deFi app on Ethereum but settling it on Bitcoin. impossible five years ago, today, Citrea shows it’s plausible. but making execution modular is the real puzzle. the critical angle (ethereum danksharding & modular rollups) ▸ ethereum’s roadmap: danksharding, proto-danksharding, blobs. the bet is: if you make data cheap, rollups will flourish. rollups keep execution, ethereum provides data availability + settlement security. elegant, in theory. ▸ celestia and its cousins: they double down on modularity. split consensus from data from execution. each layer does one thing, devs assemble the pieces they want. ▸ KRNL (KRNL_xyz) steps sideways. It says: blockspace scaling isn’t enough. what you really need is execution scaling functions, not just data, moving in parallel. but here’s the rub: ethereum’s danksharding inherits security from L1. rollups are forced to publish proofs, validity is baked in. with execution sharding, you start to wonder: if computation’s flying around on random nodes, what happens when a shard goes rogue? who attests, who arbitrates? It reminds me of the late 2021 mini-wave of “execution layers” that never quite landed. remember Fuel’s earliest version? Or Cartesi’s VM approach? bright ideas, but they tripped on proving costs or developer adoption. KRNL’s different, but the scars of those attempts matter. → case study: citrea citrea case study: bitcoin settlement meets evm compute. citrea’s interesting here. It’s the first EVM-equivalent rollup secured by Bitcoin. that line alone would’ve been dismissed as impossible five years ago but what it really shows is how composability could play out. ▸ settlement: Bitcoin, the cleanest ledger in the game. ▸ compute: EVM, with all its libraries and developer momentum. ▸ the glue: kernels that let you write workflows where, say, a DeFi app borrows against ETH but finalizes in BTC. this is the dream scenario for institutions. banks don’t want to bet the farm on Ethereum governance fights, but they trust Bitcoin’s immutability. If they can still program logic in solidity and then settle to BTC… that’s compelling. but I keep asking myself: do we really need new middleware for this? Or can L2 bridges and zk-proofs handle most of the heavy lifting? KRNL’s wager is that middleware is the missing layer. Open questions: » If you spread execution across kernels, how do you stop logic from fragmenting into incoherence? » what’s the attack surface when nodes collude to falsify execution before it hits settlement? → risks & gut feel there’s a danger in assuming modular = better. scenarios have played out where projects split their stack into “microservices” of blockchains, each with their own governance, their own fee token, and users hated it. too much friction. there’s also the historical problem of middleware capture. protocols that try to be “neutral glue” often end up invisible. TCP/IP level plumbing that accrues little value. KRNL might succeed technically and still struggle economically. on the other hand… execution sharding feels like the missing piece. Ethereum’s scaling is data-rich but compute-starved. rollups add throughput but don’t solve cross-chain workflows. If KRNL nails verification, it could sit in the sweet spot: not another chain, not another rollup, but the connective tissue. → wrap what I’ve seen, reading papers and watching teams scramble: execution is the choke point no one wants to admit. storage you can shard, consensus you can modularize, but compute? compute gets political fast. KRNL’s kernels are one of the first credible attempts to shard execution while keeping composability intact. citrea is the proof-of-concept that BTC + EVM can coexist if stitched properly. the rest, security assumptions, developer adoption, institutional trust. that’s where the research still has to go. that’s where I’ll leave it.

LTC & BTC: A Deep Dive Into Supply, Scarcity, and Undervaluation When most people look at cryptocurrency, they see price first. Bitcoin trades in the tens of thousands, Litecoin trades in the tens or hundreds... and at a glance, that’s all they notice. But underneath those price tags lies a deeper story about supply, scarcity, and how markets assign value. This analysis reveals something striking: Litecoin (LTC) may be profoundly undervalued compared to Bitcoin (BTC), not because of hype or speculation, but because of math, mining, and monetary mechanics. - Bitcoin cap: 21 million - Litecoin cap: 84 million (exactly 4× BTC) These caps are hard-coded. No more coins can ever exist. That makes both assets “deflationary” in the sense that supply is limited, unlike fiat currencies printed arbitrarily with ultimately no limitation. How Much Is Already Mined? Bitcoin (2025): 19.92M mined (94.9%). 1.08M left. Litecoin (2025): 76.29M mined (90.8%). 7.7M left. At present, Litecoin has more left to mine percentage-wise (9.2% vs 5.1%). Bitcoin will always be “ahead” on the scarcity curve. Halvings and Scarcity Pressure Both BTC and LTC use a halving schedule, where block rewards (new coins paid to miners) are cut in half every four years. Bitcoin: Currently 3.125 BTC per (10min)block; halves again in 2028. (210k blocks) (450/BTC or $54 million USD daily) Litecoin: Currently 6.25 LTC per (2.5min)block; halves again in 2027. (840k blocks) (3,600/LTC or $432k USD daily ) Here’s where things get interesting. Bitcoin today (2025): ~5.1% left to mine. Litecoin will reach ~5% left: late 2028‼ That means Litecoin in 2028 will look, in terms of scarcity, almost exactly like Bitcoin does today. Even more compelling: after Litecoin’s 2027 halving, its inflation rate (~0.8% annually) will be almost identical to Bitcoin’s current inflation rate. The Valuation Discrepancy Bitcoin vs. Litecoin supply math: If Litecoin has 4× the supply, one might expect its value per coin to be about ¼ of Bitcoin’s. Reality today: Litecoin trades at 1/1000th of Bitcoin’s price. Why This Matters... This discrepancy is more than trivia. It’s a case study in how markets function. If markets ever begin to price Litecoin more on its scarcity profile, instead of just narrative and perception... the rebalancing could be explosive. Even a move from 0.001 BTC per LTC toward 0.01 BTC (just 1% of Bitcoin’s price) would represent a 10× appreciation in Litecoin’s relative value! This analysis shows why you can’t just look at surface prices. You need to ask: How much supply is left? How fast is it being issued? When does scarcity align across different assets? These questions effectively highlight potential mispricing. Litecoin’s fundamentals suggest it should command a higher ratio to Bitcoin than it does today. Whether the market ever closes that gap depends on adoption, narrative, and demand... but the asymmetry is clear. Litecoin in this frame is not "just another altcoin,” It's an asset with structural undervaluation baked into today’s prices... -trading at 1/1000th the value of Bitcoin, despite having a supply cap only 4× larger and following the same halving-driven scarcity curve... For anyone building a portfolio, this kind of analysis can shape financial well-being. It proves that by digging into supply mechanics, halvings, and inflation curves, you can spot opportunities the broader market ignores.
