AZTEC OTC TRADING OTC (Over-The-Counter) trading is huge for whales and institutions moving large volumes without market impact. But transparency exposes them, thereby exposing their strategies. Aztec Network's open-source private OTC system changes that by enabling fully confidential, peer-to-peer swaps on its privacy L2. The Problem Traditional OTC on chains like Bitcoin or Ethereum leaves traces, analytics firms track patterns, sizes, and wallets (like Arkham). This risks front-running and strategy leaks. The solution aztecnetwork brings off-exchange trading to crypto with zk-proofs for end-to-end confidentiality. What is Aztec's OTC System? It's a proof-of-concept open-source platform for non-custodial P2P OTC swaps. Built on Aztec's hybrid zkRollup. It uses programmable privacy for private escrow contracts, order matching, and atomic settlements. No Intermediaries. How it works (buyers & sellers) Sellers; - Deploy a private escrow contract (only you know it exists at this stage) - Initialize contract and set the terms (asset type, quantity, price) - Deposit your assets into the contract - After it’s been deployed, call a private API (the order book service) Buyers; - Discover available orders through our privacy-preserving API - Select trades that match your criteria - Complete the seller's partial note with your payment - Execute atomic swap – you get their assets, they get your payment How it is done ( Aztec) Aztec uses Partial Notes to let multiple users privately contribute to a single transaction at different times. Sellers create incomplete payment commitments that buyers can finish without revealing the seller's identity. How Crypto ETFs Differ from Traditional ETFs By design, ETFs are structured to hold and track the performance of an underlying asset, index, or basket of assets. A Traditional ETF is a regulated investment vehicle that tracks the performance of conventional stocks, bonds, and commodities. Examples include: Stock Equity ETFs: S&P 500, Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF. Bond ETFs: iShares U.S. Treasury Bond ETF, Vanguard Total Bond Market Index Fund ETF. Commodity ETFs: iShares Silver Trust (SLV), Invesco DB Oil Fund (DBO). Sector-based ETFs: Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLK), Global X Robotics & Artificial Intelligence ETF (BOTZ). A crypto ETF allows investors to gain exposure to the performance of crypto assets like Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, or XRP through familiar, regulated investment channels, without actually buying any crypto. Simply said, the key difference between a traditional ETF and a crypto ETF lies in what they hold and track.

To understand how severe Bitcoin’s privacy problem really is, consider the following scenarios: 1. Personal Safety Risk You’re travelling through a region with a moderate to high violent crime rate. You need to spend some of your Bitcoin. If every merchant or peer you transact with can see your wallet balance, transaction history, and wealth, you are effectively broadcasting a “rob me” signal. In an adversarial world, total transparency equals personal danger. 2. Business Confidentiality Risk Your company receives a Bitcoin payment from a supplier. That supplier can now observe your wallet balance, trace all incoming and outgoing transactions, and infer your revenue, cost structure, and key counterparties. They can roughly estimate your margins, pricing power, and customer base all through public chain data. This is a total breakdown of commercial privacy. Bitcoin’s UTXO model and transparent ledger make every transaction a permanent, analyzable data point, destroying the concept of business confidentiality. 3. Consumer Exploitation Risk As a private individual purchasing goods or services online, you face algorithmic exploitation. Corporations employ data analytics and price discrimination models to identify your spending capacity. If they can see your entire financial footprint on-chain, they gain perfect informational asymmetry. You become a predictable node in an economic panopticon, a consumer with no negotiating opacity and no right to financial discretion. 4. Fungibility and Guilt by Association You sell cupcakes and receive Bitcoin as payment. Unbeknownst to you, one of the coins you received once passed through an address tied to criminal activity. Because Bitcoin’s ledger is permanently public, chain-analysis companies can label your coins as “tainted.” You might now be treated as a suspect, or worse, find your coins rejected by exchanges or counterparties. Bitcoin’s lack of fungibility turns every coin into a traceable bearer instrument with an attached moral history, the opposite of sound money. Monero fixes all of this. Monero was engineered from first principles to restore financial privacy and fungibility, not as an optional layer, but as a protocol guarantee. Through Ring Signatures, Stealth Addresses, and Confidential Transactions, Monero conceals the sender, receiver, and amount of every transaction at the protocol level. Each output is indistinguishable from millions of others, making chain analysis impossible in practice. Monero’s adaptive block size and tail emission sustain decentralization and long term miner incentives, while its RandomX algorithm ensures CPU-level mining fairness. Monero reclaims what Bitcoin abandoned: the right to transact freely, privately, and safely. Which is the very essence of digital cash envisioned by the cypherpunks.

“The Shadow of Paper Bitcoin: Our Blind Trust in Exchanges” Of the 21 million bitcoins ever to exist, about 94% have already been mined. The amount of bitcoin available for purchase on exchanges has dropped from around 3 million a year ago to just 2.4 million today. However, even that 2.4 million is not necessarily all truly available for purchase. A large portion of exchange-held bitcoin belongs to individual investors or is custodied on behalf of institutions such as BlackRock. We assume we can freely buy and sell bitcoin on exchanges at any time — but it’s worth questioning how solid that assumption really is. For instance, Coinbase currently holds roughly 920,000 bitcoins, most of which belong to institutional clients like BlackRock. BlackRock’s spot ETF, IBIT, has already accumulated about 800,000 bitcoins, mainly custodied with Coinbase and partly with Anchorage Digital Bank. The real issue is that no one can say for sure how much bitcoin on exchanges is: owned by individuals, owned by institutions, and actually available for trading as liquid supply. This lack of transparency creates fertile ground for what’s known as “paper bitcoin” — bitcoin that exists only on paper, not on-chain, and is traded through internal exchange ledgers. While exchanges like Upbit are thought to have higher proportions of individual holders, major U.S. exchanges such as Coinbase are primarily custodial platforms for client assets. This means there’s a significant margin for error. If, one day, every user and institution decided to withdraw their bitcoin to self-custody wallets at the same time, it’s highly likely that many would discover their coins simply aren’t there. Ultimately, we are trusting the numbers shown on exchanges — but what’s really happening behind the scenes is something no one can say with absolute certainty.

Privacy is finally having its long-awaited moment in the crypto world. This year alone, "crypto privacy" hit an ATH on Google searches, zcash pumped over 700% in 3 months and privacy apps like Railgun are processing $150-250M monthly. Ever since bitcoin genesis, we've been fighting for decentralization(Freedom from government and banks surveillance, and the right to manage our money). When I was onboarded to crypto, one of the benefits of defi that we were taught was that we were finally free from the banks and the government, that our money, safely stored in our wallets couldn't be tracked by authorities. But ironically, in our decentralised finance, EVERYONE can spy on your finances - The bartender you tipped at the bar, your boss or fellow employees etc.. and many times this visibility can lead to life threatening issues, because people know how much is in your crypto wallet. Eric Hughes wrote in the Cypherpunk's Manifesto (1993): "Privacy is the ability to selectively reveal oneself to the world." This idea has become one of the core pillars of crypto, since cryptocurrencies were born from the cypherpunk ideals. In fact, bitcoin white paper promises privacy through pseudonymity - your wallet address serves as your identity instead of your name. But there was a flaw, transactions are PUBLIC. Anyone can track your address, monitor your spending, trace your entire financial life. We mistook pseudonymity for privacy. But this year we've seen things change, the data speaks for itself: > Zcash's shielded pool grew from 1M to nearly 4M ZEC > Major institutions finally entered the space We've also seen some notable privacy developments: > Ethereum Foundation formed a dedicated privacy team and launched Kohaku (privacy wallet SDK) >Paxos partnered with Aleo to launch USAD - a private, COMPLIANT stablecoin > OFAC lifted sanctions on Tornado Cash (blacklisted in 2022) > Zcash wallet Zashi integrated with Near for privacy-preserving cross-chain swaps > Noir (ZK programming language) saw a massive uptick in developer activity It's very obvious that the institutions are here and the infrastructure is maturing. Privacy is going mainstream!!! ------------------------------------------------- We've got some technologies leading this revolution: > Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZK) > Trusted Execution Environments (TEE) > Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) [I made a table each of them and a bit of comparison, check it out in the Images] Here's a brief note on each of them: > ZK: Prove something without revealing it. Used in: Zcash, Mina, Aztec, StarkNet > TEE: Secure hardware enclaves that even the OS can't access. Used in: Oasis, Secret Network, Phala > FHE: Compute on encrypted data without ever decrypting it. Used in: Fhenix, Zama, Inco Network Each has its place. ZK for verification, TEE for practical computation now, FHE for the future(so many potentials). --------------------------- Finally , Privacy isn't about hiding illegal activity. It's about preserving human dignity in a digital world. The cypherpunks knew this in the 90s, Satoshi tried to solve it with Bitcoin. Now, three decades later, we finally have the tools to make it real. TL;DR: Decentralization without privacy is f*ckery . I hope you enjoyed the thread, lmk your thoughts in the comments.

How MyriadMarkets Lets Anyone Turn Opinions into On-Chain Predictions When people talk about decentralized finance, they often focus on trading, lending, or yield farming. But another branch of DeFi has been gaining quiet momentum prediction markets. These platforms allow people to forecast the outcome of real events and earn rewards for being right. Myriad Market is one of the most active names in this space, offering a system where anyone can turn a simple opinion into a verifiable on-chain prediction. What a Prediction Market Really Is At its core, a prediction market works like a marketplace for opinions. Each event such as “Will Bitcoin reach 80,000 dollars by December?” becomes a market with two possible outcomes: yes or no. Traders buy shares in the outcome they believe will happen. The market price of those shares reflects the collective belief of all participants. If most people believe the answer is yes, the price for the “yes” side will rise, showing that the crowd expects the event to occur. If it turns out to be true, those holding the correct side share in the winnings. This idea transforms public sentiment into measurable data. How Myriad Brings It On-Chain Myriad Market takes that traditional concept and runs it entirely on blockchain. Instead of using a centralized company to record predictions, every market and every trade is written to a public ledger. That ensures transparency and prevents manipulation. Users connect a digital wallet, usually funded with USDC or another supported token, and pick the event they want to predict. Each trade they make becomes an on-chain transaction. When the event ends, smart contracts automatically settle the market based on the verified result. This process removes the need for a trusted middleman. The blockchain handles everything from record keeping to payouts so the results are as fair and traceable as the code that governs them. Why This Matters Most people already make predictions every day. They discuss what a coin’s price will be, who will win a match, or how a political decision might turn out. Myriad gives those same predictions financial weight. By linking opinions with a token-based system, it allows anyone to test how accurate their views really are. For traders, this becomes a way to hedge or express market sentiment. For casual users, it becomes a learning tool that teaches how probabilities and incentives shape behavior. The fact that everything happens on-chain also makes it impossible to alter outcomes once they are recorded. The Role of USDC and Real Value A major step in Myriad’s growth was its shift from experimental tokens to stable assets like USDC. This change introduced real monetary value into the prediction process. It turned what was once a curiosity into a functioning economic environment. When users stake USDC on a prediction, they are not dealing with abstract points. They are making a financial statement about what they believe will happen. That changes the psychology of participation and increases accountability within the system. A Glimpse of Collective Intelligence Prediction markets like Myriad are more than just platforms for profit. They serve as living experiments in collective intelligence. Each market becomes a small data model that measures what thousands of people believe about the future. When aggregated, these signals can be remarkably accurate. Economists have long argued that markets often predict outcomes better than experts do, because they combine many perspectives into one value. Myriad brings that theory into the blockchain era, letting anyone contribute to the pool of shared insight.

BLOX (Nicholas Crypto Income ETF) •Objective: blend of crypto-industry companies + income via options contracts on those holdings. •Yield: As of 09/30/2025 the 30-day SEC yield was negative (-0.80%). That is a strong red flag. •The fund is very new (inception 6/16/2025) and is actively managed. •Fit vs your goal: This one is more growth + crypto-tech exposure than reliable high income. The negative yield figure shows risk of principal erosion or unpredictable income. Not aligned with “sustainable NAV + 20-30% yield”. 3. WPAY (Roundhill WeeklyPay Universe ETF) •Strategy: Fund-of-funds equal-weighted across “WeeklyPay™” single-stock ETFs (leveraged/augmented versions of single stocks paying weekly distributions) according to the index/structure. •Yield: Some sources show ~8% yield (TTM $4.26 on ~$53 price → ~8.0%) (StockAnalysis). But other sources note issues. •Important: The fund is very new (inception Sep 4 2025) so no long track record. Also the index is concentrated (~67% of assets in Top 10 holdings) and levered. •Also the yield may not be from sustainable earnings; with leveraged/single stock exposure the NAV can be volatile. •Fit vs your goal: Yield is far below your 20-30% target, and the risk of NAV fluctuation is high. So again not ideal for “sustainable NAV + 20-30% yield”. ⸻

Users generate proofs of validity locally and submit them to the network. The network’s role becomes lighter: verifying and aggregating proofs, tracking state commitments, and managing shared public state. Systems like Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, or Aptos often struggle with scalability, privacy, and user experience, or compromise on self-custody and censorship resistance. Miden combines performance, privacy, and safety without sacrificing composability or decentralization. It supports both public and private transactions, allows horizontal and vertical scaling, and is designed to be safe for developers while remaining compatible with existing programming languages.

.strategy confirmed that preferred dividends will be classified as return of capital (ROC). At face value, this is great news! Holders of STR* paper can defer taxes until they sell or until basis is covered - whichever is sooner. But there's a catch. Strategy must keep current and accumulated earnings and profits (E&P) at zero or negative for each year it wants to classify dividends as ROC. I.e. Only in the absence of positive E&P does the dividend become return of capital. If E&P is positive, distributions are considered dividends to the extent of current and accumulated E&P, and only anything beyond that is treated as ROC. digitalphong briefly alluded to this on the earnings call, but did not go into details. Let me share my thoughts; I am sure the community will dig into this more in the coming days and weeks. Big picture, Strategy CANNOT generate operational income if it wants to treat STR* dividends as ROC. Any activity that generates a profit runs the risk of pushing E&P > 0. This makes it challenging to monetize Bitcoin or consider other income generating activities like Metaplanet's option selling. Thankfully, the IRS has ruled that CAMT will not apply to bitcoin "income," making it is highly unlikely that that "income" will count toward toward E&P that contributes toward dividend distribution. ⏸ Technically, it is possible to ring-fence operations away from the distributing entity (Strategy) such that any income remains at the subsidiary level, and no consolidated return is filed at the parent level. Not something we may want to see as economic value may not accumulate to the commons, which we all want to see, but am mentioning this for completeness. At any rate, saylor needs to talk to tax professionals here, and not query ChatGPT. For anyone wanting to learn more about the considerations around ROC, I'd encourage you to look into REITs and MLPs. Simple version is: they are able to designate distributions as ROC even though they use cash generated by the business to do so because depreciation and amortization makes their E&P ≤ 0. MSTR does not have a similar shield. Finally, a word of caution. This is a complex tax area where treatment depends heavily on specific facts, structure, and jurisdiction. The IRS does not f*ck around, particularly if setups appear designed primarily for tax avoidance. Again, talk to tax professionals, Saylor, and do not ask just ChatGPT.

The system isn’t “broken.” It’s doing exactly what it was built to do: fund deficits with politicized rates, hide risk in expanding credit, and quietly tax savers through dilution. When credit compounds faster than productive capacity, something has to give… and in fiat regimes, it’s the currency. That’s the distortion so many people feel but can’t quite name. For decades, LawrenceLepard (along with a long line of “gold bugs”) rang the bell about this reality. They stood in the headwinds when it was unfashionable to question the orthodoxy, doing the homework on real rates, debt dynamics, and monetary history. Bitcoiners should appreciate that work. Without that community keeping the hard‑money flame alive through long winters, the story of Bitcoin would have been slower to land. Gold was the first great firewall against the worst incentives of paper money. It gave individuals and nations an off‑ramp… a way to store the output of their time in something harder to manipulate. For centuries, that was the best tool available. It trained millions to care about scarcity, discipline, and settlement that doesn’t rely on political permission. In that sense, gold didn’t just preserve wealth; it preserved an ethos. Bitcoin extends that ethos with new properties that fit an internet‑native world. It doesn’t “hate” gold; it outcompetes it as a monetary good and, over time, will likely demonetize gold for everyday monetary use. Why? • Transportability: Move any amount, across borders, in minutes…. no armored cars, no vault logistics. • Divisibility: 100,000,000 sats per bitcoin makes micro‑settlement native, not an afterthought. • Absolute supply cap: 21 million, enforced by rules anyone can verify—not by anyone’s discretion. • Verifiability: Don’t trust… run code. Every participant can audit the ledger at home. Add to that 24/7 global liquidity, predictable issuance, censorship resistance, and self‑custody with bearer‑style finality, and the result is a monetary network that compresses the cost of assurance while widening access. When the cost to test authenticity trends toward zero and the cost to move value collapses, liquidity migrates. That’s not ideology; it’s engineering meeting incentives. None of this diminishes what gold accomplished. Gold preserved the ethos; Bitcoin perfects the mechanism. One taught the world why discipline matters; the other shows how discipline can be enforced without trusting a handful of institutions. One is the steam engine of monetary restraint…. revolutionary in its time, still useful in places. The other is the electric motor….. cleaner, faster, and built for the networks we actually live on. This is why I think of Lawrence as a bridge…. someone who didn’t just hammer on the old problems, but who has been willing to widen his lens as a new tool emerged. That takes intellectual honesty and humility. It’s easy to defend your priors forever; it’s harder to update them in public. I applaud that. His work helps connect the sound‑money warriors of decades past with the new breed of builders, miners, coders, and allocators finding their way into Bitcoin today. To my fellow Bitcoiners: remember whose shoulders we’re standing on. The debates about real rates, about the meaning of savings, about what happens when money becomes an instrument of policy rather than a measuring stick - all of that groundwork was laid by people who were right too early and paid a social price for it. Gratitude is not just good manners; it’s good strategy. It makes the tent bigger and the mission clearer. To my friends in the gold community: if Bitcoin sometimes feels like it’s “coming for” gold, reframe it. Bitcoin operationalizes the very principles you’ve defended: scarcity, settlement you can trust, freedom from arbitrary dilution. It doesn’t erase your contribution…. it scales it. Keep an open mind and run the experiment alongside us. Continued

Related Terms: a. Smart contract: the code that powers most dApps. b. DAO: decentralized autonomous organization, often managed via a dApp. c. DeFi: decentralized finance, a popular category of dApps. Examples: 1. Uniswap – a dApp that lets users swap crypto tokens without intermediaries. 2. LensProtocol – a social media dApp built on blockchain. 3. opensea – an NFT marketplace dApp for buying and selling digital collectibles. Fun Fact: The first recognized dApp was Bitcoin itself, a decentralized application for sending and storing digital money without banks.

Michael Saylor says Bitcoin will reach $1,000,000. He wants to own 10% of the entire supply. But what happens if the Bitcoin crashes? Here’s ow the MicroStrategy system really works: Saylor started as an engineer. Graduated from MIT. Founded MicroStrategy in 1989 with two classmates. For years, they sold business software to companies like McDonald’s and Coca-Cola. In 2000, the dot com bubble came. MicroStrategy’s stock went from $333 to $7 after an accounting scandal. Saylor paid $10M to the SEC but stayed in control. For the next 20 years, the company survived quietly. Then came 2020. MicroStrategy had half a billion dollars in cash and almost no growth. So he converted all of it into Bitcoin. 21,454 BTC for $250M. The first public company to do it. He borrowed money, issued debt, and sold new shares. Every time the stock went up, he sold more. Every dollar went straight into Bitcoin. By 2025 he holds 641,205 BTC worth about $68 billion. They paid $47 billion for it. Almost all of it was financed with bonds, convertible notes, and stock offerings. The system is simple: 1.Issue new debt or preferred stock. 2.Use it to buy Bitcoin. 3.Stock price goes up with BTC. 4.Raise more money again. 5.Repeat. It’s a loop that feeds on confidence. As long as Bitcoin rises, the cycle continues. But what happens if Bitcoin crashes? If Bitcoin stays above $60k, the model works perfectly. If it falls below $30k, the coverage over its $8B in debt shrinks dangerously. At that point, dilution isn’t enough. They might have to sell part of their Bitcoin. That’s the risk no one talks about.

A zkRollup makes blockchains faster and cheaper by moving most work off-chain while keeping key data on-chain. It’s like handling tasks in a separate room and submitting only final results for verification. Zero-knowledge proofs confirm these results without revealing details. On Bitcoin, BitVM2 enables this by optimistically verifying complex computations, including zk proofs such as Groth16 or FFLONK. As long as Layer 2 state updates are published to Bitcoin and verifiable by proofs, it qualifies as a zkRollup. GOAT Network(goatnetwork) builds on this with a decentralized economy offering sustainable yield, strong security, and a growing ecosystem. Users earn and interact on Bitcoin without sacrificing safety. Basic flow in a Bitcoin zkRollup: >>Peg-In (Deposit) Deposit BTC via a BitVM2-based transaction on Bitcoin. Layer 2 nodes detect it and mint WrappedBTC on Layer 2 for ecosystem use. >>Transactions and Blocks A sequencer collects transactions, builds blocks, and broadcasts them across Layer 2 for state consensus. >>Publishing State Updates The sequencer periodically posts state differences to Bitcoin, ensuring Layer 1 holds the truth. >>Peg-Out (Withdraw) Burn WrappedBTC on Layer 2 to trigger a Bitcoin covenant returning real BTC to your address. This guarantees asset withdrawal to Bitcoin anytime, even if Layer 2 fails. In short, zkRollups bring scale and speed; BitVM2 enables Bitcoin verification; networks like goatnetwork create safer, rewarding user experiences. It’s fast. It’s secure. Bitcoin and Government Shutdowns: The Hidden Liquidity Cycle 1 ⃣ Most investors miss this pattern. Every major US government shutdown in history has created the same sequence in Bitcoin: a liquidity drain, a correction, and then a powerful rally once the shutdown ends. Let’s break it down with real data. 2 ⃣ The current 2025 shutdown has lasted over 34 days - almost the longest ever. Bitcoin started near $115K when it began, surged to $123,874, and has since corrected to around $103K–$108K. A 13–18% drawdown. Classic mid-shutdown behavior. 3 ⃣ To understand what comes next, look at the historical record. 2013: Bitcoin jumped from $133 to over $1,000 around the shutdown - an 8x surge. 2018–2019: The 35-day shutdown saw BTC fall 20%, then climb 50% in the following 3 months. Pattern: weakness during, strength after. 4 ⃣ Why? Liquidity. During shutdowns, the US Treasury General Account (TGA) pulls hundreds of billions from circulation. Spending halts. Cash gets trapped inside government accounts. Liquidity dries up. Risk assets struggle. 5 ⃣ When shutdowns end, the opposite happens. The Treasury immediately starts spending again - back pay, contracts, delayed programs. This injects hundreds of billions back into the system. It’s like flipping a liquidity switch back on. 6 ⃣ Bitcoin thrives on liquidity. It’s not just a hedge against inflation - it’s a global liquidity barometer. When dollars flood back into markets, Bitcoin responds first and fastest. 7 ⃣ Shutdowns also raise the odds of rate cuts. Economic slowdown + missing data = a more dovish Fed. Lower rates weaken the dollar and boost demand for non-sovereign assets like BTC. 8 ⃣ There’s a psychological layer too. Every shutdown reminds the world that government reliability is fragile. That loss of trust drives capital toward neutral assets. Bitcoin benefits from both the liquidity return and the credibility erosion. 9 ⃣ So, what does history suggest for now? If the shutdown ends soon and the liquidity snap-back follows the 2019 pattern, a 30–50% rally over the next 3 months is realistic. That puts targets in the $134K–$155K range. In summary: Shutdowns drain liquidity and tighten markets. Reopenings flood liquidity and spark rallies. Bitcoin, the purest expression of global liquidity sensitivity, rides that wave better than any other asset. History doesn’t repeat, it rhymes through liquidity. Bitcoin BTC Macro LiquidityCycle

PMI could fall from here into greater contraction, but what does that mean for bitcoin? BTC has been expanding while PMI is contracting (below 50). This chart is misleading. Where is the bitcoin implied pricing axis? It hides the inverse correlation of the last 3 years and makes it appear positive. I ran three different correlation calcs, with the help of chatGPT. 1) PMI above 50 and rising compared to rising BTC. There was a -0.02 correlation, IOW no correlation to rising PMI above 50 and rising BTC. 2) PMI above 50 and falling compared to falling BTC. There was a -0.01 correlation, IOW no correlation. 3) PMI below 50 compared to change in BTC price. There was a -0.21 correlation, suggesting that when PMI is below 50 there is a slight negative correlation. Next, I added lags. I tested if lagging BTC by 1, 2, or 3 months would make any correlation appear. It did not. I added lags for PMI of 1, 2, and 3 months to see if bitcoin led. There was a very slight consistently positive correlation on each of these time frames, but nothing significant. What I think this shows is that there is no statistical correlation here at all really. The apparent similarity is likely from another underlying variable or variables.

Why Crypto Can't Build Anything Long-Term Most crypto founders aren’t building : they’re pivoting. From NFTs in 2021 → DeFi in 2022 → AI agents in 2023 → prediction markets in 2024/25. Same builders. Same cycle. Different story. Let’s talk about why crypto structurally can’t build anything that lasts. 1. The 18-Month Product Cycle Narrative appears → capital floods in → everyone pivots → 6–9 months of hype → narrative dies → pivot again. It used to be 3–4 years (ICO era). Now? You’re lucky to get 18 months. You can’t build real infrastructure or PMF in that time. 2. The Sunk Cost Fallacy (Maxxed Out) In normal startups: pivot when something doesn’t work. In crypto: pivot before you even know if it works. Why? Because pivoting raises money faster than building. Option A: build for 3 years and maybe raise again. Option B: chase the next trend and raise now. Guess which wins? 3. The Halting Problem Most crypto projects are always almost finished. “Just one more feature from PMF.” But before they finish… the narrative shifts. Now it’s AI, or RWA, or prediction markets. The market punishes finishing a finished product has limits. An “almost finished” one has infinite potential. 4. Capital Follows Attention, Not Completion VCs don’t fund products. They fund stories. New narrative, no product: $50M raised Working product, struggling narrative: $5M Old narrative, real users: can’t raise The result? “Narrative-maxxing” — optimize for hype, not impact. 5. Team Retention = Trend Retention Your best dev leaves for a project that just raised $100M. Your marketing lead gets poached by the new “AI + DeFi” startup. No one wants to build the “boring but working” project. They want chaos, hype, and exit liquidity. 6. The User Attention Problem Crypto users don’t stay because your product is good. They stay because it’s new — or there’s an airdrop. Once the hype moves on, they move too. You can’t build sustainable products for unsustainable users. 7. The Infrastructure Paradox The only lasting things in crypto — Bitcoin and Ethereum — were built before the hype. No tokens, no VCs, no exit pressure. But nobody builds between cycles anymore. No hype → no funding → no builders. 8. The Structural Trap Token models incentivize exits, not endurance. If you can exit before maturity, why wait? The space rewards speed over substance. By the time you finish, someone copied your idea and shipped faster. So what now? Crypto’s biggest innovation might not be blockchain. It’s monetizing pivots. The product isn’t the app. It’s the narrative. And until the incentives change, building long-term will always lose to building what’s hot. Crypto doesn’t fail because founders are lazy - it fails because the system rewards starting, not finishing. The real challenge? Build something that lasts after the hype dies.

From the 1940s through the 1970s, the pattern was coherent: higher rates disciplined debt. Credit expansion followed real output. The dollar was tethered to gold, and debt to constraint. Then, post-1971, the inversion began. Nixon killed convertibility, and suddenly the economy no longer had to earn growth - it could borrow it. Look closely at the divergence after 2008. That’s the singularity point. Debt explodes vertically while yields collapse horizontally. The market is no longer pricing risk, it’s pricing coordination. The state has become the market, and the bond market has become theology. Every era of this chart reflects a regime of belief: •1945-1971: Bretton Woods discipline - debt expansion tethered to production. •1971-2000: Fiat globalization - debt expansion tethered to consumption. •2008-2025: QE reflexivity - debt expansion tethered to narrative. We are now in the fourth phase: permanent monetization, where deficits are no longer errors but features of the system’s design. The state borrows not to spend but to sustain the illusion that debt still matters. The reason Max Anderson is right when he says this is “the only chart you need to understand investing for 30-40 years” is because it encodes the end of the interest rate cycle as we know it. There is no returning to pre-2008 dynamics. The system is trapped in an equilibrium that requires debt to rise exponentially faster than GDP just to stay coherent. When your debt/GDP ratio crosses the event horizon - as it did post-2020 - your options collapse into two: 1. Inflate nominal GDP through monetary debasement. 2. Default - either explicitly (through restructuring) or implicitly (through currency devaluation). The Federal Reserve, Treasury, and global financial system have already chosen door 1. Inflation is now structural, not cyclical - because it’s the only politically survivable way to liquidate unpayable promises without calling it default. The red line’s periodic spikes, those yield surges, are the market’s screams of disbelief. But each time, the blue line swallows them. Rates collapse not because inflation is gone, but because the system cannot survive true price discovery anymore. This means one thing for investors: The next 30 years will be a slow-motion transfer of real value from holders of paper to holders of scarcity. Gold, Bitcoin and productive assets are hedges against a timeline where fiat must decay to preserve the illusion of stability. The real red pill isn’t that data is fake. It’s that reality itself has been financialized. GDP, CPI, unemployment - they’re all derivatives of the same political equation: how long can the system postpone truth without collapsing belief. So here’s the translation: •The blue line is trust decay. •The red line is belief volatility. •The space between them is the price of denial. This chart is the eulogy of the old world’s monetary physics. If the 20th century was the age of leverage, the 21st will be the age of reckoning through substitution. Fiat will decay. Double Spending in crypto Double spending is when someone tries to use the same cryptocurrency more than once. The attacker doesn’t create new coins, but tries to trick the network into accepting the same coins in two different transactions. If the network is slow to confirm transactions, both payments might look valid at first. This is called double spending, because the same coins are being spent twice. How Do Hackers Pull This Off? Hackers do this via different methods and one of them is the 51% attack, when someone controls more than half of a blockchain, allowing them to rewrite parts of the blockchain. The other methods varies depending on the resources and strategy of the attacker → Race attacks → Finney attacks → Zero-confirmation attacks → Selfish mining → Sybil attacks and others You may wonder, has this ever happened before? Yes, it has. Although not on the main Bitcoin network, it occurred on smaller blockchains like Bitcoin Gold and Ethereum Classic. This was done through 51% attacks. The hackers were able to reverse transactions and steal funds, which led to the loss of more than $65 million from the cases of Bitcoin Gold and Ethereum Classic alone. After the attack on Ethereum Classic, Ethereum’s developers created a new hard fork of the mainnet, which is what we now have as the current Ethereum blockchain. This was done to recover the stolen funds by creating a new blockchain where the hackers’ transactions were reversed, while the old blockchain continued as Ethereum Classic, where those coins remained. Although not everyone left the Ethereum Classic blockchain, so the Ethereum Classic community continued. The sad thing, though, is that the blockchain suffered more than three additional attacks. You may be thinking, “Dang! That’s terrible! Couldn’t they stop the attack?” Well, they did improve the system. One step they took was doing a Thanos Upgrade, which modified their Ethash consensus algorithm into what is now referred to as Etchash. If you are not yet following my page, do so now, as I will be talking more about consensus algorithms next. This modification of its previous system made future attacks harder and improved overall security. Consensus mechanisms played a major role in reducing the risk of double spending. Since blockchains don’t have a central authority watching them, the consensus mechanism acts as the backbone of their security. There are different types of consensus mechanisms, like Proof of Work and Proof of Stake. The main idea is that these systems help everyone agree on one version of the blockchain by deciding which transactions get added and in what order, so all users see the same correct record. With the consensus mechanism acting as a gatekeeper, most types of double spending are very difficult, because transactions must be agreed on by the network before they are confirmed. You are probably scared right now, but lol! You don’t need to be. Given that blockchain technology is still very much alive and thriving, it’s clear that the double-spending problem has been taken care of, for the most part. So, as a regular crypto user, double spending is probably not something you should lose sleep over, but blockchains as a whole can be (and have been) affected by it. This is my second post in my r3tard guide to Bittensor TAO series. In this post I'm going to cover what a subnet is and a bit more about tokens and how they compare to other networks. Sorry, it gets a little more complicated in language now, but this is level 2 after all. You can read my first post (level 1) in the link under this post. The structure of how a subnet is made is at it's core the same across every single subnet. They have: A) The base subnet layer where tokens are distributed by the system B) The Incentive mechanism (IM) layer where the team have to decide what output they want miners to achieve and build an IM around it that is competed for by miners and scored for by validators C) Product layer - a monetisable product from the output needs to be made, or face reduction in funding. Teams that deliver value, or sell their vision well, will get funded, teams that don't... don't Regarding subnet outputs: The output can be anything you could think of, ranging from ideas such as- 1) The provision of compute chutes_ai lium_io 2) Prediction of the future price of BTC SynthdataCo 3) The improvement of agent code ridges_ai bitsecai The incentive mechanism has to be scored around a benchmark, which is what the validators judge them on. In the cases of the above that might be: 1) Was the compute provided 2) Was the prediction correct 3) Which miner did the best code improvement This makes Bittensor a highly flexible incentive mechanism protocol that can capital fund any idea as long as it can either make money, or people might want to support a nice cause for a period. ----------------------- Tokens The idea of buying subnet tokens is pretty simple. Buying a subnet token at it's core is just like buying any coin on Solana or Eth. The tokens launched are still the same concept in terms of the fact that they are a project/company with their own team. Some teams are legendary, and some are When you buy a token on Sol, you do so with Sol or USDC on chain. The token was minted depending on the teams preference, and they have choice over their tokenomics.... On Bittensor it's different as all the launches are the same, as are the tokenomics. Once a token on Sol is live, it's symbiotic connection to the network it was launched on mostly ends there. There might be a market on chain, and it might find it's way to a CEX but it doesn't really drive any value back to SOL itself aside from being the unit of account in pools, and provide transaction volume on the network. On Bittensor, capital funding is heavily tied to subnet performance, so teams have to drive value back to their token through fundraising (getting speculative buyers), or by gaining real world revenue. If they fail to do so funding dries up. How their capital funding is provided is judging which subnets put most back into their pool, and guess where that comes from? Yes it's the amount of TAO itself driven back into the pools. You can think of this as a permanently ongoing Y combinator. The ultimate capital funding game. So, every subnet is now battling to put TAO into their pools (by buying subnet tokens) in order to stay funded, thus aligning every team back to TAO. This is the fundamental difference. Bittensor projects are aligned to TAO. SOL (or other L1 projects) are not aligned to SOL ------------------------ Why Bittensor will be valuable AF Where other L1 protocols such as Sol or Eth operate on number of users on their network creating the value, on Bittensor each project (subnet) is in effect it's own network. Bittensor is a network of networks. Where we can look at the likes of Bitcoin, Solana or even Facebook as being Metcalfe's law followers (and you have seen the growth of value in those networks), Bittensor, being a network of networks follows a different law... Reed's law, which should grow in value and size much faster than Metcalfe's law based networks. Dr. notthreadguy

You can only control whether you lace up. In Bitcoin: you can't control the macro, the regulations, or the market. You can only control whether you show up and stack. The runners who won championships weren't always the most talented. They were the ones who did the work when it didn't feel like it was working. That's DCA. So if you're DCA'ing while price is down, you're doing the 5am runs in February. Nobody's watching. Nobody's cheering. Do you know the essential requirement for a solution to qualify as a Bitcoin Layer 2? It's the presence of a forced withdrawal feature. Forced withdrawal leverages BitVM to inherit Bitcoin's Proof-of-Work (PoW) security and censorship resistance. When a user initiates a forced inclusion via a Bitcoin transaction, the build_on_bob state is reconstructed from Bitcoin data, making the L2's stability dependent on the L1's immutability. This allows users to safely recover their assets even if the L2 experiences downtime or malicious activity, thereby enhancing the overall system's trustworthiness. In BOB, BTC becomes equivalent to native BTC through BitVM (scheduled for implementation in early next year, currently under testing on the testnet). If we entrust our BTC to a Bitcoin L2 and can still recover it to the original Layer 1 even if the L2 fails, we can use the L2 with peace of mind and consider it on par with native BTC. While many so-called Bitcoin L2s exist today, they don't truly qualify as such—they're essentially EVM-based L2s that rely on wrapped BTC. This has led to widespread disappointment among people regarding Bitcoin L2s, but you haven't been disappointed. After all, you can't be disappointed in something that doesn't exist. However, BOB makes this possible through BitVM, building a more secure BTC DeFi environment. This creates a setting where users and institutions can confidently manage their BTC assets with safety.

The more I read about 0xMiden, the clearer it becomes: if we were designing blockchains from scratch today, they’d look a lot less like the networks we’re used to… and a lot more like an edge-first system. Traditional chains were built for a world without ZK proofs, so they inherited the same bottleneck: the network executes everything, everyone re-executes everything, and privacy is sacrificed so the validator set can check your homework. That design carried us through Bitcoin and Ethereum - the first two big inflection points - but it was never meant to go global. Miden flips that model in a way that feels inevitable in hindsight. >> Users execute their own transactions locally. >> Users store their own state. The network only verifies compact proofs and tracks commitments. It removes execution bloat, it reduces state bloat, it makes privacy the default, and it brings scale without centralizing the network. Your device does the heavy lifting; the chain just verifies receipts. And because verifying a ZK proof is exponentially cheaper than running the underlying computation, even complex smart contracts become feasible without punishing the network. This, to me, is the real third inflection point: Bitcoin gave us self-custodied money. Ethereum gave us programmable trust. Edge blockchains like Miden give us scalable privacy by design. And that unlocks something we haven’t had: applications that are fast enough, private enough, and safe enough for everyday use - without throwing away the principles of censorship-resistance or composability. When people say the future of crypto is at the edge, this is what they mean. Not marketing. Not rollup tweaks. A full rearchitecture where the network stops being the bottleneck, and users finally become the engine. This feels like the direction the entire industry shifts toward once everyone catches up.

ZetaChain: The Universal Chain That Aims To Connect All of Web3 The blockchain world has grown rapidly, but it has grown in pieces. Ethereum has its ecosystem. Solana has its own. Bitcoin stands alone. Layer 2 networks operate separately. Sidechains, app-chains, subnets and zk-rollups each form their own islands. For everyday users, this means constant switching. For developers, it means fragmented liquidity. For institutions, it means complexity and operational risk. ZetaChain (ZETA) is stepping into this challenge with one of the boldest visions in modern Web3. It is building a universal chain that allows applications to connect directly with every blockchain, whether they are EVM based, non-EVM, Layer 1 or Layer 2. This is not just bridging. It is native interoperability. — — — A Chain Built to Unify Web3 ZetaChain introduces a model where applications can become omnichain dApps. Instead of building separate versions for different networks, developers can build once on ZetaChain and interact with every major chain automatically. This approach solves the fragmentation problem at the root by offering: Unified liquidity Unified messaging Unified user experience Unified contract execution A DeFi protocol can access Bitcoin liquidity without wrapping. A social app can read Ethereum and Solana identities at the same time. A game can execute assets across chains without confusion for the player. The result is a smoother, cleaner Web3 experience. — — — The Power of Omnichain Smart Contracts The real innovation lies in omnichain smart contracts. These contracts run on ZetaChain but control assets and data across external chains. For example: A user can deposit on Polygon and borrow on Avalanche. A liquidity pool can combine assets from multiple ecosystems into one shared vault. A protocol can settle interactions across chains without trust assumptions or centralized bridges. This is a major shift in how developers think about architecture and liquidity design. ZetaChain is giving Web3 something like the "internet layer" it has always needed. — — — Solving the User Experience Problem Users today switch wallets, networks, RPCs and apps constantly. It is one of the biggest barriers to real adoption. ZetaChain’s universal approach simplifies the entire process: Users interact with one chain The protocol handles all the cross-chain complexity Transactions feel seamless regardless of where assets originate This is the type of user experience that will drive mainstream adoption because it removes friction at every level. — — — The Role of ZETA The ZETA token powers the network through: • Transaction fees • Cross-chain messaging security • Validator incentives • Gas abstraction for omnichain operations As more dApps migrate to omnichain models, ZETA becomes the coordination asset that keeps everything functioning securely and smoothly. Its value accrues as universal interoperability becomes a core requirement for modern applications. — — — Why ZetaChain Matters Now The future of blockchain will not be one chain dominating the others. It will be a world where many chains coexist, each optimized for different experiences, but all connected through a reliable interoperability layer. ZetaChain is one of the few networks approaching this as a native layer, not an afterthought. It is not competing to be the fastest or cheapest chain. It is competing to be the unifying chain. If Web3 is ever going to feel like one coherent digital world instead of dozens of fragmented ecosystems, chains like ZetaChain will be the reason.

Most of us grew up in crypto knowing one simple truth: Bitcoin is king… but Bitcoin is limited. It’s the most secure chain in the world, the most decentralized, the most battle-tested yet it can’t run the things we use every day: • Smart contracts • DEXs • Lending • NFTs • DAOs • On-chain automation In other words, Bitcoin became the world’s best store of value… but not the world’s best platform. For years, builders tried to fix this. Sidechains, federations, rollups, bridges… all interesting, but all with compromises. Then botanix walked in with something new. Something clean. Something surprisingly elegant. Let me break it down the way you’ll feel it instantly The Problem Bitcoin Couldn’t Solve If Bitcoin is the “world’s digital gold,” what’s missing is a smart-contract layer powerful enough to build an entire economy around it. But we had three walls: • Lightning → great for payments, not apps • Liquid → federation, not decentralized • Rollups → Bitcoin doesn’t have the opcodes yet • Bridges → hacked every other month Everybody wanted Bitcoin smart contracts. Nobody could build them without asking users to trust a middleman. Botanix solves that without touching Bitcoin at all. What Botanix Really Is (Simple Version) Let me strip away the noise: Botanix is an EVM chain built on top of Bitcoin, anchored to Bitcoin, designed to evolve into a permissionless system secured by BTC itself. Meaning: > It runs Ethereum smart contracts > It supports the entire EVM ecosystem > All value is backed 1:1 by real BTC > Long term no federation, no sidechain council, no custodians (once the full proof-of-stake system is active) > No Bitcoin soft fork needed (Important reality check: today’s mainnet still uses a federation for peg security, but Spiderchain is the intended trust-minimized end state.) It’s the first time Bitcoin truly gets an application layer that feels like Ethereum… but aims to remain Bitcoin anchored and Bitcoin backed. Now, the magic: the Spiderchain. The Spiderchain -The Innovation Everyone’s Talking About Here’s the simplest way to understand it: Imagine a vault where the guards keep rotating every 10 minutes, and each vault is controlled by a random group of guards no one controls. That rotating vault system is the Spiderchain. Here’s how it works (in full design): > Every Bitcoin block creates a new multisig > Those multisigs hold the BTC backing Botanix > The signers are chosen randomly from Orchestrator nodes > You never know who you’ll end up with, so collusion is nearly impossible > The set rotates forever like a web constantly shifting This design gives Botanix Bitcoin-level security, but with Ethereum-level programmability. Why the Spiderchain is genius: > There’s no single point of failure > Attackers can’t predict or control who signs what > Even if someone gets majority today, they can’t steal yesterday’s funds > It’s decentralized by design, not by marketing It’s the closest design we’ve seen to a trust-minimized BTC smart-contract layer. (Again: this is the final architecture. Today, Botanix runs a federated model while Spiderchain rolls out in phases.) Synthetic BTC - Bitcoin You Can Actually Use On Botanix, the currency is synthetic BTC (sBTC). this is simply: BTC locked inside Spiderchain multisigs (or today's federation multisig)→ sBTC minted 1:1 on Botanix. When you return sBTC, the multisig releases your real BTC back to you. Why this matters: > No custodial bridge in the final design > No traditional peg operators > No dependency on a small council in the spiderchain model. Your BTC becomes usable in smart contracts without ever leaving Bitcoin’s security envelope. The Peg Mechanism (Explained Without Confusion) You'll love this part because it feels simple. Peg-in (BTC → sBTC) 1. You send BTC to a Spiderchain multisig 2. Botanix sees it 3. It mints sBTC for you 4. You start using it like ETH on an EVM network Peg-out (sBTC → BTC) 1. You burn sBTC 2. A new multisig releases the same amount of BTC back to you 3. Botanix picks UTXOs using LIFO for better security It's just pure cryptography. Orchestrators - The Blockchain’s Backbone In the full spiderchain architecture botanix validators are called Orchestrators. They: > stake BTC > sign multisigs in the Spiderchain > build Botanix blocks > process peg-ins and peg-outs If they misbehave? > they get slashed > they get kicked > they lose their stake This keeps everyone honest. Botanix uses Proof-of-Stake, but inherits randomness and fairness from Bitcoin’s Proof-of-Work. The Security Model - Why Botanix Is Hard to Attack I'll make this extremely digestible: Security Ingredient 1: Randomness from Bitcoin Bitcoin block hashes decide who participates in multisigs. It's random. It's unpredictable. It's not gameable. Security Ingredient 2: Forward Security Even if you hack the system today, you can’t steal funds from the past. This is massive. Security Ingredient 3: Stakes plus Slashing If you try to steal from a multisig, someone else will report you and earn your entire slashed stake. Collusion becomes irrational. Security Ingredient 4: Distribution To attack Botanix, someone would need to: > Own majority of the Orchestrator stake > AND get lucky enough to dominate random multisigs > AND remain undetected > AND avoid slashing The math is brutal. (Note: this applies to the full Spiderchain PoS system i.e the end-state Botanix is moving toward.) Fully Ethereum-Compatible - No New Language Needed Developers don’t need to learn: > Rust > Move > Cairo > Custom VM languages Botanix is the EVM equivalent. Meaning: > All Solidity smart contracts work > All Ethereum tooling works > All EVM dApps can deploy > No performance limits of ZK rollups This alone accelerates adoption 10x. What Botanix Makes Possible Once sBTC becomes programmable, Bitcoin stops being idle capital. Here’s what becomes possible: > Bitcoin-native DEXs > Bitcoin-backed lending > Bitcoin yield markets > Bitcoin NFTs > Bitcoin perpetuals > Bitcoin stablecoins > Bitcoin DAOs > On-chain automation powered by BTC This is a new design space: DeFi on Bitcoin without sacrificing decentralization. Actual BTC. Actually programmable. Actually secure in spiderchain final model. Why Botanix Matters Bitcoin controls trillions in value. Ethereum controls trillions in activity. Botanix merges both. It takes: > Bitcoin’s decentralization > Ethereum’s composability > PoS efficiency > Multisig security > Open participation …and blends them into a chain that could host the next wave of Bitcoin-native applications. This isn’t “yet another L2.” It’s foundational infrastructure. The kind that changes what’s possible on Bitcoin forever.

As of November 21, 2025, Bitcoin (BTC) trades around $82,000–$87,000 USD (with some sources varying slightly due to exchange differences and intraday swings), down significantly from its 2025 all-time high of approximately $126,000 reached in early October. $74,000 was a key level in prior cycles (e.g., the 2024 ATH around $73–74k and a common support/reference point), but right now BTC sits ~10–15% above that price. Realism of Bitcoin Dropping Back to $74k Over the Next Month (December 2025) A drop to $74k would require another ~10–15% decline from current levels (or up to ~20% from recent weekly highs around $90–95k). Yes, this is entirely realistic — even probable in a bearish scenario — for several reasons: • Bitcoin remains highly volatile — 10–20% moves in a single week (or day) are common, especially during corrections. We’ve already seen BTC fall ~35% from its October 2025 peak of $126k to the current mid-$80k zone in just 6–7 weeks. • Ongoing heavy selling pressure → Spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded record outflows in November 2025 (~$3–4 billion+), institutional demand has cooled, and broader risk-off sentiment (fears of AI/tech bubble, macro uncertainty) is weighing on speculative assets. • Technical picture — BTC is in a descending channel since the October top, with weakening momentum. A break below the $80–82k zone could easily accelerate toward $74–75k (a psychological level and MicroStrategy’s approximate cost basis, often cited as strong support). • Historical precedent — Post-ATH corrections of 30–50%+ are normal in bull cycles (e.g., 2021 saw multiple 30–50% drawdowns before the final top). We’re only ~35% off the high so far — room for more downside is typical. Counter-Arguments (Why It Might Not Happen) • Strong long-term support around $70–80k from ETF buyers, corporate treasuries, and halving-cycle expectations. • Some analysts still forecast stabilization or mild upside into year-end ($90–110k+ ranges) if outflows slow and holiday-season retail flows return. • The overarching 2025 bull market narrative (post-halving, institutional adoption, potential U.S. strategic reserve developments) remains intact. Bottom Line Dropping to $74k (or lower) over the next month is realistic and within normal volatility bounds for Bitcoin right now — it would “only” extend the current correction another 10–20%, which happens frequently. It’s not a base-case certainty, but definitely not far-fetched given the momentum. Conversely, a quick rebound above $100k would require a sharp sentiment reversal (e.g., ETF inflows resuming strongly), which looks less likely in the very short term based on current flows. Always trade/invest with caution — crypto markets can swing wildly in either direction.

The source of the selling that started on Oct 10: The big story connecting MSCI (the major index provider) to the Bitcoin market revolves around a proposed rule change that could exclude companies heavily loaded with digital assets from key equity benchmarks. MSCI's Proposed Rule Change A preliminary list of ~38 affected companies is circulating, and feedback from investors reportedly leans toward exclusion.MSCI's Proposed Rule ChangeMSCI is consulting on treating "digital asset treasury companies" (firms where crypto/Bitcoin makes up ≥50% of total assets) more like investment funds than operating businesses. Investment funds are ineligible for MSCI's mainstream stock indexes (e.g., MSCI USA, MSCI World, Nasdaq 100 inclusions).This directly targets companies like: Strategy Inc. (formerly MicroStrategy, ticker MSTR) — the largest corporate Bitcoin holder with ~650,000 BTC Some crypto miners (Marathon Digital, Riot Platforms, etc.) A preliminary list of ~38 affected companies is circulating, and feedback from investors reportedly leans toward exclusion. Timeline and Potential Impact MSCI's consultation ends soon, with a final decision expected around January 15, 2026.If exclusion happens: Passive funds/ETFs tracking MSCI indexes would be forced to sell holdings. JPMorgan estimates ~$2.8 billion in outflows from MSCI-tracked funds alone for Strategy/MSTR. Up to $9–11 billion total if Nasdaq, Russell, and others follow suit. Effect on Bitcoin Price Action Strategy (MSTR) has been a popular leveraged Bitcoin proxy for traditional investors — its inclusion in major indexes funneled indirect BTC exposure into pensions, 401(k)s, and broad-market ETFs for years.The looming exclusion risk has already crushed MSTR's premium: The stock is down >60% from its November 2024 peak and trading barely above the spot value of its Bitcoin holdings (mNAV ~1.1× or lower). MSTR has underperformed Bitcoin itself by a wide margin in recent months, largely because of this “index overhang” rather than pure BTC price moves. Broader Bitcoin market pressure comes amid a rough crypto drawdown — BTC is down ~30%+ from its October 2025 all-time high, with the total crypto market cap off over $1 trillion. Forced selling of MSTR (and potentially miners) could spill over: If index funds dump MSTR shares → MSTR price crashes → margin/liquidity issues for the company → potential (though unlikely) need to liquidate some BTC → additional downward pressure on Bitcoin spot price. It would also remove one of the main channels for “stealth” institutional Bitcoin exposure via regular stock portfolios. Current Market Sentiment Markets are pricing in a high probability of exclusion — that's part of why MSTR and mining stocks have been leading the crypto sell-off this week, even as spot Bitcoin ETFs see mixed flows. S&P Dow Jones already effectively snubbed Strategy from the S&P 500 earlier in 2025 for similar “not a real operating company” reasons, so precedent exists. In short: The potential delisting of Bitcoin-heavy companies from major equity indexes is creating a structural headwind for Bitcoin-tied stocks and adding to the current bearish price action in the crypto market. Watch January 2026 closely; if the rule passes, expect a wave of mechanical selling in MSTR and related names that could feed back into Bitcoin sentiment. Now that this news is public, perhaps we can form a bottom. Time will tell.

If this hypothesis is right, it would mean that the structure of the Bitcoin market changed, perhaps definitively, with the penetration of ETFs (something already witnessed in the stock market with the increase of passive flows). Then, one could expect more clustering of volatility around the mean (low vol) and at the tails (large vol events) of the distribution: instances of a calm market and of wild turbulences will become more frequent. **Summary: The “Real Reason” Behind the October 10 Crash** Finally, the full picture of why the market crashed hard on October 10 and never really bounced back is coming into focus. Here’s a beginner-friendly breakdown ────────────────── ① There was a major buyer holding up this entire bull run Companies like MicroStrategy (MSTR) and others that hold massive amounts of Bitcoin (so-called “DAT” companies) have been the big buyers driving the past year’s bull market. ────────────────── ② How the DAT company “mechanism” worked - They buy huge amounts of BTC with their own money → company market cap balloons - High market cap → gets added to major stock indices - Index funds automatically buy the stock - More buying → market cap rises even higher ↑ This created a giant feedback loop, pushing DAT company stock prices higher and higher. ────────────────── ③ Then on October 10, MSCI dropped a bombshell MSCI (the world’s second-largest index provider) said: “Are companies that hold massive amounts of Bitcoin actually operating companies… or should they be treated as investment funds?” If they’re classified as “funds”… ▶ Can’t be included in indices anymore (= buyers disappear) ▶ Any that are already in indices get kicked out ▶ Funds are forced to sell the shares automatically In other words, the scenario of a violent crash in DAT company stocks suddenly became very real. ────────────────── ④ Smart money ran for the exits immediately The October 10 plunge wasn’t random. Pros instantly realized: “Ah, this is bad.” “DATS are going to get sold off.” “This is going to spill over into Bitcoin too.” And they all moved to de-risk at once. That’s exactly why there was no meaningful rebound. ────────────────── ⑤ Key upcoming event MSCI’s final decision comes on January 15, 2026. If they’re treated as funds → DAT companies get removed from indices → domino forced selling → Bitcoin could get dragged down even harder. If they’re treated as regular companies → All the uncertainty vanishes overnight → a new bull run could restart. ────────────────── Conclusion: October 10 was the day smart money priced in a future crash risk ahead of time. The reason we never bounced: - The market’s strongest buyer (DAT companies) suddenly had a cloudy future - Fear spread that the main buyer might disappear completely It was an extremely rational reaction. Selling begat more selling, support lines broke, and the drop continued (exactly as technical analysis had been warning). So… is everyone down money right now? Or are some of you actually up? No matter what the market throws at us, let’s keep moving like it’s a sports match—beautiful formations and all

Keiser’s confidence comes from a long track record of early predictions. He was covering Bitcoin when it traded for cents and publicly projected six-figure prices while it was still near a dollar. I wanted to give everyone something meaningful, a gift… This comes from Global Macro Investor (GMI) and a deep, long-running body of research developed by RaoulGMI and myself. Many of you already know The Everything Code, which is our framework for understanding the macro landscape and why major central banks are debasing their currencies to manage aging demographics and overwhelming debt loads. I call this a gift because these four charts, while only scratching the surface of The Everything Code, give you the big-picture context you actually need in moments like this. They stop you from getting lost in every Bitcoin pullback and explain why Raoul and I never panic, even when, to borrow one of his expressions, everyone’s acting like monkeys throwing poo at each other. Once you understand The Everything Code, you stop trading short-term noise and expand your time horizon. You cannot unsee it. The starting point is what we call The Magic Formula: GDP growth = population growth + productivity growth + debt growth. Population growth and productivity growth have been falling for decades. Debt growth is the only thing filling the gap. The private sector has been deleveraging since 2008, mainly households, but debt levels are still around 120% of GDP. The public sector sits at roughly the same level. Here’s the problem… If the government is running debt at 100% of GDP and the private sector is sitting on another 100%, and for simple math we call rates 2% even though they are really closer to 4%, then the entire 2% trend growth of the economy is being consumed by servicing private-sector debts. That is a completely unproductive use of GDP. And then there’s the issue of public-sector debts. There’s just not enough organic growth to service the existing debt load. To understand why this dynamic persists, you need demographics. Birth rates peaked in the late 1950s and have been declining ever since. This shows up about sixteen years later in the labor force participation rate as each generation enters the workforce (chart 1). That means the labor force participation rate is not going to rise any time soon. It is set to keep drifting lower. This is a structural problem. Aging populations, falling birth rates, and rapidly expanding automation make the backdrop even more deflationary. AI and robotics are replacing humans at scale, and we are only at the beginning. This reinforces the need for ongoing stimulus to keep the system functioning. With weak population growth and sluggish productivity, the only way to keep GDP expanding is through debt. Now here’s where it gets interesting… Government debt growth is completely offsetting the demographic decline and policymakers know exactly what they are doing (chart 2). And what happens next? All debt growth in excess of GDP gets monetized (chart 3). Basically, since 2008, magic money has effectively been paying the interest. Governments issue new debt to cover old interest, and once rates fall enough, central banks absorb it onto their balance sheets. So to wrap this up, demographics drive the decline in the labor force. Governments offset that decline with more debt. That debt eventually gets monetized through quantitative easing (QE) style operations, not always directly by the Fed, but through the coordinated ecosystem of the Fed, the Treasury, and the banking system. And the bottom line is that there’s still a massive wall of interest that needs to be monetized, far more than GDP can ever cover. Liquidity is literally the only game in town. And what thrives in a world of perpetual debasement? Bitcoin (chart 4). I know this correction has been painful, but it’s all part of the journey. These periods feel brutal in the moment, then they fade and the trend resumes. This too shall pass… To quote Walter White from Breaking Bad, later echoed by LynAldenContact, nothing stops this train. Solv Protocol's relationship to restaking is primarily as a yield aggregator and liquidity layer for Bitcoin (BTC) that utilizes restaking mechanisms specifically for BTC to generate and diversify returns for its users. SolvProtocol core innovation is SolvBTC, a liquid, 1:1 Bitcoin backed token that allows BTC holders to put their idle assets to work in decentralized finance (DeFi) while maintaining liquidity. ​The connection to restaking can be understood through two main points: ​1. Yield Sourcing via Restaking Protocols ​Solv Protocol uses restaking platforms and mechanisms to source high quality yield for the Bitcoin backing the SolvBTC token. ​Restaking for BTC: While protocols like EigenLayer initially focused on restaking staked Ethereum (ETH) and Liquid Staking Tokens (LSTs), platforms like Babylon have emerged to enable restaking for native BTC. ​Integrating with Providers: Solv Protocol leverages these underlying protocols (such as Babylon, EigenLayer, and Symbiotic) to take the staked BTC assets and "restake" them. ​Diversified Rewards: This enables the staked BTC to secure other decentralized protocols (Actively Validated Services or AVSs) and earn additional rewards on top of the base staking yield. Solv Protocol abstracts this complexity away from the end user, distributing the accumulated restaking yields and other DeFi earnings back to SolvBTC holders. ​2. Liquid Staking and Enhanced Capital Efficiency ​SolvBTC itself functions as a Liquid Staking Token (LST) for Bitcoin, which is a prerequisite for liquid restaking. ​LST Generation: When a user deposits BTC into Solv Protocol, they receive SolvBTC. This token represents their staked Bitcoin plus accrued yield, and it can be used across multiple blockchains in other DeFi protocols. ​Capital Efficiency: This architecture achieves the high capital efficiency that restaking promises: ​The original BTC is earning a base staking yield. ​The same BTC is simultaneously earning additional yield by securing other networks via restaking. ​The resulting liquid token, SolvBTC, can also be used as collateral or for liquidity provision in other DeFi applications (lending, trading) to earn further yield. ​ Solv Protocol acts as a unified infrastructure (Staking Abstraction Layer or SAL) that makes the complex process of BTC restaking accessible, liquid, and multi chain, transforming Bitcoin from a passive asset into a dynamic yield generating asset in DeFi

Zcash currently uses public-key encryption as part of making payments anonymous. The encryption we use has the property that the ciphertext can't be linked to the public key (for the destination address) used to encrypt it. But in the case of a quantum adversary, /contd if they know the public key then they can find the private key and decrypt. Working through the Counterparty chapter clarified something that’s been consistent across every attempt to put assets or logic on Bitcoin: Bitcoin is not a state machine — and every protocol that treated it like one eventually ran into the same wall. Ordinals and Atomicals understand this. They use Bitcoin purely as a data availability layer; the real rules, asset semantics, and ordering all live inside the indexer. Wallets are merely interpreters. Different indexers produce different “realities” because Bitcoin is not defining the state — the indexer is. RGB goes further in the correct direction. It abandons global state entirely, moves the state machine to the client, uses cryptographic commitments for correctness, and relies on Bitcoin only for history + data availability. Bitcoin validates Bitcoin; RGB validates RGB. The separation is clean and coherent. Counterparty, in contrast, tried to encode protocol-level state transitions inside Bitcoin’s UTXO spend semantics — as if “spending a UTXO” could express higher-level asset logic. That assumption is incompatible with the UTXO model. Bitcoin’s semantics are minimal: a UTXO is unspent or spent; a script passes or fails. It does not maintain balances, asset supplies, or state transition rules. After tracing all historical paths, two sustainable models emerge: (1) Stateless protocols — Stamps, Ordinals, Atomicals Data = result. Interpretation is off-chain. (2) Off-chain state machines — RGB, Taproot Assets State is local; Bitcoin provides commitments and irreversible history. Everything else is wishful thinking. Asking Bitcoin to “understand your protocol’s state” is asking it to be something it fundamentally is not. Bitcoin is a history machine. Ethereum is a state machine. Confusing the two is what caused Counterparty’s limitations — and the lesson keeps repeating. Bitcoin BitcoinOG bitcoinbuilder

To anyone getting bored with Bitcoin price action: The S&P500 index is known to only have a few days during a year when most all the investment gains are made, what are the statistics on that and what is it like for Bitcoin? The well-known statistic about the S&P 500 illustrates the high concentration of returns in a small number of trading days, underscoring the risks of market timing. Based on historical daily data for the SPY ETF (a close proxy for the S&P 500) from 1993 to November 25, 2025, the average annual return across 32 full years was 9.88%. However, if the 10 best trading days each year are excluded, that average drops sharply to -12.25%. In other words, those top 10 days (out of roughly 252 trading days per year) account for essentially all the positive performance, turning what would otherwise be a losing strategy into a winner. This pattern holds over longer periods too—for instance, over the past 30 years, missing the 10 best days overall would have reduced total returns by more than half, while missing the 30 best days would have slashed them by about 83%. Bitcoin exhibits an even more extreme version of this phenomenon, consistent with its higher volatility. Using daily closing price data from September 17, 2014 (the start of reliable exchange-traded data) to November 25, 2025, Bitcoin’s average annual return across 11 full years was an astonishing 172.25%. Excluding just the 10 best days each year flips this to -12.43%—meaning nearly all gains are crammed into those few explosive sessions, with the rest of the year effectively underwater. Extending the analysis, missing the 30 best days per year for Bitcoin would reduce the average annual return to a mere 1.45%, highlighting how its upside is hyper-concentrated compared to the S&P 500. To arrive at these figures, the calculation involves: 1Fetching daily closing prices and computing simple daily returns: ( r_t = \frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}} ), where ( P_t ) is the closing price on day ( t ). 2Grouping returns by calendar year. 3For each year with at least 10 trading days, computing the full annual return as ( \prod (1 + r_t) - 1 ). 4Sorting that year’s daily returns in descending order and recomputing the “missed” annual return using all days except the top 10: ( \prod (1 + r_t \text{ for the bottom } n-10) - 1 ), where ( n ) is the number of days that year. 5Averaging the full and missed annual returns across all qualifying years. This per-year approach captures the “few days during a year” dynamic directly, as opposed to a lump-sum over the full period (which would understate the concentration by spreading misses across decades). Both assets reward staying invested through volatility, as attempting to sidestep downturns often means missing the exact days that drive compounding. Still feel like “timing the market” Anon?

The early material is plain on what the target was: the trust structure of fiat issuance and of banks operating inside state-backed credit cycles. In 2009, the point was that conventional currency requires trusting a central bank not to debase, and trusting banks not to abuse fractional reserves and privacy. That is a critique of a system of trust and incentives, not a manifesto to “replace central banks” as an abstract political end in itself. Read the Genesis block headline for what it is: a timestamp welded to a newspaper line about a bailout, and a contextual jab at the government–bank rescue loop. It’s about the state stepping in to socialise losses and the banking sector relying on that backstop. It is not some childish “burn all central banks” rallying cry; it’s evidence of the climate that made a cash-like system necessary in the first place. So when someone says “everything he said is wrong” and then waves the February 2009 passage like a flag, they’re sawing off the branch they’re sitting on. That passage doesn’t say “Bitcoin was meant to replace central banks”; it says the existing model forces people to trust central banks and banks, and that history shows those trusts get breached. It’s diagnosis, not your preferred religion. The rest is rhetorical overreach dressed up as certainty. A digital cash system can coexist with fiat, be used by people who still live under governments, and even be priced or accounted in state units. None of that contradicts the design goal. What contradicts it is pretending the goal was a utopian demolition project, then acting smug because you’ve misread your own exhibit. Get the target right: the problem was not “central banks exist”; the problem was a world where money and payments are mediated by institutions that routinely break trust, with the state standing behind them when they do. If you can’t keep that distinction straight, stop telling anyone else what the system was “always meant” to do.

Result: As demand grows → block capacity expands → confirmations stay smooth. --- 2. Larger Network = Faster Propagation More full nodes worldwide = faster propagation of block data.
