Why Bitcoin is the Only Engineered Truth and Voluntary Opt-Out Capable of Protecting Your Time and Energy from the Devaluation of Political Currency In an era where governments print money at will, the value of your hard-earned savings erodes silently. Inflation, often dismissed as a natural economic phenomenon, is in reality a subtle tax on your time and energy. Every hour you work, every ounce of effort you expend, is converted into currency that loses purchasing power over time due to deliberate policy decisions. This devaluation isn't accidental; it's inherent to fiat currencies, money backed by nothing but government decree and public trust. Amid this financial sleight of hand, Bitcoin emerges not as just another asset, but as the singular engineered truth: a decentralized, immutable system that offers a voluntary escape hatch from this coercive monetary regime. It protects your wealth by enforcing scarcity and transparency in a way no other invention can. This article explores why Bitcoin stands alone in this role, safeguarding the fruits of your labor against the relentless grind of political currency manipulation. The Curse of Fiat Currency Devaluation To understand Bitcoin's revolutionary potential, we must first grasp the flaws of the system it challenges. Fiat money, untethered from physical commodities like gold since the 1970s, derives its value solely from government mandate. Central banks, such as the Federal Reserve, can expand the money supply at their discretion, often to fund deficits, bailouts, or stimulus programs. This leads to inflation, where more units of currency chase the same goods and services, diminishing each unit's worth. Historical examples abound. In Venezuela, hyperinflation reached 65,000% in 2018, rendering the bolívar worthless and forcing citizens to barter or flee. Zimbabwe's 2008 crisis saw inflation hit 79.6 billion percent monthly, turning savings into dust overnight. Even in stable economies like the United States, the dollar has lost over 96% of its purchasing power since 1913, when the Fed was established. What cost $1 then requires about $30 today. This devaluation isn't just numbers on a ledger; it steals your time. The hours you worked last year buy less food, housing, or education this year, effectively forcing you to run faster on a treadmill that's speeding up. Governments benefit from this system. Inflation acts as a hidden tax, reducing real debt burdens while eroding citizens' wealth. Borrowers, often states or corporations, win, while savers and wage earners lose. In a fiat world, your energy is funneled into a currency designed to depreciate, compelling constant consumption or risky investments to stay afloat. Traditional hedges like gold offer some protection but are cumbersome, taxable, and subject to confiscation, as seen in the U.S. in 1933. Stocks and real estate tie you to volatile markets influenced by the same political whims. None provide a true opt-out; they're all entangled in the fiat web. Bitcoin as Engineered Truth Enter Bitcoin, launched in 2009 amid the global financial crisis. Unlike fiat, Bitcoin isn't declared valuable by decree, it's engineered to embody truth through mathematics and code. At its core is the blockchain: a distributed ledger where every transaction is recorded immutably across thousands of nodes worldwide. No single entity controls it; consensus is achieved via proof-of-work, where miners compete to solve complex puzzles, expending real energy to validate blocks. This isn't arbitrary; it's a deliberate design to make altering history prohibitively expensive. Bitcoin's "truth" lies in its verifiability. Anyone can audit the entire supply, capped at 21 million coins, ensuring no hidden inflation. Fiat systems rely on opaque central banks; Bitcoin's protocol is open-source, scrutinized by millions. This engineering eliminates trust in fallible institutions, replacing it with cryptographic proof. As APompliano notes, Bitcoin is humanity's best bet against currency debasement because it can't be inflated or confiscated easily. In a world of lies and manipulation, Bitcoin is truth incarnate: predictable, unchangeable, and resistant to political interference. This truth extends to its scarcity. While fiat can be printed infinitely, Bitcoin's halving events every four years reduce new supply, mimicking digital gold but with superior properties like divisibility (down to satoshis) and portability. As adoption grows, demand for this fixed asset drives value appreciation, countering fiat's dilution. It's not speculative hype; it's a mathematical inevitability in an inflationary environment. The Voluntary Opt-Out Mechanism What sets Bitcoin apart is its voluntary nature. Fiat is imposed; you're forced to use dollars, euros, or yuan for taxes, debts, and daily life, with no easy escape. Bitcoin, however, is an opt-in system. You choose to acquire it, hold it, or spend it without permission from any authority. Wallets are pseudonymous, borders irrelevant, send value globally in minutes without intermediaries. This opt-out defunds the state indirectly. By shifting savings to Bitcoin, you withdraw from the inflationary cycle, starving governments of seigniorage profits from money creation. It's peaceful resistance: no violence, just code. In countries like Argentina or Turkey, where currencies crumble, citizens flock to Bitcoin for stability, proving its real-world utility as an escape. Unlike centralized alternatives, Bitcoin's decentralization ensures no one can shut it down, attempts to ban it only highlight its resilience. Critics argue cryptocurrencies could replace fiat entirely, but Bitcoin's voluntary ethos ensures it coexists, allowing gradual adoption. It's not coercive; it's empowering. Protecting Time and Energy At its essence, money represents stored time and energy, your life's work quantified. Fiat devalues this by design, forcing you to work harder for diminishing returns. Bitcoin reverses this. As a deflationary asset, its value tends to rise over time due to scarcity and network effects, preserving and potentially multiplying your purchasing power. Holding Bitcoin means your past efforts appreciate, not depreciate. Consider: Since 2010, Bitcoin has outperformed every major asset class, turning modest investments into fortunes amid fiat erosion. It's a hedge against inflation, as seen in 2022 when U.S. inflation hit 9.1%, yet Bitcoin rebounded as a safe haven. Institutions like MicroStrategy and Tesla allocate billions to Bitcoin for this reason, viewing it as superior to cash reserves that bleed value. Moreover, Bitcoin's energy-intensive mining ties it to real-world costs, creating a "proof-of-energy" that mirrors human effort. This isn't wasteful; it's a feature ensuring security and aligning value with expended work. In contrast, fiat printing requires no such sacrifice, leading to moral hazard. Why Only Bitcoin? Other cryptocurrencies exist, but none match Bitcoin's uniqueness. Altcoins like Ethereum introduce features like smart contracts, but often at the cost of centralization or infinite supply. Bitcoin's proof-of-work is the most secure, with a hashrate dwarfing competitors, making attacks infeasible. Its market cap, over $1 trillion as of late 2025, provides liquidity and stability absent in smaller tokens. Bitcoin's immutability is key; changes require overwhelming consensus, preventing founder-led manipulations seen in other projects. It's not just another crypto, it's the original, battle-tested protocol with the strongest network effects. Skeptics like Eugene Fama predict Bitcoin's demise, but its survival through bans and crashes proves otherwise. Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) are fiat in disguise, offering surveillance without protection. In volatility lies opportunity; Bitcoin's risk is offset by its asymmetric upside in a devaluing world. It's the only asset truly decoupled from political currencies. Conclusion Bitcoin isn't mere speculation, it's a lifeline in a sea of devaluation. As the only engineered truth, it enforces honesty in a dishonest system. As a voluntary opt-out, it empowers individuals to reclaim their time and energy from fiat's grasp. In a future where debt spirals and inflation rages, Bitcoin stands as the ultimate protector. Whether you're a skeptic or believer, the math is clear: opt in, or watch your efforts fade. The choice is yours, voluntarily

How to read OrderFlow? Here comes another quick guide on how to read OrderFlow like a pro and how you can profit from market-generated information. /Introduction: OrderFlow is not another indicator or strategy. It’s simply a visualization of how the market actually works. Instead of only seeing open, high, low, and close on a standard candlestick chart, OrderFlow lets you see the real-time interaction between buyers and sellers, including the volume traded at each price level. /How the market works: If you trade the market, you need to understand how it works first! Markets operate as a two-way auction. On one side, market buyers transact with limit sellers. On the other, market sellers transact with limit buyers. Market orders never trade with other market orders, and limit orders never trade with other limit orders! Limit orders sit in the OrderBook and provide liquidity. Market orders execute immediately by consuming that liquidity. From here on, we’ll refer to traders who execute at market as "aggressive traders", and traders who place limit orders and wait for execution as "passive traders". So when and why does price move? Let's say a large aggressive sell order hits the market; for example, a 5M contract market sell. To execute the order we need a 5M limit buy order on the other side. If we look at the current OrderBook (see picture, right side, in blue = limit buys), we can see that at the current price (87,950) there aren’t enough contracts resting on the bid. The order can’t be fully filled there, so price has to move lower to find more passive buyers and enough liquidity to complete the execution. Price does not move lower because there are more buyers than sellers. Price moves because one side is more aggressive, starts crossing the spread and there isn’t enough liquidity at the current price! /OrderFlow: If you understand how the two-way auction works, you can watch it play out in real time using OrderFlow and so-called footprint charts (provided, for example, by ExochartsC). On the left side of the picture you see a footprint candle chart, showing aggressive sell orders on the left side of each candle and aggressive buy orders on the right. Those are actually executed orders: market orders that got matched with limit orders. You could also say that the left side of each candle shows limit buy orders executed by market sell orders. But for OrderFlow analysis, we focus on the aggressive side of the market, the market orders, because only aggression consumes liquidity and drives price discovery. So It shows intent, because aggressive orders reveal who is actively forcing price to move. Thus we say we got market sells on the left and market buys on the right. Now it gets really interesting when price does not follow the aggression. For example, you see a lot of aggressive market buying (large numbers on the right side of the candle), but price doesn’t move higher. That tells you passive limit sellers are providing liquidity and absorbing the aggressive buyers. The buyers are essentially "hitting a wall". That’s extremely valuable information you can use in your trading. /How to trade with OrderFlow (OI, CVD, ...) (next post coming soon...) 2025 is ending… and if you’ve been in crypto long enough, this year probably felt strange. Not painful like a bear market. Not euphoric like a real bull run. Just… flat. Controlled. Uneventful. We were conditioned by history to expect fireworks. 2017 ICO mania, overnight millionaires, pure chaos 2021 NFTs, DeFi summer, BTC at $60K+, retail FOMO everywhere So naturally, expectations for 2025 were sky-high. Halving done. Liquidity narrative ready. Macro supposedly lining up. And yet… nothing close to the classic cycle played out. Bitcoin primed at $121k ETH shipped upgrades, price barely cared Memecoins pumped for days, not months Retail never truly arrived No grandma asking about Solana. No across-the-board 10x. No euphoric “everything only goes up” phase. Instead, what we got was something very different. A market that feels engineered A cycle that feels capped A space that suddenly looks… institutional And that raises the uncomfortable question: Has crypto turned into just another Wall Street playground? Let’s break it down. The institutional takeover is real Not loud. Not emotional. Surgical. BlackRock. Fidelity. TradFi giants. They didn’t come for decentralization. They came for asymmetric upside and control. They accumulated aggressively during 2022–2023 They pushed ETFs through regulation-friendly channels They hedge with derivatives, dampening volatility They play multi-year games while retail chases candles The result? A market that moves slower. Cleaner charts. Less chaos. But also… less opportunity for uninformed retail. It feels less like the Wild West. More like the NYSE with wallets. The halving that didn’t ignite The 2024 halving was supposed to be the catalyst. Instead, it was absorbed. Miners are now corporations, not cypherpunks Energy costs are hedged and optimized Supply shock was priced in years ago by quants No panic buying, no reflexive melt-up The halving didn’t fail. It just wasn’t dramatic - because the players changed. Regulation tightened the noose 2025 was the year compliance went mainstream. SEC pressure on DeFi MiCA turning Europe into paperwork hell UAE and others tightening KYC Every serious project now needs lawyers before devs This isn’t about protecting investors. It’s about controlling access. Small builders get squeezed. Big players navigate effortlessly. AI stole the spotlight While crypto chopped sideways, AI exploded. Capital rotated into GPUs and models VCs chased AI narratives Blockchain funding slowed Institutions focused on tokenization and CBDCs The irony? Crypto was built to disrupt. Instead, TradFi adopted the parts it could control. Volatility down, upside capped They call it market maturity. But let’s be honest. Flash crashes are bot-driven Pumps are fund-coordinated Retail exits become liquidity The house is smarter now Lower volatility sounds good — until you realize volatility was the opportunity. So… is this depressing? A little. It does feel like the soul of crypto is being polished into something safe, regulated, and profitable for institutions. But zoom out - this isn’t the end. It’s a transition. And transitions create opportunity for those who adapt. Here’s the bullish case no one talks about enough. Real utility finally matters Hype is fading. Builders remain. Layer-2s scaling real usage Zero-knowledge tech maturing RWAs tokenizing real value DeFi becoming actual financial infrastructure By 2026–2028, crypto won’t just be speculation. It’ll be plumbing. Retail doesn’t disappear — it evolves Retail isn’t dead. It’s learning. On-chain analytics are public Wallet tracking exposes whale behavior ETFs normalize crypto exposure Education replaces blind FOMO The next retail wave won’t be manic. It’ll be smarter. Macro still favors crypto Zoom out beyond price charts. Fiat currencies continue to weaken Inflation isn’t “solved” Emerging markets rely on stablecoins Bitcoin as digital collateral keeps strengthening Institutions can’t fake organic global adoption. Innovation never dies — it reloads Crypto moves in waves. The next one could be: AI + blockchain convergence Decentralized social Privacy tech Quantum-resistant systems Institutions bring capital. Builders bring disruption. That tension is where breakthroughs happen. Final thoughts as 2025 closes This wasn’t the bull run many expected. But it might be the foundation for something bigger. Crypto didn’t die. It grew up. The easy money phase is gone. The asymmetric opportunity phase isn’t. Stack smart. Build skills. Follow fundamentals, not noise. Let institutions lay rails - you position for what runs on top. 2026 and beyond won’t reward tourists. They’ll reward conviction. The bull run that wasn’t… might just be the calm before the real shift. So tell me - Are you bearish because it feels controlled? Or bullish because control always cracks eventually? Onward. Here is the summary of the response: PoW and PoS are two primary consensus mechanisms used by blockchains to secure the network and validate transactions. The key difference lies in the resource used to achieve consensus: - Proof-of-Work (PoW): Uses computational power and energy consumption to secure the network. Miners compete to solve complex mathematical puzzles to propose new blocks and earn rewards. - Proof-of-Stake (PoS): Uses economic capital (staked tokens) to secure the network. Validators are selected based on the size of their stake to propose or vote on new blocks. • Key Features and Benefits Of Proof Of Work: - Security tied to energy burned - Non sovereign alternative to money - Examples: Bitcoin, Ethereum Classic • Key Features and Benefits Of Proof Of Stake: - More scalable and energy efficient - Validators are incentivized to act honestly through economic penalties - Examples: Ethereum, Algorand, Fantom

From my perspective mUSD fees are not designed to maximize revenue but to enforce discipline and long term stability. The Teenager Who Took Over Twitter and Lost Everything In July 2020, Twitter experienced one of the most embarrassing security breaches in its history. Some of the biggest accounts on the platform, including those belonging to Elon Musk, Barack Obama, Bill Gates, and Kanye West, suddenly began posting the same message. The tweets claimed that if people sent Bitcoin to a specific address, they would receive double the amount back. Many people initially believed the hack was carried out by a powerful foreign group or an advanced cybercrime ring. However, investigators later discovered that the main person behind the attack was a seventeen-year-old boy named Graham Ivan Clark, who lived in Florida. Graham did not hack Twitter by breaking complex code or exploiting deep technical flaws. Instead, he used social engineering. He contacted Twitter employees and pretended to be part of the company’s internal IT team. By speaking confidently and sounding legitimate, he convinced them to give him access to internal tools that allowed him to reset and control high-profile accounts. After gaining access, Graham and others involved in the scheme used the hacked accounts to run the Bitcoin scam. Although the attack was successful for a short period, it did not last long. Graham made a critical mistake by bragging about what he had done in private online chats. Screenshots of these conversations began circulating, and investigators were quickly able to connect the dots. Law enforcement tracked him down within days. His home was searched, and his laptop and phone were seized. At the age of seventeen, Graham was arrested and charged, and his life changed permanently.

Why Liquidity Matters More Than Exchange Names in 2026 What does liquidity really mean when trading crypto today? Liquidity is simply how easy it is to buy or sell without moving the price too much, In 2026, that matters more than ever because crypto trades 24/7 and price swings can be fast, Good liquidity shows up as tight spreads, deep order books close to market price, and low slippage. Volume alone isn’t enough, real liquidity is about how markets behave when things get volatile, This is why many traders now look at order book depth within 1–2%, spread stability, and execution quality, not just big volume numbers. Which exchanges actually carry most of the market liquidity in 2026? A small group of platforms now handles most global spot and derivatives activity. The most liquid exchanges this year are: Binance Still the largest by overall volume, with deep liquidity on major spot pairs and strong dominance in perpetual futures, though conditions vary by asset during volatility. Bitget Has grown quickly into a top-tier venue, with especially deep derivatives liquidity and expanding spot markets. Strong BTC and ETH perpetual depth, plus steady spot activity on major pairs. Coinbase Liquidity is concentrated in fiat-based spot markets like BTC/USD and ETH/USD. Fewer assets and derivatives, but stable execution on major pairs. Bybit Liquidity is mainly in derivatives, especially BTC and ETH perpetuals. Spot markets are smaller, but futures depth is often strong. Kraken A long running exchange with solid spot liquidity in fiat pairs. More conservative structure, limited derivatives and altcoin depth. KuCoin Broad asset coverage with liquidity spread across many tokens. Stronger in popular altcoins, while newer listings can have wider spreads. MEXC Liquidity often centers around new and high-volatility listings. Depth can shift fast, making execution less consistent across markets. Why do derivatives now dominate liquidity and what does that change for traders? By 2026, more than 70% of crypto trading volume comes from derivatives, especially perpetual futures. These markets offer leverage, easier shorting, and high capital efficiency, so price discovery often happens there first. Spot markets still matter for long term holders, fiat access, and actual asset ownership, but they carry less volume overall. This shift means traders often use derivatives for liquidity and hedging, while relying on spot markets for settlement and longer term positions. It also increases liquidation risk and short term price swings during stress. The Bottom line Liquidity shapes execution quality, costs, and risk more than almost any other factor in crypto trading today. Binance, Bitget, Coinbase, Bybit, Kraken, KuCoin, and MEXC each play different roles, with liquidity strengths that depend on asset type and market structure. Choosing an exchange in 2026 means looking past headline volume and focusing on depth, spreads, and how markets behave when conditions aren’t calm. FAQ •What does liquidity mean in crypto? How easily you can trade without moving the price. •Which exchanges are most liquid in 2026? Binance, Bitget, Coinbase, Bybit, Kraken, KuCoin, and MEXC. •Where is Bitcoin liquidity strongest? Mostly on large exchanges in both spot and perpetual futures markets. •Why do derivatives dominate? Leverage, efficiency, and constant demand drive higher activity. •Is volume enough to judge liquidity? No depth, spreads, and execution matter more.

Vitalik Buterin is quietly describing 'Ethereum 3.0' - and most people are sleeping on it While CT keeps running the "ETH is dead" loop, VitalikButerin keeps dropping posts that are... honestly structural. His latest take is basically: now that PeerDAS is already live on mainnet, and ZK-EVMs are "alpha" (performance is there, safety hardening remains), Ethereum is moving from replicated work -> truly distributed work. He frames it with two historical extremes: BitTorrent (2000) = insane bandwidth + decentralization, but no shared truth. Bitcoin (2009) = shared truth + decentralization, but low bandwidth, because every node has to redo everyone else's work. Ethereum with PeerDAS + ZK-EVMs is the first time we get a real third option: high bandwidth + consensus + decentralization - not as a whitepaper, but as live code (PeerDAS now, ZK-EVM rollout starting in 2026). In human terms: > PeerDAS makes data availability cheaper to verify because nodes can check small random samples instead of downloading everything. > ZK-EVM validation is the shift where you don't need every node to re-execute every block to trust it - you verify a proof. And that's why Vitalik is confident saying "the trilemma is solved" in practice. What happens next (the part that matters for markets, not just nerds): the next ~4 years are basically an aggressive "scale the base layer safely" roadmap - higher gas limits, repricings / state tweaks to keep it stable, and eventually ZK becoming the primary way blocks get validated. The other underrated part: distributed block building. The long-term goal is a world where a full block is never assembled "in one room" - which is how you reduce censorship risk, reduce single points of interference, and make inclusion more geographically fair. So yeah... if you wondered what the real ETH bull case looks like in 2026-2030, it's this shift: from "everyone repeats everything" -> "the network splits the load, but keeps Bitcoin-level guarantees".

Fogo: Designing Market Infrastructure Where Rules, Not Narratives, Win The podcast with RobertSagurton is less about fogo as a product and more about a diagnosis of why most onchain markets fail to mature. The core argument is uncomfortable but precise: crypto’s main problem is not speculation, meme coins, or retail behavior, but infrastructure that was never designed for professional grade markets. Speculative assets are not inherently broken. What breaks them are chaotic launch mechanics, shallow liquidity, unclear execution rules, and systems that reward latency arbitrage instead of real price discovery. With proper market structure, even highly speculative assets can sustain liquidity without collapsing into extraction games. This is where onchain trading still lags centralized venues. Most blockchains optimize for general purpose computation, not trading. They are slow to cancel orders, fragile during volatility spikes, and highly vulnerable to latency based arbitrage. Without infrastructure that prioritizes market makers, liquidity decays and markets stagnate. Fogo starts from this failure mode. It is not a blockchain for everything, but a blockchain for trading. Its architecture centers on a Central Limit Order Book, minimal latency, and execution logic modeled closer to CME or Binance than DeFi first abstractions. This narrowing of scope is intentional. Specialization is the strategy. A key design choice is equality enforced at the protocol level. There are no privileged applications, special execution paths, or hand tuned advantages. All DEXs and perpetual protocols operate under the same rules. Permissionless here is not marketing, but a structural constraint. Hyperliquid is acknowledged as a meaningful step forward. It proved that low latency onchain trading is possible. But its limits are structural: closed source code, speed ceilings, and limited composability. These constraints introduce trust assumptions and cap ecosystem evolution. Fogo takes the core insight and removes the ceiling by being open, composable, and fully observable. This reflects a broader pattern. Meaningful innovation rarely comes from incremental change within existing networks. Bitcoin did not evolve into Ethereum. Ethereum did not evolve into Solana. Each leap required a new architecture because entrenched systems resist radical change. The case for onchain markets is practical, not ideological. Transparent rules, equal access, and permissionless launches remove gatekeepers, listing fees, and opaque advantages. Rules are visible and enforced by code. High frequency trading is framed correctly: not as a villain, but as infrastructure. Market makers provide liquidity, narrow spreads, and improve execution quality for everyone. Co location reduces information asymmetry by compressing latency in a controlled environment. Open source is non negotiable. Closed systems invite suspicion. Transparency lowers barriers to entry, accelerates ecosystem development, and makes manipulation harder to hide. Trust is not declared. It is engineered. Launching an L1 is a brutal, multi year grind with a high probability of failure. Networks built for narrative or status rarely survive. Networks built to solve a specific structural problem at least have a chance. Fogo’s positioning reflects restraint. Compatibility with Solana, operating effectively as a different RPC layer, higher speed, and a focus on lower stakes applications to survive early instability. This is survivability engineering, not maximalism. The takeaway is not about tokens or memes. It is about infrastructure that enforces fairness, minimizes latency, and aligns incentives at the system level. Markets do not need better stories. They need better rules. In the long run, winners are not the loudest or the most speculative. They are the ones who design environments where execution is fast, access is equal, and rules matter more than narratives. fogo RobertSagurton im_jowee

Post 7 of talking about citrea_xyz How batch proofs work:- Batch proofs are what make zk-rollups like Citrea fast, cheap, and secure. Instead of sending every transaction to Bitcoin one by one, Citrea groups many transactions into a single batch. Here’s the flow in human terms: • users make transactions normally • Citrea executes them off-chain • all transactions are grouped together • a zero-knowledge proof is generated to prove every transaction was valid • that single proof is published on Bitcoin Bitcoin doesn’t recheck each transaction. It just verifies the proof. Why this is powerful: • thousands of transactions → one Bitcoin verification • massively reduced fees • faster confirmation times • full Bitcoin security preserved Think of batch proofs like submitting one perfectly checked report instead of thousands of homework pages.

I was digging through the NY Fed’s data this morning and found something pretty incredible. Their Corporate Bond Market Distress Index (CMDI) just hit 0.06. That is effectively an all-time low. If you aren't familiar with this index, it basically measures how hard it is for companies to borrow money and how stressed the market is about defaults. To put 0.06 in perspective: > During the Covid crash (2020), this number was around 0.60. > During the 2008 Financial Crisis, it was near 0.80. We are currently at the complete opposite end of the spectrum. The bond market is signaling that conditions are healthier than they have ever been. There is zero fear in the system. When the corporate bond market is this boring and stable, yields get compressed. We’ve already seen the High Yield Bond ETF (HYG) return over 8% last year, which makes those bonds expensive to buy now. Historically, when traditional credit markets get too expensive and offer low returns, capital is forced to move further out on the risk curve to find growth. Investors stop buying bonds and start looking for assets with higher upside. That capital rotation usually benefits assets like Tech and Crypto. We are in a macro Goldilocks zone. As long as that index stays near zero, the liquidity backdrop for Bitcoin and the broader market is incredibly strong. But this is also where caution matters. A reading of 0.06 means the market is priced for near perfection. This is classic Minsky behavior. When risk feels absent, leverage rises and hedging drops. Any surprise, inflation, rates, geopolitics, would hit a market that is not prepared for it. So, the question is: Do you trust this silence, or are you hedging for the inevitable volatility that follows a period of zero risk? h/t: The Kobeissi Letter

Bank runs are not a failure of confidence. They are just a consequence of design. In traditional banking, deposits are not fully held. They are promised. The same unit of money is lent multiple times, while the system assumes not everyone will ask for it back at once. When that assumption fails, the system breaks, people have to trust traditional banking. The solution offered has always been the same, withdrawal limits, emergency closures, central bank intervention, or inflation to paper over the gap. These measures protect the system, not the depositor. Scarce digital currencies change this dynamic at the root. With Bitcoin, there is no maturity mismatch. No rehypothecation by default. No hidden leverage behind a balance sheet entry. If you hold the keys, you hold the asset. There is no promise. There is only ownership. A bank run is impossible when reserves are provable, fixed, and held directly. You do not need to trust that liquidity exists. You can verify it. Scarcity matters because it removes discretion. No authority can create more units to stabilize a failure. No institution can dilute holders to rescue itself. Traditional banking relies on confidence and backstops. Scarce digital money relies on math and finality. One system asks you to believe withdrawals will be honored. The other allows you to exit at any time without permission. Not “better prompts” Not “bigger models” But making intelligence itself verifiable, auditable and user owned. Why is this hard? Because intelligence isn’t static like a ledger entry. So when OpenGradient says the hardest problem is Verifiable Intelligence, it’s not marketing. It’s recognizing the same pattern crypto has followed for 15 years and pushing it one layer higher. The future isn’t just decentralized money or compute. It’s decentralized trust in intelligence itself. And like every major crypto shift before it, it starts by replacing belief with proof. P2P (Peer-to-Peer) trading is a method of exchanging cryptocurrencies directly between individuals without intermediaries like traditional exchanges. In P2P trading, buyers and sellers are matched on a platform, but the actual transaction happens directly between them. The platform acts as an escrow service, holding the cryptocurrency until both parties confirm the transaction is complete. How it works: A seller lists their cryptocurrency with a price, a buyer accepts the offer, pays the seller directly via bank transfer or other payment methods, and once payment is confirmed, the platform releases the crypto from escrow to the buyer. StandX Maker Points System StandX offers a “Maker” (Market Maker) points system where your limit orders are rewarded even if the trade does not get executed. So how can you earn points by simply waiting on the order book without taking risk? Let’s review the system with technical details, but in a simple way. 1 ⃣ What’s the logic? Normally, on exchanges, when a trade is executed (fill), you pay fees or you make a profit/loss. On StandX, simply posting your order to the book (Limit Order) and keeping it within a certain proximity to the price is enough to earn points. The goal is to provide liquidity (depth) to the exchange. 2 ⃣ Key term: What is BPS (Basis Points)? The system measures your distance to price in “bps” (basis points). Don’t let this term intimidate you. It simply means a percentage slice. • 100 bps = 1.00% (one percent) • 10 bps = 0.10% (one-tenth of a percent) So when someone says “the 10 bps range,” they mean 0.10% below or above the current Bitcoin price. 3 ⃣ Earning tiers (Distance to price) To earn points, there are 3 different zones based on your distance to the reference price (Mark Price). The closer you are to the center, the higher the multiplier: Zone 1 (High Return): 0 - 10 bps (0% to 0.10%) This is the closest zone to price, where your order has the highest chance of being filled. • Reward: You earn points at a 100% rate based on your order size. Zone 2 (Medium Return): 10 - 30 bps (0.10% to 0.30%) This is a slightly safer distance. • Reward: You earn points at a 50% rate based on your order. Zone 3 (Low Risk): 30 - 100 bps (0.30% to 1.00%) This is the widest band where you can move away from price up to 1%. • Reward: You earn points at a 10% rate based on your order. 4 ⃣ Let’s do an example calculation Using an example scenario where Bitcoin is priced at 90,000 USD, let’s list the exact price equivalents for 10, 30, and 100 bps (basis points) both downward (Long/Buy) and upward (Short/Sell). Dollar equivalents of basis points First, to understand the calculation, let’s clarify the percentage slices (bps) on 90,000$: • 10 bps (0.10%): equals a 90-dollar difference. • 30 bps (0.30%): equals a 270-dollar difference. • 100 bps (1.00%): equals a 900-dollar difference. Point zones for Buy (Long) orders If you want to collect points by placing orders below the price, the valid ranges when moving down from 90,000 dollars are: • 100% Maker points zone (Highest Points - 100%): This is the closest zone to price. If you place your order between 89,910 dollars and 90,000 dollars, you earn the highest points. • 50% Maker points zone (Medium Points - 50%): This is a slightly safer distance. If you place your order between 89,730 dollars and 89,910 dollars, you earn half points. • 10% Maker points zone (Low Points - 10%): This is the farthest and safest zone. If you place your order between 89,100 dollars and 89,730 dollars, you earn low points. Point zones for Sell (Short) orders If you want to collect points by placing orders above the price, the valid ranges when moving up from 90,000 dollars are: • Highest Points - 100%: If you place your order between 90,000 dollars and 90,090 dollars, you earn the highest points. • Medium Points - 50%: If you place your order between 90,090 dollars and 90,270 dollars, you earn half points. • Low Points - 10%: If you place your order between 90,270 dollars and 90,900 dollars, you earn low points. Important note: For your orders to earn points, they must remain on the book for at least 3 seconds. Because the price moves constantly (for example, when it moves from 90,000 to 90,005, all boundaries change), instead of placing orders exactly on the boundary line, placing them slightly inside the range (toward the middle) prevents you from losing points during price fluctuations. 5 ⃣ Examples of Market Maker points you can earn based on order size: In the StandX Maker Points system, the amount of points you earn per day is calculated by multiplying your order’s total dollar value by its proximity to the price. • In the example scenario, the Bitcoin price is assumed to be 90,000 USD. Based on this price, the daily points you can earn with limit orders sized at 1 BTC, 100 DUSD, 500 DUSD, 1,000 DUSD, and 10,000 DUSD: Remember: to earn points, your order must remain on the book for at least 3 seconds without being executed (without a trade). 1. Order Size: 1 BTC (Approximately 90,000 USD in value) In this scenario, since Bitcoin is 90,000 USD, your order value is also that amount. • If you are very close to price (0-10 bps, i.e., 0.10% distance): You earn 90,000 points per day. • If you are at a medium distance (10-30 bps, i.e., 0.30% distance): You earn 45,000 points per day. • If you are far from price (30-100 bps, i.e., 1.00% distance): You earn 9,000 points per day. 2. Order Size: 10,000 DUSD When your order’s total value is 10,000 dollars, your earnings are: • If you are very close to price (100% Return): You earn 10,000 points per day. • If you are at a medium distance (50% Return): You earn 5,000 points per day. • If you are far from price (10% Return): You earn 1,000 points per day. 3. Order Size: 1,000 DUSD When your order’s total value is 1,000 dollars, your earnings are: • If you are very close to price (100% Return): You earn 1,000 points per day. • If you are at a medium distance (50% Return): You earn 500 points per day. • If you are far from price (10% Return): You earn 100 points per day. 4. Order Size: 500 DUSD When your order’s total value is 500 dollars, your earnings are: • If you are very close to price (100% Return): You earn 500 points per day. • If you are at a medium distance (50% Return): You earn 250 points per day. • If you are far from price (10% Return): You earn 50 points per day. 5. Order Size: 100 DUSD When your order’s total value is 100 dollars, your earnings are: • If you are very close to price (100% Return): You earn 100 points per day. • If you are at a medium distance (50% Return): You earn 50 points per day. • If you are far from price (10% Return): You earn 10 points per day. As a GOAT Network Ambassador, I've been diving deep into the tech powering Bitcoin's evolution. The goal is to take goatnetwork to the trenches, it just my be our way out of the trenches. Let's unpack BitVM2 and how it positions GOAT as Bitcoin's yield capital. BitVM2 builds on the original BitVM (Bitcoin Virtual Machine), a framework for executing complex computations off-chain while verifying them on Bitcoin's layer-1. Introduced in late 2024, BitVM2 refines this by reducing the challenge-response rounds from hundreds to just a few, making verifications faster and cheaper without needing soft forks. At its core, BitVM2 uses fraud proofs and zero-knowledge (ZK) techniques to enable Turing-complete smart contracts on Bitcoin. Settlement hits your wallet natively on the destination chain. So: No bridge state to exploit. No shared liquidity honeypot. No “paused withdrawals” moment. The only thing securing the swap is L1 finality + economic obligation. Loved the new Saylor interview today. Ever since the Bitcoin treasury company boom and bust, there has been a LOT of lazy criticism of Bitcoin treasury companies from Bitcoiners. Which is ironic, because a lot of the criticism comes from a high time preference perspective, something that Bitcoiners are not known to have :) I do think Danny and Saylor talked past each other a bit, but the thrust of Saylor's argument is totally valid and he rightfully argued for the reorientation of focus regarding companies that don't hold Bitcoin. We saw some of these TC's trade at huge multiples (at least relative to what we've seen before), there was a natural market correction, and then a bunch of Bitcoiners shut their brains off and threw the baby out with the bathwater. It should be common sense by now that the price of an equity doesn't always reflect its fundamentals, which is why mispricings exist and why consensus isn't ever formed, and why some people make money and some people lose money. I think a good analogy would be comparing the mania to the dotcom bubble. Equities that were largely propped up by retail investors during a hype phase. Want a recap of what happened during the dotcom crash? Amazon stock went down -94%. Intel went down -72%. Apple went down -65%. Microsoft went down -60%. These companies didn't recover for YEARS, and yet they went on to fundamentally change the world. I can see a critique pop up that asks "Do these companies really compare to BTC TCs?" Why wouldn't they? Isn't the idea of monetizing the best form of capital the biggest idea in all of finance? Is Strategy not revolutionizing fixed income right now? You know, a $300 trillion idea? Strive is taking part, Metaplanet is taking part. More to come, undoubtedly. Is there really only room for 200 companies to hold gold? Why would it be any different for Bitcoin? It continues to blow my mind when I see the cognitive dissonance from Bitcoiners who can look at a company with thousands of Bitcoin on the balance sheet and think that it is doomed. Even if you take a company that had a bad downturn, it trades below NAV, and you assume zero multiple expansion ever, a reasonable Bitcoin return rate means you're out of the hole before too long. If you are a Bitcoiner and believe that Bitcoin is going to $1 million, congratulations: You believe a small web design operating business out of the UK will add $2.5 billion dollars of value to it's balance sheet from here. And that's assuming they never buy another Bitcoin of course. AND zero assumption of any other multiple expansion. Treating these companies as failed like it's some foregone conclusion is a grave error, and it really shows a lack of critical thinking. PIPE unlocks added to bad perception and a decent number of these companies were leveraged going into a Q4 where we have always seen BTC performance within the traditional cycle structure. They were simply leveraged at the wrong time, and if Bitcoin moved like it always did, there would have been a much different story for the end of 2025. There is simply way too much tribalistic negativity about people building on the frontier, and quite frankly, we as a community should be doing a lot better than posting red charts and laughing while we're mutually bullish on the asset that they are buying.

Web3 Series: Episode 2 Before we talk about tokens, NFTs, DeFi, or “the next big thing,” we need to understand why Web3 was born in the first place. Web3 did not start as a trend. It started as a reaction. The early internet (Web1) was simple and open. You could read information, but you couldn’t really interact. Then came Web2: social media, platforms, apps. We could create, share, and connect, but there was a cost. Over time, power became centralised. A few companies owned the platforms. They owned the data. They controlled access, reach, monetisation, and even identity. Creators built audiences they didn’t own. Users produced data they didn’t control. Accounts could be taken, censored, or demonetised overnight. (Remember when you lost your Instagram account for no just reason?) This growing imbalance raised a fundamental question: What if the internet didn’t need a middleman? What if ownership, identity, and value lived with the user instead of the platform? That question is what gave birth to Web3. Web3 is rooted in ideas that predate the hype: – Cryptography – Peer-to-peer systems – Bitcoin (2008) as the first real breakthrough – Blockchains as a way to coordinate trust without central authority At its core, Web3 is an attempt to return ownership to individuals, using code and cryptography instead of trust in institutions. Everything you see today; DeFi, NFTs, DAOs, on-chain identity, are expressions of that original idea. If you don’t understand the problem Web3 is trying to solve, you’ll always misunderstand the technology. Until next time, you are not special and you don't need to be to understand this technology.

Time is not money, motion is money. (Ramblings from a Retardmaxxer) I went down the time-is-motion rabbit hole last weekend for unrelated reasons, but those 1 or 2 hours wasted made me think about blockchain and why I like working in this industry. Aristotle thought time was/is a number or measure of physical motion. If everything froze in the universe time would cease to exist, because time needs a change of state to measure. It needs changes to be perceived. I was speaking to the smartest commodity trader I know about this and some mutual friends organically manifested in our conversation. Our friends, are precious metals miners in sub-Saharan Africa, and we started discussing why blockchain (Solana) should shape the future of their industry. *deep breath* Commodity trading is expensive because like I said, time is motion and motion is money, literally. Every day that metal sits (motionless) between the mine face and good delivery, someone's paying carrying costs. Let's use Greenland as the example because it's perfect. You've got maybe eight weeks of operating window. The capital expenditure is enormous. Equipment leases have terms. Permits have validity windows. And between extraction and monetization, you're looking at six to eight weeks minimum, and that's for gold, which moves fast. Base metals, we're talking years. Each step in that chain requires proof, letter of credit, permit, assay report, transport documentation, warehouse receipt, depository confirmation. Each proof takes time. Each day costs money. You can't hedge it all perfectly, not the price variance, not the transport cost, not even the lease rates. That variance degrades your ROI hugely *Trump voice*. It makes otherwise viable deposits uneconomic. This is pure time value of money mechanics. The longer your capital is tied up in unmonetizable inventory, the worse your return. So the discount rate is killing you. The supply chain problem isn't really about time as duration, it's about time as arrested motion. The metal sitting in customs isn't experiencing "time passing" it's experiencing stopped motion. Capital locked in working inventory isn't "waiting", it's frozen and thats expensive. THE TOKENIZATION ARBITRAGE If time is "the measure of motion," then a supply chain that takes six weeks isn't measuring time, it's measuring how much motion isn't happening. Metal in the ground: No motion (economically speaking) Metal extracted but waiting for permits: No motion Metal in transit but unverified: No motion (can't be monetized) Metal in warehouse awaiting assay: No motion Metal awaiting good delivery certification: No motion Each "step" where motion stops is where time becomes expensive. The carrying costs, the financing charges, the opportunity cost, these aren't payments for time's passage. They're payments for arrested motion. However, if you can take metal in the bush (Zimbabwe, UAE, wherever) and oracle it into a tokenized vault position immediately, you've just collapsed six weeks into six days. Maybe six hours. You're no longer financing a supply chain, let someone else do that. You're monetizing an authenticated asset. The moment provenance hits the blockchain, that metal becomes liquid. Tradeable. Borrowable against. You've turned working capital into instant settlement. This is exactly what Glencore ($70B marketcap) figured out the analog way. They don't own more mines than Rio Tinto. They own the flow. They put metal in the pipe continuously and get paid for shipments from three months ago while extracting today. Rio owns the assets but Glencore owns the velocity. And thats why Rio Tinto is looking to acquire them. You need more motion. This should be the goal, compressing the time horizon from months to days. That compression is the arbitrage. Every day you shave off via increased velocity is basis points back in your pocket. PHILOSOPHICAL RAMBLINGS Supply chain friction isn't really about logistics, it's about epistemology dressed up as finance. How do I know this metal is real? How do I know the assay's legitimate? How do I know it hasn't been double-pledged? Historically, knowing cost money. You paid intermediaries to verify. You paid insurance to cover their mistakes. You paid lawyers to write contracts that anticipated every fraud. The entire financing stack exists because proof was expensive and trust was scarce. This is why we are in Blockchain, it has the potential to invert this. Cryptographic verification makes proof cheap. The oracle doesn't ask you to trust, it gives you a signature you can check yourself. We all know this, at least most of us who have been around the space for more than a few years do. Bitcoin has very attractive properties, but from a trading perspective, it lacks something compelling. Bitcoin proved you could create a supply chain from nothing, mine value through proof-of-work, settle instantly, no physical substrate needed. Beautiful but hollow. There's no time value to arbitrage because there's really no supply chain to finance. The real world still has metal in the ground. Equipment in the Arctic. Ships crossing oceans. All of it requiring capital, all of it subject to time decay. So what if you marry the two worlds? Take crypto's settlement mechanics and apply them to physical commodity flows. You get instant liquidity for real assets. The price signal can finally reach all the way down to the ore body, not just Rio Tinto's massive operations but the small miner in Greenland, the artisanal operation in the Zim bush, eventually the space mining company pre-selling asteroid platinum. THE FINANCING ARB In commodity markets, everything is a financing arb. Glencore built a $70 billion company on this insight. The question is always: Can you monetize faster than your cost of capital? Traditionally, no. The verification stack was too expensive, too slow. You had to be huge to absorb the friction costs. Tokenization changes the math. Suddenly, verification is cheap, settlement is instant, and liquidity is global. The small operator can compete on velocity, not just on scale. Capital flowing to its most productive use because the cost of knowing, the epistemological tax, just collapsed to near zero. THE PRACTICAL IMPLICATION Right now, the market is screaming for supply. Every viable ounce, from granny's silver drawer to subsurface deposits two miles down. The price signal wants to find metal wherever it is. But that signal can't penetrate the verification costs. The friction is too high. So capital pools in the usual places, the big miners, the established supply chains, the players who can afford the friction. Remove that friction and watch what happens. The price signal reaches everywhere. The invisible ore bodies become visible. The uneconomic deposits become economic. The supply curve shifts right because the cost curve just shifted down. That's what tokenization does. It's not better trade finance. It's instant monetization of authenticated assets. It's taking the time value of money and turning it into a weapon, compressing settlement windows, collapsing supply chains, capturing the spread between "metal in ground" and "metal in market." Six weeks to six days. That delta is billions of dollars annually, just sitting there, waiting to be arbitraged. And like I said thats just Gold, imagine the implications for base metals/other minerals. We've been measuring the wrong variable. Finance obsesses over duration, how long capital is deployed, how long until maturity, how long the carry period lasts. But duration is just a proxy for what we actually care about: velocity. Capital sitting still for six weeks isn't expensive because six weeks passed. It's expensive because the capital stopped moving. Motion arrested. Velocity dropped to zero. And when velocity hits zero, carrying costs explode because you're financing dead weight, value that exists but can't flow. Tokenization/Blockchain OS doesn't just "speed things up." It restores motion. It keeps capital in continuous flow. It increases velocity. The asset goes from illiquid to liquid instantly, which means capital never arrests. And this is why blockchain is interesting, it has the potential to eliminate the friction that arrests motion. TLDR: Antiquated supply chains should use blockchain TLDR2: Accelerate

While there is good reason to believe that global liquidity has not peaked in nominal terms, there is a major misconception. Many assume liquidity has been rising continuously, but that ignores the momentum component. Although the level of liquidity has increased, its momentum has clearly rolled over, explaining why Bitcoin's sell-off late last year. Equities, on the other hand, tell a different story. Last year's gains were driven mainly by earnings growth rather than liquidity, making them a weak proxy for liquidity conditions. Chart 1 shows that our Global Liquidity 12-week RoC does a good job at identifying risk-on and risk-off phases. The Nasdaq has broadly followed this pattern. When liquidity momentum slowed last year, equities held up because strong earnings growth offset the drag from liquidity. Bitcoin is different. It has no earnings, margins, or buybacks, making it the purest proxy for global liquidity. As shown in Chart 2, Bitcoin closely tracks the 12-week RoC of global liquidity. Contrary to claims that Bitcoin is mispricing liquidity, the evidence suggests the opposite: global liquidity momentum has been contracting, and Bitcoin has reacted expected. Now it is turning up again. There was no external event distorting Bitcoin's price discovery - liquidity momentum did.

Government debt has exceeded $10 trillion, and Japanese government bond yields are now at multi-decade highs. This shift alone has serious implications for global liquidity. For decades, Japan survived because interest rates were near zero. That era is over. As yields rise: • Debt servicing costs accelerate • Government revenues are increasingly absorbed by interest payments • Financial stability becomes fragile The global impact starts here Japan is not an isolated economy. It is one of the largest international investors: • Over $1T in U.S. Treasuries • Hundreds of billions in global equities and bonds Capital flowed overseas because domestic yields were uncompetitive. That incentive is fading. With higher local yields and currency hedging costs rising, many foreign assets no longer make sense for Japanese investors. This points to one thing: Capital repatriation. Large-scale repatriation doesn’t happen quietly. It creates global liquidity gaps. Add the yen carry trade into the equation Over $1 trillion borrowed cheaply in yen and deployed into: stocks, crypto, and emerging markets. As Japanese rates rise and the yen strengthens: • Carry trades unwind • Forced selling increases • Correlations spike across risk assets At the same time: • U.S.–Japan yield spreads are shrinking • Japan has less incentive to keep capital abroad • Global borrowing costs trend higher Bottom line Japan is trapped between: High debt Currency sensitivity Inflation that limits aggressive money printing For 30 years, ultra-low Japanese yields acted as a hidden anchor for global rates. For your consideration, I present some classical literature and other works that gave rise to the ideas that later influenced the cypherpunks and others contributing to the Bitcoin movement—in chronological order: → We (1924) by Yevgeny Zamyatin The pioneering dystopian novel critiquing total collectivism and loss of individuality — foundational influence on later anti-authoritarian works. → Anthem (1938) by Ayn Rand A compact novella depicting the suppression of the self in a collectivist society and the triumphant rediscovery of "I" — direct thematic echo to Bitcoin's emphasis on personal sovereignty. → 1984 (1949) by George Orwell The classic on totalitarian surveillance, rewritten history, and centralized power — a stark warning that resonates with cypherpunk/Bitcoin privacy and anti-state motivations. → Atlas Shrugged (1957) by Ayn Rand The magnum opus of productive creators withdrawing from a coercive, centrally planned system — widely seen as the philosophical blueprint for Bitcoin's "opt-out" from fiat control. → The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress (1966) by Robert A. Heinlein A libertarian lunar colony's revolution through decentralized voluntary cooperation against Earth authority — embodies scarcity mindset and anti-statism. → The Codebreakers (1967) by David Kahn A comprehensive history of cryptography from ancient times to the mid-20th century — foundational for understanding the cryptographic roots that cypherpunks (and later Bitcoin) built upon for privacy and trustless systems. → True Names (1981) by Vernor Vinge Groundbreaking novella introducing cyberspace, digital identities, and cryptography for privacy — prophetic for pseudonymity and decentralized systems in crypto. → The New Libertarian Manifesto (1983) by Samuel Edward Konkin III Outlines agorism (counter-economics via voluntary black/grey markets) as a path to bypass state coercion — seen as an ideological precursor to Bitcoin's voluntary, decentralized money that enables opting out of fiat systems. → Neuromancer (1984) by William Gibson The cyberpunk cornerstone defining digital networks, hacking, and decentralized tech economies — shaped the cultural imagination that birthed Bitcoin. → Snow Crash (1992) by Neal Stephenson Features private hard-currency systems, virtual worlds, and decentralized economies beyond government control — key influence on blockchain concepts. → A Cypherpunk's Manifesto (1993) by Eric Hughes A seminal short essay (not a full book, but often treated as foundational reading) calling for cryptography to enable anonymous transactions and resist surveillance — directly in the lineage that led to Bitcoin's privacy ethos. → Heavy Weather (1994) by Bruce Sterling A cyberpunk novel set in a chaotic future with climate collapse and a digital currency resembling early cryptocurrency ideas — one of the closer fictional predictions of decentralized money. → The Great Simoleon Caper (1995 short story) by Neal Stephenson A concise tale explicitly depicting a private, digital cryptocurrency-like system in a near-future setting — one of the earliest fictional portrayals of decentralized digital money, often cited as eerily predictive. → The Sovereign Individual (1997) by James Dale Davidson & Lord William Rees-Mogg Non-fiction forecast of cryptography enabling individual sovereignty, the decline of nation-states, and digital currencies — often dubbed the most accurate pre-Bitcoin prophecy. → Cryptonomicon (1999) by Neal Stephenson Cryptography meets attempts to create private digital gold-like money escaping fiat — massive direct inspiration for early Bitcoin and cypherpunk developers. → Crypto: How the Code Rebels Beat the Government—How They Will Save Privacy in the Digital Age (2001) by Steven Levy Chronicles the cypherpunk movement, public-key cryptography battles, PGP, and early fights against government crypto restrictions — direct heritage explaining the privacy-through-code ethos that underpins Bitcoin.

i've been following arch for a while, mainly because i'm curious how they think about using BTC. this latest blog starts from a very familiar idea: bitcoin as digital gold. that comes from a few basics: • fixed supply • transparent issuance • deep liquidity because of that, institutions already see BTC as very strong collateral. what Arch looks at next is usage. not how BTC is stored, but how it's actually used. they're saying bitcoin is starting to be used inside real financial markets, not just held in wallets. the first big concept they introduce is THE BITCOIN YIELD CURVE this ends up being a key part of the whole post. in simple terms, a yield curve exists when markets can put a price on: • time • how easy it is to get liquidity • how risky something is early bitcoin markets couldn't really do this because there wasn't enough depth, derivatives were limited, or institutions weren't active yet… today, yeah… that looks different. you can already see pricing signals: • CME futures give a clear reference price • when futures trade above spot, that shows a financing cost • funding rates show short-term demand for liquidity • lending markets show different rates over time this is all happening live. once markets can price these things, more advanced financial products become possible. then they point to the main problem: EXECUTION INFRA. bitcoin's scripting system can't handle complex financial agreements between multiple parties. because of that, institutions move activity offchain: • they negotiate lending deals manually • they use custodians to hold collateral • they rely on legal contracts to enforce terms this works, but it adds: • trust in third parties • slower settlement • operational friction that's the gap Arch is trying to close. they explain capital markets as a few basic layers: • issuance • trading • clearing • settlement bitcoin already does settlement very well (global transparent..) what's missing is a layer that can: i) manage obligations between parties ii) update collateral when conditions change iii) react to what's happening on bitcoin iv) still settle everything directly on bitcoin that's the layer Arch is building. their setup includes a few main pieces: • ArchVM runs financial logic talks directly to bitcoin UTXOs and scripts • Titan indexer watches the bitcoin mempool in real time important because some decisions happen before blocks confirm • rollback / reapply handles reorgs by recalculating state keeps everything in sync with bitcoin • settlement final results always land on bitcoin no wrapped BTC no synthetic assets no bridges logic runs offchain + results settle onchain. they then connect this to things institutions already do today. CME basis trades: • buy BTC on the spot market • sell BTC futures • earn the difference lending supports this: • borrowing BTC • hedging positions • managing exposure over time right now, this goes through custodians like Anchorage or Coinbase Prime where terms are agreed manually & collateral depends on trusted third parties… Arch keeps the same strategies: • same market behavior • same risks *BUT* replaces manual coordination with programs that enforce the rules automatically. on yield, they draw a clear line. older bitcoin yield came from: • custodial lending • rehypothecation • token incentives capital markets yield comes from: • basis trades • structured credit • options and volatility products returns come from real market activity & pricing is visible & risk can be measured. their point is that bitcoin markets are already mature enough for this. what was missing was infra that lets all of this happen while keeping BTC native. at a high level, the idea is simple. bitcoin moves from sitting idle to being used inside real financial workflows. the capital is already there & the pricing signals already exist. Arch positions its stack as the piece that connects everything and lets it all settle directly on bitcoin. that's the core argument they're making here…

This pattern signals strong bearish momentum and typically indicates that sellers have gained control, potentially leading to further declines. The best time to play a falling window is when it appears after an uptrend has pivoted at a resistance level, suggesting a change in direction and the beginning of a downtrend. To play this setup, identify the falling window pattern after a pivot at resistance, especially when price gaps down, leaving a visible space between the previous close and the next open. Confirm the bearish sentiment by watching for follow-through with additional bearish candles below the gap. Consider entering a short position below the low of the second candle in the gap to capture downside momentum. A stop-loss can be placed above the high of the gap, as a close above this level may invalidate the bearish setup. The psychology behind a falling window reflects a shift in sentiment, where sellers have taken over, likely due to a failure at resistance. After a pivot at resistance, bullish confidence weakens, and the gap down signals that sellers are eager to push prices lower. This break in momentum often causes buyers to step back, while bears capitalize on the shift, confirming a potential trend reversal. The falling window underscores the power of sellers in this new trend direction, encouraging additional selling pressure. INSTITUTIONAL WALLS: BITCOIN’S 100K LINE WHO SETS THE ORDERS, WHO BREAKS IT? The core misconception about Bitcoin is that we still read it like an independent market. News hits, price reacts, buyers and sellers find balance. That is the story most people stick to. Recent price action points to something else. Crypto is no longer just an asset looking for direction. It has become a mechanism that reveals where liquidity concentrates and how risk appetite is managed. From the outside it looks like a free market. Inside, dominant flows often define the boundaries in advance. You do not need to memorize chart patterns to see it. Watch how perfectly synchronized venues have become. THE CRIME SCENE: PERFECT SYNCHRONIZATION Coinbase, Binance, Bybit. Pick any screen. Even on second by second candles, you will often see near perfect alignment. What used to be minutes of exchange-to-exchange spreads now closes in milliseconds. Yes, arbitrage bots close gaps fast. But on certain days it is not just “gap closing.” You see moves that start at the same time, push in the same direction, and deepen at the same pace. That level of coordination tells you more about market structure than about investor psychology. SEPARATE VENUES, SAME FLOW Large players do not operate on a single exchange. They manage spot, perpetuals, and options at the same time, spreading risk across the network. Price is not formed in one place anymore. It is shaped within the network’s aggregate liquidity. When a move appears on one venue and instantly echoes everywhere, it is often less about “news spreading” and more about a simple fact: the same capital flow goes live across multiple platforms at once. The language of that flow is simple. Price moves toward where liquidity is concentrated. It moves quickly through where liquidity is thin. BITCOIN’S NEW ROLE: THE HIGH BETA REALITY Bitcoin no longer behaves like a standalone “safe haven.” Institutionally, it is increasingly treated as a high beta expression of global risk appetite. It rallies harder in risk-on regimes and unwinds faster when risk-off takes over. ETFs accelerated this shift. The center of gravity moved from spot venues toward futures and options that institutional risk desks watch closely. To understand why price stalls at certain levels, spot charts are not enough. Options positioning, gamma dynamics, and hedging flows matter. That is why levels like 100K can behave not only as psychological resistance, but as a mechanical wall. LIQUIDATION MECHANICS: THE REAL ENGINE Crypto is not unique only because it is volatile. Liquidations turn price into a trigger system. Price drops into a key zone. Leveraged positions get forced out. Those forced exits push price further. A chain reaction builds. From the outside it looks like panic. Inside it often behaves like a mechanical acceleration. That is why some selloffs feel less “emotional” and more “structured.” What matters is not only the drop, but where it speeds up and where it stops. WHY TRADFI LIKES THIS FIELD: FLEXIBILITY AND SPEED In traditional markets, regulations and circuit breakers make it hard to run the same intensity of leverage cleanouts. Crypto is more flexible. Liquidity is more fragmented, leverage is more accessible, and moves can expand faster. This is not always about malicious intent. Often it is simply about turning market fragility into an advantage. Survivors in this game are not the ones who stare at patterns. They are the ones who read liquidity. CONCLUSION: THE CENTER OF GRAVITY HAS SHIFTED “Leave centralized exchanges” can be an emotional reaction, but the market’s center of gravity already moved. Even DEXs need reference prices. Oracles, arbitrage, and where volume concentrates all tie back to the same reality. Bitcoin is still an open market. But the players at the table have changed. Retail follows price. Bigger flows manage liquidity. And that is where the 100K wall begins. Sometimes “who gives the orders” is not a name. It is a mechanism. I saw this post the other day and I casually mentioned timing, algorithm, and emotional pull, but that alone was vague because it didn’t really do justice to what I was seeing. so I went deeper and asked Grok, and it explained a few things, and I was shocked to see it mentioned the exact thing I had in mind. As at the time of making this post, that tweet had exploded with over 3K likes, 200+ replies, and 350K views in just a few days. Here are a combination of reasons why it blew up on X, considering the fact that this is a period where Bitcoin is around six-figure territory, hmm (murky waters). So here’s what I found. 1. The “what if” nightmare that surrounds Satoshi Nakamoto as the single biggest mystery in all of crypto. This is something almost everybody fears that the ghost founder who vanished and never touched 1.1M BTC, (5% of the total supply), currently worth over $150B. The idea that he could suddenly reappear and dump everything is, in crypto terms, the equivalent of the creator himself losing faith in the technology. So that single thought alone triggered a massive FUD among believers and his followers, and it spread like wildfire, because fear travels much faster than hope on X. 2. The open-ended, extremely engaging question format. “What price would Bitcoin dump to? ” It’s perfect engagement bait, It’s emotional, and the broken-heart emoji just hits differently. It invited wild guesses, with people mentioning anywhere from $20K, to a minor 20–30% dip, to basically nothing significant beyond short-term volatility. Everyone feels qualified to answer with their own number and reasoning, which naturally resulted in over 200 replies, tons of quote tweets, arguments, and people tagging friends to see what they think. 3. Timing and market psychology hitting a very sweet spot. Bitcoin still feels very early in 2026 after hitting both ATHs and sharp pullbacks between late last year and now. In these euphoric phases, people are often over-leveraged and quietly nervous about market tops. So any hypothetical “big price move” suddenly becomes much scarier. so the tweet gently taps directly into a lingering trust anchor many people still hold "as long as Satoshi is still holding, Bitcoin is safe".

Are ETFs a trap for Web3? Between 2023 and 2025, the retail market was buzzing with a single word: ETF Everyone was checking the news for the "Bitcoin ETF." We were told that the arrival of the BlackRock and Fidelity was the final battle web3 needed to win. We thought their entry was the stamp of approval that would send our portfolios to the moon and keep them there. In many ways, we got exactly what we asked for. But by late 2025, with several market manipulation, the downsides started becoming impossible to ignore. During the last bull cycle, the rise of the Spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs felt like a victory parade. We thought institutions would bring "Infinite Liquidity." We believed the market would stop crashing by 50% overnight because "serious people" were now in charge. Prices did hit new highs, but other things started to shift. - The New Market Manipulation Entered In the old days, Whales were rich individuals or early adopters. Today, the whales are trillion-dollar institutions with high-frequency trading (HFT) bots. They can move the price just enough to liquidate thousands of small traders, extracting value with mathematical precision. -The "Paper" Supply: With ETFs, many people are buying "Paper Bitcoin": a claim on a stock rather than the actual coin. This allows institutions to influence the price without ever moving a single satoshi on the actual blockchain. - The Centralization Trap We wanted to Be Our Own Bank, but we ended up letting the Big Banks be our custodians once again when they started buying shares in exchanges, launchpads and wallets. - The Honeypot Risk: A massive percentage of the world’s Bitcoin is now sitting in a few institutional vaults. This creates a single point of failure that can crash the market. - Governance Hijacking: Institutions now hold enough tokens to "out-vote" the actual community on every major project decision. The Institutions gave us the price action we wanted, but it appears like Web3 is loosing the decentralization it needed, which appears to defeat the purpose of why Bitcoin was invented. Ethereum just flipped post-quantum security from "research topic" to "top strategic priority." The Foundation announced a dedicated team focused on this, with Justin Drake steering the engineering phase. They're talking real timelines: 2026 for serious roadmap execution, including wallet upgrades, testnets, and a $2M global bounty pool to pull in the best cryptographers. Why now? Vitalik dropped a pretty sobering take there's roughly a 20% chance quantum computers could break today's elliptic-curve cryptography before 2030. That's not "someday"; that's potentially 3–4 years away in the worst plausible scenarios. Google's Willow chip and steady qubit progress keep moving the needle faster than most expected.What actually breaks? Shor's algorithm on a large-scale quantum machine can derive private keys from public keys. For Bitcoin and Ethereum, that mainly hits spent outputs or reused addresses where the public key is exposed on-chain. Unspent coins with never-revealed pubkeys get a longer grace period because reversing hashes Keccak-256 on ETH, SHA-256 on BTC is much harder for quantum attackers.Ethereum has advantages here: account abstraction lets wallets rotate to quantum-resistant signatures without forcing users to sweep funds. They can hybridize keep ECDSA for now, add lattice-based (like Dilithium/ML-DSA) or hash-based options as fallback. The "lean Ethereum" vision Drake's pushing ties into this: simplify the protocol, boost scalability to 10k+ TPS, modernize staking/consensus, and bake in PQ crypto from the ground up. Bitcoin's path is trickier decentralized governance means upgrades move slower. BIP-360 already sketches quantum-resistant address formats, but full migration needs broad consensus and miner/node buy-in. Some devs are accelerating talks, but it's not at Ethereum's action speed yet. Coinbase even set up an advisory board with heavy hitters (Aaronson, Boneh, even Drake) to stress-test the whole ecosystem.Bottom line: this isn't panic time, but dismissal is bad risk management. The asymmetric nature sucks attackers can wait silently for a breakthrough, while chains have to telegraph upgrades years ahead. Ethereum treating it as an engineering problem (not a crisis) gives it a real edge. Chains or wallets that stay hybrid-ready or fully migrate early will look prescient.If your stack isn't at least thinking about PQ signatures in 2026, it's already lagging. Evolution beats extinction every time.

The heart of the setup is the TSS Vault (Threshold Signature Scheme). Instead of one person holding the keys, multiple validators each hold a piece. No single validator can move funds alone. Only when enough honest validators agree does the vault sign a Bitcoin transaction. This is how users can trustlessly use DeFi style apps on Bitcoin without handing custody to anyone, including validators. Validators also participate in Midl’s delegated proof of stake system. That means staking BTC and Midl tokens, staying online, processing transactions correctly, and coordinating with other validators. Downtime, refusal to process transactions, or malicious behavior isn’t just frowned upon, it gets penalized. Real responsibility, real consequences. Behind the scenes, validators execute EVM level smart contract logic, batch multiple user actions into efficient flows, and help return real Bitcoin and Runes back to users after each dApp interaction. The magic users feel, one Bitcoin confirmation, no bridges, no wallet switching, exists because validators are doing disciplined, technical work every single block. What I find powerful is this: someone using a Bitcoin wallet for the first time doesn’t need to understand any of this. They just click, sign, and receive. But under the hood, people running Midl validators are carefully stitching together Bitcoin’s security with modern app logic, and that’s how Bitcoin quietly grows beyond just send and receive. That’s the kind of infrastructure Midl is building, not flashy, not loud, just solid systems that make Bitcoin feel usable without asking users to become experts first.

Omer Husain, Manager for Bitcoin DeFi at Input Output, explains how they are building an end to end Bitcoin DeFi liquidity stack. The goal is to enable Bitcoin holders to earn real yield. To do that, they need access to stablecoins for investment, with Bitcoin locked non custodially as collateral to borrow those stablecoins, alongside defined borrowing terms and interest rates that are attractive for participation. He outlines three core requirements: A credit market that creates stablecoin liquidity A yield application that deploys capital into real world, off chain yield opportunities A trust minimised BitVM based bridge that allows users to use Bitcoin as collateral without custodial risk End to end, for users, the experience is intended to be as simple as using an earn product on a centralised exchange. Rather than pulling ADA out of staking, which is already safe and attractive, this approach allows external liquidity, especially in the form of Bitcoin, to enter Cardano.
