Instead of issuing debt with a maturity date, they issued perpetual preferred stock. In simple terms: Investors receive 12.25% annually (similar to interest) No obligation to ever repay principal Holders rank above common shareholders in distress scenarios Strive used this instrument to swap out existing debt, resulting in: No repayment deadline A lighter balance sheet Continued flexibility to accumulate Bitcoin The big question: can Strategy do the same? In theory: yes In practice: very hard Strategy is many times larger than Strive, and the annual payout cost could be even higher than its current interest expense. On the other side, we have very bullish views from the likes of Tom Lee and the very respected Raoul Pal. Pal argues that crypto never truly followed a four year time cycle at all. In his view, those cycles only appeared to exist because crypto's short history happened to line up with global liquidity cycles driven by central banks. Bitcoin and crypto, he says, are simply the most liquidity sensitive assets in the world (they rise when financial conditions ease and struggle when liquidity tightens.) There is a distinction between the original and the synthetic. The original is what is given by reality itself. The synthetic is what is made in imitation. This is not a religious claim. It is an observation about how truth, nourishment, and value work across biology, economics, and human attention. The question is not whether something is man-made, but whether it honors the reality it imitates or conceals it. Does it complement what is real, or does it replace it with a signal that looks convincing enough to distract? Does it nourish, or does it poison while wearing the mask of nourishment? Gold and silver have bodies. They have weight. Their scarcity is written into the structure of the earth. Their value exists whether anyone agrees with it or not. Bitcoin and Ethereum have price, but price is not value. They are signals without substance. Gold is the body Bitcoin will never have. Silver is the body Ethereum will never have. No protocol can conjure what took millennia to form. This is not ideology. It is physics. Fruit has flavor that arrives with nourishment. Sweetness evolved as a signal pointing to something real. Synthetic chemicals mimic the signal while withholding what the signal was designed to indicate. The taste is there. The food is not. The body receives the message that nutrition has arrived, but nothing arrives. A promise made and broken at the cellular level. So ask a harder question: what is the synthetic actually feeding? If it is not feeding you, it is feeding something else. And what does that something require? A humanity distracted from the tangible, disconnected from consequence, trained to respond to signals while substance goes unexamined. This condition has a name older than any modern system: heedlessness. Not ignorance. Not denial. Heedlessness is being awake while asleep, present but absent, looking without seeing. The truth is not hidden. Attention has simply been redirected. The struggle is not against lies. Lies are easy to detect once attention returns. The struggle is against the conditions that make truth irrelevant to daily life. Walk through a grocery store. The real food sits at the edges because it spoils, because it is alive. The synthetic dominates the center: shelf-stable, engineered for craving, optimized for consumption rather than nourishment. This is not an accident. It is an architecture. The same architecture governs value. Synthetic stores of wealth, digital abstractions, algorithmic scarcity occupy more and more human attention. The original is dismissed as inconvenient, heavy, obsolete. Who wants to hold something real when a password is lighter? Who wants to real food when a synthetic food tastes better to our senses? Maybe you dislike what is good for you and maybe you crave what is bad for you. Reflect. These are not separate problems. The synthetic food inside the body and the synthetic value occupying the mind feed the same system. Both require disconnection. Both depend on attention fixed on signals rather than substance. Both produce humans who consume but are not nourished, who transact endlessly but hold nothing real. So where do these rivers meet? What benefits from bodies filled with chemicals that do not nourish and minds occupied with values that do not exist? What thrives when humanity mistakes the signal for the thing itself, the price for the value, the flavor for the food? The question is not rhetorical. Follow the effects. Trace what synthetic consumption produces in the body: disruption, inflammation, dependency managed but never resolved. Trace what synthetic value produces in the economy: abstraction, surveillance, systems no individual controls. Ask who profits not from human flourishing, but from managed dysfunction. The original asks only for attention. The synthetic survives on inattention. Reality still offers what is real to those willing to look directly at it again. The invitation is simple: look.

Bitcoin's recent drop has people looking for a simple reason. While market sentiment and broader economic factors always play a role, a key technical argument is gaining attention. It's not about the 21 million supply cap changing, but about how the price is discovered. The core idea is that Bitcoin's price is no longer set only by people buying and selling the actual asset. Instead, it's heavily influenced by a massive derivatives market. This includes futures, options, and perpetual swaps, where traders bet on the price without ever owning the underlying Bitcoin. This creates a huge amount of "paper" or synthetic Bitcoin. In essence, the financial exposure to Bitcoin in these markets can far exceed the actual number of coins that exist. When leverage is high, the price becomes extremely sensitive to trader positioning and forced liquidations, not just to fundamental supply and demand. So, when large leveraged positions get wiped out in a downturn, it can trigger a cascading sell-off in the derivatives market. This pressure then drives the spot price down sharply, even if long-term holders aren't selling their coins. In short, the crash isn't necessarily about Bitcoin's fundamentals breaking. It's about the modern market structure, where price discovery is dominated by leveraged bets, creating violent swings that feel disconnected from the asset's underlying scarcity.

AI Won’t Kill Bitcoin, But Its Quantum Cousin Might: The Truth About Crypto’s Future. Could a super-smart AI crack Bitcoin? It’s a question that feels ripped from a sci-fi thriller, but the reality is far more nuanced and, frankly, more interesting. While the idea of an AI simply “learning” to break Bitcoin is a myth, the convergence of AI and a new kind of technology-quantum computing-is setting the stage for the biggest cryptographic showdown in history. The AI Misconception Let’s get this out of the way: your standard AI, even a highly advanced one, isn’t going to break Bitcoin’s encryption. Why? Because modern cryptography is designed to look like random noise. There are no patterns for an AI to learn. It’s a mathematical fortress, and AI, for all its power, is still using the same classical computing tools we all are. It can’t just “outsmart” the math [1, 2]. Instead of being an adversary, AI is actually becoming one of crypto’s most powerful allies, helping with everything from fraud detection to enabling a future where autonomous AI agents can transact on the blockchain [3]. Enter the Quantum Wildcard The real, long-term threat comes from quantum computers. These machines are a different beast entirely. They play by the bizarre rules of quantum physics to solve certain problems that are impossible for regular computers. One of those problems happens to be the one that underpins all of Bitcoin’s security [5]. So, case closed? Is Bitcoin doomed? Not so fast. The catch is that you’d need a quantum computer with millions of stable qubits to pull this off, and today’s best machines are nowhere close. The consensus is that we are still 5-15 years away from a quantum computer that could pose a credible threat [7]. AI: The Threat Accelerator Here’s where it gets complicated. AI has entered the quantum race and is turbocharging it. AI is now being used to design more powerful quantum chips and, most importantly, to help correct the errors that make today’s quantum computers so unstable. This AI-quantum synergy is turning a distant physics problem into a very real engineering challenge that is progressing faster than anyone expected [9]. A Symbiotic Future While the quantum threat is a serious, long-term challenge that the crypto industry is actively preparing for, the more immediate story is one of partnership. The future of the internet will likely be built on a powerful alliance between AI and crypto. As leading thinkers from a16z and Ethereum have pointed out, AI needs crypto. As AI agents become more autonomous, they’ll need a native, permissionless way to pay for things. Blockchains provide that. In a world flooded with AI-generated content and deepfakes, blockchains can provide the “proof-of-personhood” needed to verify who is real and who is a bot [4, 10]. So, while the quantum countdown has begun, the real story isn’t about AI killing crypto. It’s about crypto becoming the foundational layer for a new, intelligent, and autonomous digital world. Assets sitting in custodial systems are easier to use within the broader financial system, which can increase short term supply in practice, even if not on chain. That’s not a conspiracy it’s how modern markets function. None of this breaks Bitcoin. It changes how it trades. In the short term, derivatives and leverage can mute moves, exaggerate corrections, and create price behavior that looks disconnected from simple scarcity logic. Over longer periods, real ownership still matters, because leverage always unwinds and paper exposure cannot fully replace the underlying asset when stress appears. Term of the week: mechanical degrossing The explanation for Bitcoin’s drop last week needs to account for four things - timing, breadth, sequencing, and correlation. Only mechanical degrossing does so. There was no discrete Bitcoin-specific catalyst. The pressure in high-beta equities and duration risk aligned with it. Selling happened before liquidation acceleration. And once exposure likely reset it stabilized, which gave us the -20% snapback in price on Friday. This happens when risk tolerance changes, not when beliefs shift. ETFs don’t generally tend to sell off due to fears/narratives, but instead for rebalancing and reducing risk. And you can see the outflows in bitcoin ETFs showing up as would be expected in mechanical exposure reduction. There also wasn’t any macro shock. You could argue macro uncertainty, but that proves the point even more as uncertainty manifests itself in sensitivity reduction, not directional conviction. As dgt10011 mentioned, Vol picked up significantly. That kind of move will push strategies from “add risk” to “reduce risk.” Things like risk parity sleeves, vol-targeting funds, and dealer gamma hedging, for instance, all can be expected to react mechanically to that shift in vol. Furthermore, the move down was clearly procedural, not chaotic, which suggests housekeeping not fear. Leverage got punished, yes, but it wasn’t what ignited the drop. In other words, the drop was just balance sheet puking, not narratives invoking “the end of Bitcoin” for the millionth time in its existence. The only real question left at this time is whether the degrossing is complete or if that was only the first pass. Degrossing tends to end quietly when risk has reset but can resume violently when vol doesn’t cooperate.

Bitcoin fell by 50 percent, and I was faced with the leader I needed to become. Moments like this come unannounced to stress-test your leadership. You can sense it. There is just a room that feels slightly different. Everyone asks themselves harder questions. People are still committed, but they are scanning the horizon, trying to work out whether the ground beneath them has shifted. They look to your response to shape their own. Thing is, your team won't expect you to have all of the answers or to predict what comes next. As the leader, you set the emotional and intellectual centre of gravity for everyone else. In unsettling moments, teams look for an anchor. That anchor is you. If you break, the company breaks. I'm reminded by Jeff Bezos' existential moment early on in his career. In the dot-com crash, AMZN share price collapsed by 95%, and stayed down for a long time. I shared with the team Jeff's stark and unemotional message: the stock is different and separate to the company. The stock responds to people's sentiment. What actually mattered was that customers were still there. Revenue was growing. Orders were coming in. The work still mattered, so they kept building, quietly and stubbornly, while the noise raged above them. Amazon did not change its mission because the market lost confidence. Today, Amazon is worth trillions. Bitcoin asks for the same discipline. Nothing about Bitcoin changed last week but its price relative to the dollar. The protocol held. The rules remained intact. It remains censorship resistant. It remains the hardest form of money. It remains what it was designed to be: freedom technology. Infrastructure built to reduce reliance on centralised power, discretion, and intermediaries. A system that makes it structurally harder to f*ck vulnerable ppl over. The leadership lesson that was crystallised here for me was that you can't persuade people into their convictions. Conviction is something people infer from your long-term behaviour, integrity and moral clarity. I should also say thank you to DSBatten Daniel Batten. His work, and especially his course on how to tell better and more ambitious stories, has stayed with me. Bitcoin needs its story to grow up again. For a while it drifted - inward looking, materialistic, reactive, disconnected from the wider world. I love how Daniel is pulling it back to first principles and telling a more authentic human Bitcoin story. And I want to acknowledge the EverGive_ team. Resilience is easy to demonstrate after the fact, but much harder to practise in real time. They've been tested, and their convictions are only growing. What stood out to me was members of my team steadying others. In particular, Oliver Tufft and Ben Wylie stepped up with a calmness and clarity that stabilised and lifted the room. Their natural leadership emerged, and that kind of conviction in teams is contagious in the best way. Proud to be building with you all.

The core argument posits that certain bitcoin mining sites, once developed into data centers with long-term leases, transition from volatile crypto bets to stable infrastructure assets. This “REIT endgame” perspective suggests these facilities appeal more to investors seeking steady cash flow, akin to data center real estate investment trusts, rather than those tracking bitcoin price swings. Cipher Mining, with its data centers deemed suitable for this transformation, and TeraWulf, with its strong track record in data center agreements and power infrastructure, are positioned to benefit from this re-rating. Conversely, Marathon Digital’s hybrid strategy, combining mining with data center ambitions and a focus on bitcoin price maximization, is seen as carrying significant risk due to the historically unattractive profitability of pure bitcoin mining. This selective approach underscores a pivotal moment for the industry, challenging miners to evolve into power and computing landlords to unlock new investor value beyond the volatile cryptocurrency market. Crypto’s biggest threat was never regulation, it’s internal decay. If builders get drowned out by grifters, we hand over the future without realizing it. This crime, scam, ponzi narrative needs to stop. It is fixable. We just need less ego and more leadership. Less extraction and more creation. Less division and more alignment. I still believe the strongest cycles are driven by real people, real conviction, and real community. The question is whether we want a future owned by institutions… or one still shaped by the people bold enough to build it. The original vision was us against the world and too quickly we devolved into you vs me. Be better.

Primary Analysis Methods Predictors generally use three distinct frameworks to forecast price movements: 1. In 2026, this increasingly involves AI-driven pattern recognition to spot trends faster than human traders. 2. Fundamental Analysis (FA): Evaluates the "intrinsic" value of a project. Sentiment Analysis: Leverages natural language processing (NLP) to scan social media (X, Reddit, Discord) and news outlets. AI & Quantum Concerns: Speculation now includes the "Quantum Threat" to cryptography and the integration of AI agents that execute trades autonomously 24/7. Machine Learning Models Professional analysts now rely on advanced computational models rather than simple intuition: LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory): A type of neural network specifically designed to predict time-series data like crypto prices. I’m honestly not sure where to begin with this post, because it misrepresents the work at a pretty basic level. 1) He clearly hasn’t read the foundational work on the power law. The core result is not “price follows a power law” in isolation. The time-based power law emerges from two underlying network relationships: Addresses ∼ t³ — viral network growth, similar to the early Internet Price ∼ Addresses² — a Metcalfe-like scaling relationship Together, these produce the observed price ∼ t⁵·⁸ power law in time. On top of that, we’ve written extensively about Bitcoin as a self-organized critical system, which provides a solid physical and network-theoretic framework for understanding why these scaling laws emerge in the first place. 2) The claim that “other assets show the same behavior” is simply false. The entire point is that Bitcoin is unique among known assets in exhibiting long-term power-law growth (a straight line on a log–log plot across multiple orders of magnitude). Traditional assets follow exponential growth tied to inflation and GDP. Anyone claiming that other assets form straight lines on log–log plots over several orders of magnitude is misunderstanding basic scaling behavior. This isn’t a subtle point; it’s an elementary distinction between power laws and exponentials. 3) The power law is not a bubble model. The power law describes the long-term structural trend. Bubbles are short-term deviations around that trend and largely cancel out over long horizons. What seems to confuse people (and I’ve clarified this many times) is that you can take the power law as a reference curve and study the residuals — what’s left after removing the long-term trend — to see whether there are secondary patterns. We did this and observed that peak deviations appeared to decay over time, roughly exponentially. This allowed us to place a conservative upper bound on how extreme future bubbles might get. If anything, the ~$200k figure was a warning against much more aggressive claims like $444k, $500k, or $1M during that cycle. But this residual analysis is not the power law itself; it’s an auxiliary observation layered on top of the main model. Given that we didn’t even get a proper bubble this cycle, the power law is, if anything, statistically stronger than before. The fit has improved over time, and the correlation coefficient — one measure of model quality — has continued to increase. Bottom line: this post misinforms people by mixing up basic concepts and misrepresenting the underlying work. If you’re going to criticize a model, at least take the time to understand what it actually says. Sherlock, it is elementary, just Bitcoin looks like a straight line in the log-log graph below.

Epstein & Crypto: Everything You Need to Know Jeffrey Epstein was an American financier who moved in circles with politicians, billionaires, and celebrities. He was charged with running a sex trafficking network involving minors. In 2019, he was arrested and later died in jail before trial. In the so-called “Epstein files” and released emails, references surfaced to his investments, contacts, and discussions related to crypto. 1/ $3M Early Investment in Coinbase In 2014, Epstein invested roughly $3 million in Coinbase. At the time, it was just a crypto startup — not the publicly listed giant it later became. Part of that stake was reportedly sold later at a profit. 2/ Investment in Blockstream and MIT Connection Epstein also participated in funding Blockstream, a company focused on Bitcoin infrastructure. His personal investment was reported to be around $50,000, routed through structures connected to MIT. Blockstream CEO Adam Back stated: “It was a small investment with no further involvement.” 3/ Donations to Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) From 2002 to 2017, Epstein donated approximately $850,000 to MIT. Part of those funds supported programs that funded Bitcoin developers. In a 2015 email, Epstein wrote: “I was able to fill the funding vacuum for developers.” 4/ Brock Pierce as a Key Crypto Contact Tether co-founder Brock Pierce reportedly communicated with Epstein for years. In a 2018 email, Epstein wrote: “Pierce taught me everything related to cryptocurrency.” 5/ His View on Bitcoin (Based on Emails) — 2011: Called Bitcoin “an interesting idea with serious problems.” — 2014: Discussed vulnerabilities of a public blockchain. — 2017: Responded negatively when asked whether he was buying BTC. LITECOIN (LTC) PRICE: WHAT DRIVES IT AND WHERE TO TRACK IT Intro Litecoin (LTC) is one of the oldest cryptocurrencies. Its price is not random, it mainly reacts to market direction, supply changes and how much the network is used. Understanding these basics helps traders read LTC moves more clearly. Why Does Litecoin Often Follow Bitcoin? Litecoin usually moves in the same direction as Bitcoin. Both use Proof of Work, have halving cycles and attract similar traders. When Bitcoin rises, large cap coins like LTC often follow. When Bitcoin falls, Litecoin usually pulls back as well. How Do Halvings and Network Activity Affect LTC? Halvings slow the creation of new LTC by cutting mining rewards. This reduces supply growth, which can support price if demand stays strong. Network activity also matters. More transactions, active wallets, and a strong hash rate often signal healthy usage and long-term value. Where Can You Track or Trade Litecoin? Common platforms used for LTC include: Binance – high liquidity Coinbase – regulated access Bitget – spot and derivatives Kraken – security-focused CoinMarketCap / CoinGecko – price tracking, no trading. Each platform serves different needs, from trading to simple monitoring. CONCLUSION Litecoin’s price is mainly driven by Bitcoin’s trend, halving cycles, and network activity. Knowing these factors helps traders avoid reacting to short-term noise. FAQ Does Litecoin move independently from Bitcoin? Usually no. Bitcoin leads the market. Do halvings guarantee price increases? No. Demand still matters. Where can I check live LTC prices? On major exchanges and tracking sites like Binance, Coinbase, Kraken, Bitget, CoinMarketCap, and CoinGecko.

Stefan Thomas is a German programmer and early Bitcoin developer who received 7,002 BTC in 2011 as payment for creating one of the first educational videos explaining Bitcoin. At the time, the coins were worth only a few thousand dollars, but as Bitcoin surged over the years, their value climbed to more than $600 million. To secure the Bitcoin, Thomas stored the private keys on an IronKey USB drive, a highly secure encrypted device. The problem is that IronKey allows only 10 password attempts before permanently wiping its contents. Thomas has already used eight attempts and can no longer remember the correct password. With only two guesses left, his situation has become one of the most well known cautionary tales in crypto history. While some cybersecurity firms claim they can help break into the device, Thomas has been extremely cautious, knowing that one wrong move could erase the fortune forever. The story highlights one of Bitcoin’s core principles and biggest risks: full self custody. Without the private key, no bank, company, or government can help recover the funds, no matter how valuable they are, turning digital freedom into a brutal test of responsibility.

My phone was face-down on the table. Face-down because if it was face-up she would see the notifications. She reached across the table and touched my hand. She said: "You seem far away." I said: "I'm right here." I was not right here. I was thinking something that changed the way I saw everything. She asked what I was thinking about. I said: "Just you." She squeezed my hand. Her eyes were doing something I never want to see again. I said: "Wait. Wait wait wait. I need to explain." She said: "Then explain." I took a breath. January 10, 2009. While the world grappled with financial collapse and bank bailouts, a cryptographer named Hal Finney sat at his computer in Temple City, California, downloading something that would change everything. "Running bitcoin," Finney tweeted on January 11th, a simple five-word message that now reads like Neil Armstrong's first words from the lunar surface. At that moment, only two computers in the entire world were participating in this radical experiment: Satoshi's machine somewhere in cyberspace, and Finney's desktop humming quietly in suburban LA. The network consisted of exactly two nodes, mining blocks, validating transactions, and keeping each other honest in a dance of cryptographic trust. Then came January 12th, 2009. At 3:30 PM Pacific Time, Satoshi sent 10 bitcoins to Hal Finney's wallet address in what became transaction number 170 on the blockchain. No banks. No clearing houses. No government oversight. Just pure mathematics moving value from one person to another across the internet, validated by code that both men trusted more than any institution. The transaction fee was zero, the confirmation took minutes, and human civilization quietly crossed a threshold it didn't even know existed. That modest transfer of 10 bitcoins, worth absolutely nothing at the time, represents the exact moment when money became programmable. Finney received those coins not knowing they would one day be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, but understanding perfectly that he was catching the first pitch in a game that would rewrite the rules of finance itself. Every cryptocurrency transaction since then traces its lineage back to that winter afternoon when two computers proved that strangers could trust math more than governments. For years, most BTC liquidity has remained underutilized, trapped in a static state, waiting for infrastructure that allows it to participate meaningfully. Traditional scaling solutions have attempted to bend or layer Bitcoin. Increase throughput. Create secondary networks. Wrap or mirror assets to chase functionality found on other chains. Each of these approaches introduces complexity, friction, or risk. Each subtly shifts the economic center away from Bitcoin itself. Capital may move, but ownership, coordination, and native utility often suffer in the process. beyond__tech takes an entirely different approach. Rather than changing the base layer, it expands the environment around Bitcoin. Liquidity, trading, and financial primitives are designed to operate natively where the asset already resides. Assets do not need to leave Bitcoin’s domain to participate in multichain ecosystems. Ownership remains direct. Auditability remains transparent. Security assumptions remain unaltered. This is an infrastructure-first philosophy. The goal is not temporary solutions, hype cycles, or incremental improvements. The goal is systemic coordination. To turn fragmented capital into a coherent, interoperable economic network. To allow liquidity to flow where it is needed without compromising trust or sovereignty. Ethereum, Solana, BNB Chain, Arbitrum, and other major ecosystems collectively hold hundreds of billions more in locked liquidity. Bitcoin L2 networks such as Bitlayer and Core are emerging, each demanding robust access to both base layer assets and external ecosystems. New standards like Runes and Taproot Assets are expanding the asset universe further, creating additional pathways for value. Individually, these ecosystems are powerful. Collectively, they are disjointed. Liquidity resides in silos, isolated by technical and architectural boundaries. Movement often requires wrapping, bridging, or synthetic representations that introduce friction, complexity, and risk. Beyond does not try to bridge these silos superficially. It builds the connective framework that lets Bitcoin’s liquidity remain anchored while interacting seamlessly with other chains. EchoPorts and other primitives create verifiable state anchoring. Interoperability layers allow assets to flow without leaving their native home. Developers gain composable building blocks rather than rebuilding bridges repeatedly. Users experience movement without losing trust or control. When liquidity remains anchored on Bitcoin, the economic center of gravity shifts back to the base layer. Markets behave differently. Builders design differently. Capital becomes productive instead of idle. Activity consolidates rather than fragments. Ecosystems coordinate rather than compete for isolated liquidity. This is not an incremental change. It is structural. Scaling Bitcoin without modifying it. Increasing utility without compromising security. Turning the strongest, most trusted asset in crypto into the backbone of a coordinated multichain financial network. Beyond demonstrates that relevance comes not from altering a foundation, but from enabling it to interact naturally and efficiently with the broader system. Liquidity returns home. Economic activity centers on BTC. Capital becomes sovereign and productive. Financial infrastructure finally grows around the asset itself, not outside it. If this trajectory continues, Bitcoin evolves from a static store of value into a living, dynamic engine of multichain finance. Not by bending to external ecosystems. Not by relying on synthetic representations. But by expanding its functional reach while preserving its security, integrity, and identity. This is ultra-large scale Bitcoin evolution. Here's what Stripe gets wrong about Bitcoin. They're right that Bitcoin is too slow for agent payments. 10 TPS with 10-minute confirmation times doesn't work when agents need sub-second settlement. But they're making the classic category error: judging Bitcoin as a payment rail when it's actually a reserve asset. Think about it from an agent's perspective. An autonomous agent that controls capital needs two things: a medium of exchange (fast, cheap, programmable) and a store of value (scarce, verifiable, trust-minimized). Stablecoins solve the first problem. They're fast, cheap, and denominated in units humans understand. Bitcoin solves the second problem. And here's why agents will prefer it over every alternative: Provable scarcity. 21 million. Period. An agent can mathematically verify Bitcoin's supply cap by running a node. No trust required. No counterparty. No central bank policy to model. For an AI system optimizing for long-term capital preservation, this is the only asset where supply uncertainty is literally zero. Thermodynamic backing. Bitcoin's security is grounded in energy expenditure. The hashrate represents real-world thermodynamic work that cannot be faked, reversed, or inflated away. For an agent evaluating asset security, energy-backed finality is a fundamentally different trust model than validator-staked finality. Settlement finality without permission. An agent holding Bitcoin doesn't need Stripe's permission, a bank's approval, or a government's cooperation to custody its own wealth. In a world where AI agents may operate across jurisdictions with competing regulatory frameworks, sovereign self-custody isn't a feature. It's a requirement. No governance risk. Tempo has "compliance integrations" and "opt-in privacy." Translation: there's a kill switch. An agent sophisticated enough to manage capital is sophisticated enough to evaluate governance risk. Bitcoin has no board, no foundation with override authority, no compliance layer that can freeze funds. The future isn't Bitcoin OR stablecoins. It's Bitcoin AND stablecoins. Agents will transact in stablecoins on rails like Tempo and settle reserves in Bitcoin. The same way corporations today transact in dollars but hold treasury in assets that preserve purchasing power. Stripe is building the nervous system for agentic commerce. Bitcoin is the skeleton. You need both. Stripe just doesn't know they need Bitcoin yet. The $1.9 trillion insight: Stripe sees payments. They don't see reserves. And in a world of autonomous agents managing autonomous capital, the reserve layer matters more than the payment layer. My website got flagged as "Dangerous" by Google yesterday. Here's what happened. I opened Chrome, typed in my own URL, and got a full-screen red warning page. "Attackers on the site you tried visiting might trick you into installing software oR revealing your passwords." My heart dropped. I'd just started getting real users. People who signed up, tried the product, and came back. And now anyone visiting was being told my site was dangerous. I immediately audited everything. Every script, every API call, every dependency. The codebase was clean. No malware, nO phishing, no suspicious code. It was a false positive. Turns out, Google's automated Safe Browsing scanner sometimes flags new crypto/finance sites. No specific page was cited. No explanation. Just a label: "Deceptive pages." The fix? Submit a review request through Google Search Console and wait. That's it. You just wait while your site sits behind a red warning screen and your users can't get in. It got cleared in about a day. But those hours felt long. A few things I took away from this: 1. Reputation systems are powerful. One automated flag and your site is effectively offline across Chrome, Safari, and Firefox 2. Set up Google Search Console before you need it. I had to verify my domain during the crisis, which cost me extra time 3. Keep your security tight anyway. When I audited my code under pressure, I was glad I'd done things properly from the start If you're building in crypto or finance, this might happen to you. It doesn't mean you did anything wrong. Most Bitcoin would be held in offline cold storage, with minimal amounts in hot wallets for creations and redemptions. This institutional-grade security model mirrors the standards set by existing spot Bitcoin ETFs, such as BlackRock's IBIT. 3/ Wealth Client Access via Brokerage Channels The trust targets Morgan Stanley's vast wealth management base, enabling regulated Bitcoin exposure through standard brokerage accounts. Clients could gain BTC allocation without managing private keys or using crypto exchanges, lowering operational barriers and integrating digital assets into traditional portfolio workflows familiar to financial advisors and institutional investors. 4/ Competitive Positioning & Market Impact If approved and actively distributed, the product could channel significant mainstream capital into spot Bitcoin, intensifying competition with established ETF issuers like BlackRock and Fidelity. Real-world impact hinges on fee competitiveness, liquidity depth, and how aggressively Morgan Stanley promotes the trust to its advisor network and high-net-worth clientele. 5/ Strategic Catalysts & Broader Digital Ambition Key monitors: SEC approval timeline, launch terms (fees, liquidity), and actual advisor adoption. Why Bitcoin’s Long-Term Price Follows a Power Law Bitcoin looks chaotic short term. But zoom out and a clear structure appears. Growth proportional to size. In many systems the rate of change scales with the size of the system: dP(t)/dt ∝ P(t) When growth depends on current size, it compounds. You see this everywhere: • populations • cities • internet networks • capital markets Bitcoin adoption behaves the same way. Users → liquidity → security → capital → more users. That feedback loop produces multiplicative growth. Now add the constraint. Bitcoin’s supply is fixed: ≈ 450 BTC per day ≤ 21 million total When demand compounds but supply cannot expand, price must absorb the imbalance. The network grows. Supply cannot. So the adjustment happens in price. Scale invariance. Systems that grow through multiplicative processes often become scale invariant. That means the structure looks similar across different sizes. On a log-log plot, Bitcoin’s long-term fit is remarkably strong: R² ≈ 0.96 Examples: • city size distributions • lightning branching • river networks • crack propagation in materials Different systems. Same scaling logic. Mathematically this property leads to a power law. The scaling law. If growth scales with system size over time, the differential relationship becomes dP(t)/dt ∝ P(t) / t The solution is a power law: P(t) = a · tᵇ On log-log axes this becomes a straight line. That is why log-log charts reveal the structure that linear charts hide. Why cycles happen. Real markets experience shocks. Liquidity leverage news macro events These create deviations from the structural trend. Those deviations behave like a mean-reverting process: dz = −κz dt + σ dW Large deviations create stronger restoring drift. So price oscillates around the structural growth path. The path is noisy. The structure is not. Bitcoin combines four ingredients that naturally produce power laws: • multiplicative network growth • a hard supply constraint • scale-invariant adoption • periodic supply halvings The cycles are noise. The power law is the signal.

The libertarian dream turned nightmare. “Be your own bank!” Yeah, until you lose your keys and become “your own broke.” “Banks hate this!” Banks love it— they’re the ones custodying your ETFs and lending against your collateral. “Financial freedom!” Freedom to lose everything in 24 hours because some whale decided to take profits. Crypto markets, you are the emperor with no clothes, the wizard behind a curtain made of spaghetti code and venture capital, the Ponzi that keeps promising utopia but delivers bagholders and regret. A smart contract can execute perfectly, but it cannot naturally answer simple questions like: ▸ What’s the current price of Bitcoin? ▸ Did a football team win a match? ▸ What’s today’s weather in Lagos? ▸ Did a shipment arrive at its destination? Without reliable external data, smart contracts are essentially running powerful code inside a sealed box. That’s where oracle networks become essential. But not all oracles are created equal. Many traditional oracle systems rely on centralized data providers, which introduces a dangerous vulnerability. Many vesting schedules are completed within a single market cycle. After that point the full supply is circulating. A blockchain protocol is often described as long term infrastructure something that could support applications, assets, and economies for decades. Yet the token distribution model often resembles a startup fundraising cycle rather than long-term economic planning. This creates a structural tension. On one side, the vision is multi-decade infrastructure. On the other, the incentives are built around relatively short liquidity timelines. Another question worth considering: If the token is essential for the network, why distribute the majority of supply over only a few years? Traditional infrastructure systems often think in decades. Some crypto networks like bitcoin distribute supply over more than a century. Whether tokenomics are designed in a way that truly supports the long-term vision many protocols claim to pursue. If blockchains aim to become real financial infrastructure, their economic design may need to evolve toward longer time horizons rather than just the next vesting cycle.

No CPI updates, no weekly jobless claims, many official reports delayed. That removes critical points of reference for the markets. In that environment, even big funds and the Fed are flying a bit blind. Models stop working properly, risk becomes harder to gauge, and uncertainty naturally pushes volatility higher. Another factor is trust. A serious shutdown could even trigger debates about the US credit rating. In these moments, large capital typically moves to safe havens: gold, silver and cash. Liquidity is also tighter than it used to be. The RRP pools have shrunk noticeably in recent months, leaving the system with less of a buffer. Funding markets might lock up if banks and dealers start holding onto cash, which could trigger sharp, sudden moves. A shutdown also affects the economy. Historically, each week can shave roughly 0.2% off GDP. If it drags on, it could push an already slowing economy closer to technical recession. But here’s the key: markets often price in the news before it actually happens. If a real shutdown hits, the typical sequence looks like this: First, shock and sell-off. Then, a liquidity response from the system. Finally, a strong rebound. History has shown this repeatedly. The real question is: who will win in this scenario? Bitcoin? Or Gold?

Here is the breakdown. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ THE PROBLEM BITCOIN'S BASE LAYER CANNOT SOLVE ALONE Bitcoin's base layer was intentionally designed to prioritize two things above everything else: security and decentralization. It does both better than any other network in existence. But that design makes a deliberate trade-off. It does not provide a flexible environment for executing complex financial logic at high throughput. This creates a structural gap. AI agents, DeFi protocols and programmable financial applications require fast execution, low fees and composable smart contracts. Bitcoin's base layer cannot supply these without modification. For years, this gap was treated as irreconcilable. Bitcoin was productive only if you handed your BTC to a custodian or a federated bridge, both of which reintroduce the trust dependencies Bitcoin was built to eliminate. GOATNetwork addresses this directly with a Bitcoin-native ZK Rollup designed to make BTC usable for everyday financial activity without relying on custodians, federations or committee-controlled withdrawals. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ THE ARCHITECTURE: FIVE LAYERS WORKING TOGETHER Understanding GOAT's ZK Rollup means understanding five interlocking components. Each one solves a specific problem. Together, they form a complete system. ◈ Layer 1: Ziren, The Proving Engine Every ZK Rollup needs a mechanism to generate cryptographic proofs. GOAT built its own, called Ziren. Ziren is a production-grade zkVM based on the MIPS32r2 instruction set, a stable RISC architecture known for deterministic execution and minimal circuit overhead. It optimizes zero-knowledge proof generation through efficient zkCompiler design, pipelined proof architecture and a cutting-edge proof system ensuring high instruction efficiency and reduced audit requirements. Ziren is the engine that mathematically certifies every transaction processed off Bitcoin's base layer. It runs efficiently on CPUs, supports GPU hardware acceleration, parallel proving and pipelined scheduling, and can scale to a distributed proving network. The performance figures are significant. Pipelined proof generation cuts block proofs to approximately 2.6 seconds and Groth16 SNARKs to approximately 10.38 seconds by running execution, aggregation and final proofs concurrently. Withdrawal proof generation is strictly controlled within 30 seconds in the worst case, what the team describes as real-time proving, a genuine breakthrough in ZK technology. ◈ Layer 2: Type-1 zkEVM, Full Ethereum Compatibility GOAT's execution environment is a Type-1 zkEVM, fully Ethereum-equivalent. This means every smart contract, every DeFi protocol and every developer tool built for Ethereum works on GOAT without modification. Developers do not need to rewrite applications. The full ecosystem of programmable financial logic becomes deployable on a Bitcoin-secured foundation. ◈ Layer 3: BitVM2, Bitcoin as the Enforcement Layer This is the most technically significant component and the one that separates GOAT from every other Bitcoin L2 in existence. Execution happens off-chain, validity is proven with ZK, and Bitcoin is the enforcement layer for disputes and exits. If any party attempts to submit a fraudulent proof, Bitcoin itself arbitrates the dispute. No external committee required. No trusted validator set. No federated multisig. GOAT BitVM2 introduces a chain-based synchronization primitive enabling operators to share collateral across multiple reimbursements, and an Atomic Swap supporting arbitrary withdrawal amounts, together delivering a user-friendly bridge experience without custodial assumptions. The impact on finality is substantial. GOAT BitVM2 compresses the challenge period from the original 14 days to less than one day, making it the most performant and closest-to-real-deployment BitVM2 architecture currently available. ◈ Layer 4: Decentralized Sequencer, No Single Point of Failure Most rollup architectures rely on a single sequencer to order transactions. That sequencer is a centralization risk. If it fails, the network stops. If it is compromised, the ordering of transactions can be manipulated. GOAT employs a permissionless decentralized ordering protocol through which all cross-chain messages, including asset deposits, withdrawals and layer two state rollups, simultaneously gain consensus from both Bitcoin and the GOAT Network layer two, eliminating reliance on any centralized entity. GOAT was the first to launch a decentralized sequencer network in the Bitcoin ecosystem and remains the only one. ◈ Layer 5: Dual Slashing, Cryptographic Accountability GOAT introduced the first dual slashing mechanism for Bitcoin Layer 2 networks. Both sequencers and operators face cryptographic penalties for dishonest behavior. Not social consequences. Not reputational risk. Provable, enforceable on-chain penalties that make attacking the system economically irrational. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ WHY THIS MATTERS FOR AI AGENTS Each layer of this architecture addresses a specific requirement that autonomous AI agents place on financial infrastructure. Agents need fast finality so their operations are not locked in pending states across multi-day withdrawal windows. Ziren's real-time proving solves this. Agents need composable execution so they can interact with DeFi protocols, payment systems and other agents seamlessly. The Type-1 zkEVM solves this. Agents need trustless asset movement so no custodian can freeze their funds or reverse their transactions. BitVM2 solves this. Agents need infrastructure that cannot fail at a single point. The decentralized sequencer solves this. Agents need cryptographic accountability across the entire system. Dual slashing solves this. As a Bitcoin-native ZK Rollup, GOAT processes transactions off-chain using zkMIPS, verifies proofs on Bitcoin via BitVM2, reduces withdrawal finality from days to hours, and uses BTC for gas fees, creating a closed-loop economy where agents earn, transact and compound entirely within Bitcoin's monetary foundation. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ THE BOTTOM LINE GOAT Network's ZK Rollup is not a marketing claim about Bitcoin scalability. It is a precisely engineered stack: Ziren for proving, Type-1 zkEVM for execution, BitVM2 for Bitcoin-enforced dispute resolution, a decentralized sequencer for censorship-resistant ordering, and dual slashing for cryptographic accountability. Together they enable BTC to function as productive capital without surrendering the properties that make it worth holding in the first place. GOATNetwork ZKRollup

A Metal Side Story " Every system begins w/ a builder." In the quiet hills of Upstate New York, a young boy named Marshall grew up surrounded by the hum of possibility. His grandfather had built a career in finance at Merrill Lynch, setting up offices and navigating the old world of money- stocks, bonds, and boardrooms. From family stories and visits, Marshall absorbed an early sense of how money moved, but he felt something missing: freedom, speed, and fairness for everyone, not just the privileged few. As a teenager and college student at Northeastern University in Boston, Marshall was drawn to the internet's rebellious underbelly. He tinkered with decentralized file-sharing networks like Napster, fascinated by how technology could bypass gatekeepers and empower ordinary people. The world of centralized control felt outdated; he dreamed of systems where individuals held real power. Then, in late 2009, while still in his early twenties and studying (though he would soon drop out to chase bigger ideas), Marshall discovered Bitcoin. It hit him like lightning: a decentralized currency of the internet, peer-to-peer, no banks required. "There will be signs," he might have thought, sensing the inevitable shift. He dove in, mining early blocks, joining forums, and connecting with pioneers who shared his vision of financial freedom and empowerment for the common person. Inspired by innovators like Steve Jobs-who rethought what was possible-Marshall moved to San Francisco in 2011, the epicenter of tech disruption. He launched QuickCoin in 2013, one of the first social Bitcoin wallets integrated with Facebook, making crypto accessible to everyday users. He contributed to the Stellar Foundation, obsessed over Dogecoin's fun yet powerful community (where he met his future co-founder, Glenn Mariën, builder of an early Dogecoin wallet), and served on the Dogecoin Foundation board. But Marshall saw limits in the early crypto ethos. Pure rebellion against banks wouldn't scale; the revolution needed bridges, not walls. He believed crypto could transform payments with transparency, efficiency, and programmability-while working within regulations to reach the masses, especially underserved communities like credit unions and small businesses. In 2017, with that conviction burning bright, Marshall co-founded Metallicus. It started small-a vision to build compliant blockchain infrastructure that merged traditional finance with digital assets. He and Glenn poured years into it: launching Metal Pay in 2018 (pairing regulated bank accounts with crypto trading), creating the XPR Network for fast, feeless transactions, developing decentralized identity for security and compliance, and architecting Metal Blockchain as a foundation for institutions. Through market crashes, regulatory battles, and endless building, Marshall held to his core ideology: crypto's original promise of freedom and empowerment, matured into pragmatic, inclusive infrastructure. He pushed for "compliance-first" systems that prevented scams and sanctioned misuse while keeping keys in users' hands. Metallicus grew into a leader in bridging worlds-banks, credit unions, and blockchain- proving that innovation could serve the little guy without selling out to Wall Street. Today, the boy from Upstate New York leads a company that's turning his teenage dream into reality: a world where money moves freely, securely, and fairly for all. As he often reflects, when the founders stood for something real-freedom, empowerment-the path forward was always about building, not destroying. And there will be signs of more to come. Bitcoin SV uses the BEEF (Background Evaluation Extended Format) specification, improving how transactions are validated at scale. In traditional blockchain validation, nodes must query their UTXO databases to retrieve previous transactions before they can verify new ones. At high transaction volumes, repeated database lookups create significant overhead: - disk reads - latency - increased infrastructure load BEEF allows transactions to include additional verification data. Instead of transaction processors retrieving this information from their databases, the sender provides it directly with the transaction. Korean Police Struggle to Find Custodian for Seized Crypto Assets South Korean police are facing difficulties finding a private company to manage seized cryptocurrency assets as repeated asset leakage incidents have raised concerns over custody security. According to the National Police Agency, three separate bids for a cryptocurrency custody service last year all failed. The tenders held on November 6, November 21, and December 2 attracted some applicants, but none met the qualification requirements. Currently, about 27 companies in South Korea are licensed to handle cryptocurrency transfers and custody services. However, many of them are relatively small firms. Major exchanges such as Upbit and Bithumb did not participate in the bidding process. The main issue appears to be the imbalance between responsibility and profitability. Managing seized crypto assets involves strict regulatory procedures and significant liability in case of loss or hacking, while the financial incentive for service providers remains limited. From the authorities’ perspective, using a company that operates both custody services and an exchange platform would be more efficient. Such firms could manage the entire process, including asset storage, liquidation, and confiscation procedures within criminal investigations. Despite this, industry participants remain cautious due to regulatory uncertainty surrounding digital asset custody businesses in Korea. The police plan to revise the bidding conditions and budget before issuing a new tender after April. In short: The government needs a company to safeguard seized crypto, but the responsibility is high and the economic incentive is low—so few firms are willing to take the job. Metaplanet released a few disclosures today - here's how I read them: First to recap - three disclosures: 1) the establishment of Metaplanet Ventures K.K. in Tokyo 2) under MP Ventures, an investment of up to ¥400 million in JPYC (Japan's first regulated yen stablecoin) 3) the creation of Metaplanet Asset Management Inc. in Miami. I don't think the timing or nature of these announcements is a coincidence - under two weeks before the AGM. In my view, this is laying the groundwork for what's to come. Also, it's a further step towards building a vertically integrated operating company around its Bitcoin treasury — and this optionality is currently not priced into the stock valuation, as I layed out in my quoted post below "Metaplanet Valuation Framework". 1) Metaplanet Ventures Metaplanet Ventures will deploy approximately ¥4 billion over two to three years across venture investments, an incubator program, and an open-source grants program — all funded by cash flows from the Bitcoin Income Generation business. They explicitly state that companies incubated through this program "with strong strategic alignment may be acquired or integrated into the Metaplanet group." Pure speculation on my part but my read here is that this is a precursor to announcing Project Nova at the AGM on March 25, which will be seeded through this vehicle and potentially fully integrated. 2) JPYC Investment Metaplanet is investing up to ¥400 million in JPYC Inc.'s Series B. JPYC completed its first close in late February, raising about ¥1.78 billion (~$12 million) led by Asteria Corporation, with participation from BitFlyer Holdings, JR West Innovations, and entities linked to Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance. So that puts Metaplanet at ~20% of the round. The valuation hasn't been publicly disclosed as far as I can see, but JPYC has raised approximately $18 million in total across four rounds. While not exactly like for like in terms of TAM, we can look at some reference points. Circle went public in June 2025 at a valuation of ~$6.9 billion, with about $60 billion in USDC circulation at the time. USDC has since grown to ~$75 billion. Circle generated $2.7 billion in revenue for full-year 2025; so listed at ~2.5x revenue. Tether, I beleive generates >$10 billion annually in profit on $187 billion in assets. These are obviously massive numbers, and reflective of the USD stablecoin market having by far the largest TAM. The JPY stablecoin TAM is obviously much smaller, but Japan has over $10 trillion in household savings earning near-zero interest, a massive domestic payments ecosystem, and is now building one of the most advanced stablecoin regulatory frameworks globally. If JPYC captures even a fraction of domestic settlement and remittance flows, this investment could provide a very significant return. Furthermore, JPYC will be the settlement layer for Metaplanet's own financial services — lending, collateral, tokenized securities, wallet infrastructure. So it's ultimately a vertical integration for them. 3) Metaplanet Asset Management Let me start by saying that I spent ten years working in the asset management industry, investing long only and hedge funds - so I'm quite familiar with the economics. Asset management is one of the best business models in finance. Once you raise the capital, fees are recurring. Unlike deal-based investment banking or trading, your revenue compounds as AUM grows. And in a sector like Bitcoin-related financial products — where the investable universe is expanding rapidly — the opportunity to build a first-mover franchise is substantial. The filing lists its business as "development of asset management business, including Bitcoin-related investment products, capital markets advisory, and related regulatory infrastructure." They specifically mention perpetual preferred securities and related fixed income instruments (Digital Credit), actively managed derivative strategies, equity and credit strategies focused on Bitcoin treasury companies, and index products. Once again pure speculation, but this could potentially also be a vehicle to issue preferred securities into the US market. What This Means for Valuation The market is pricing Metaplanet as a static pile of Bitcoin. These disclosures prove they are building a diversified and fully integrated Bitcoin financial services company with multiple revenue streams, strategic equity stakes, and a capital markets platform that spans Japan and the US. That's not to mention, the value of their current capital markets access and ability to arbitrage and capture flows to grow BTC/share. In addition to a proven track record with BIG, generating ~$55M revenue in 2025 and expected to achieve >$100M in 2026. Jan, you touched on a very important point. I largely agree with you - but there is an interesting nuance in the Bitcoin ecosystem worth mentioning. Bitcoin itself does not provide native staking or yield. Its design is intentionally minimal: security, scarcity, and decentralization. But yield around BTC does exist through Layer-2 infrastructure, particularly through Stacks. Stacks is a Layer-2 network that brings smart contracts and dApps to Bitcoin without modifying the base protocol. In other words, it allows BTC capital to participate in DeFi and Web3 while remaining anchored to Bitcoin’s security. Key ideas behind Stacks: • Proof of Transfer (PoX) – miners spend BTC to mine Stacks blocks and earn STX • Stacking – STX holders lock tokens and receive rewards paid in BTC • Clarity – a predictable smart-contract language designed for security • Nakamoto upgrade – faster blocks and stronger Bitcoin-level finality • sBTC – a 1:1 BTC-backed asset enabling BTC liquidity in smart contracts So while Bitcoin itself remains purely scarcity-driven, its Layer-2 ecosystem is gradually turning BTC into productive capital. This is not just another geopolitical headline. Oil shocks have a history of breaking financial markets. Let me explain: US officials say Iran has laid sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway responsible for moving roughly 20% of the world’s oil supply. That might sound like a distant military story, but financially it is one of the most sensitive choke points on Earth. The Strait of Hormuz is about 21 miles wide, but the actual shipping lanes used by oil tankers are only about 2 miles wide. Almost all tanker traffic is forced through that tiny corridor. Now imagine what happens if mines appear there. Iran reportedly has more than 5,000 naval mines ready to deploy. It does not take thousands to disrupt global energy markets. Even a few hundred placed inside the shipping lanes could make the route too dangerous for tankers. And markets do not wait for mines to explode. They price the risk immediately. Insurance rates for oil tankers spike. Shipping companies hesitate to enter the area. Some vessels reroute while others delay shipments completely. Suddenly one fifth of global oil supply is at risk. When traders see that kind of threat, oil prices can move extremely fast. Analysts already warn crude could surge toward $150 to $200 per barrel if the Strait becomes unsafe. That is where the real economic pressure begins. Energy sits at the core of the global economy. When oil jumps sharply, transportation becomes more expensive, manufacturing costs rise, and food prices follow. Inflation pressures return and central banks are forced to keep policy tighter for longer. Risk assets usually suffer in that environment. Stocks weaken. Liquidity tightens. Speculative markets feel the pressure first. Now here is the part most people miss. Markets do not need the worst case scenario to happen. They only need investors to believe it might. If traders begin to think the Strait of Hormuz is becoming too dangerous to use, the fear alone can trigger massive volatility across global markets. However, for years, it hasn't been truly optimized for large-scale payment transactions or stablecoins. Projects like Utexo are trying to change that by combining: - Bitcoin's security - Lightning's speed - Stablecoin liquidity Utexo could help transform Bitcoin into the global payment infrastructure for the digital dollar. TRON teams up with Mastercard in global crypto collaboration TRON has joined Mastercard’s Crypto Partner Program as the payments company expands coordination with blockchain, fintech, and banking participants working on digital asset payments. The move places TRON among more than 85 companies participating in a Mastercard-led initiative to link blockchain-based payment infrastructure with existing financial networks. According to statements from TRON DAO and Mastercard, the program is designed to support collaboration on practical use cases, including cross-border remittances, business-to-business transfers, payouts, and settlement. Mastercard expands partner network for on-chain payments Mastercard said the Crypto Partner Program was created to bring together crypto-native firms, payment providers, and financial institutions as digital assets move toward broader real-world use. The company explained the endeavor as a place to engage in dialogue and collaborate as blockchain-based payment activity increasingly works in tandem with traditional finance, providing the background support to real-world financial activities. In its release, Mastercard reported that enterprise and institutional applications are becoming increasingly popular, especially for payments out, cross-border money movement, settlement, and B2B transfers. According to the company, it is aimed to integrate the speed and programmability of digital assets with the current card rails and global trade flows. TRON DAO claimed that its involvement was based on the view that the next stage of on-chain payments will be collaborative. The organization also stated that integrating blockchain infrastructure with payment networks is increasing in importance as digital assets come to closer to usefulness. The program expands upon previous Mastercard Bitcoin program activities, such as its Start Path accelerator track to blockchain and digital asset startups and its Engage platform, which includes a crypto card program. Stablecoins and settlement tools form core of program At the center of Mastercard’s broader crypto strategy is its Multi-Token Network, or MTN, which the company uses as a private settlement layer connecting tokenized bank deposits and regulated stablecoins across financial institutions. Mastercard also highlighted its Crypto Credential tool, which replaces wallet addresses with human-readable identifiers and automates compliance checks intended to reduce transaction errors. The partner program includes exchanges and digital asset firms such as Binance, PayPal, Ripple, Circle, Gemini, Paxos, OKX, and Bybit. It also includes infrastructure providers such as Fireblocks, Chainalysis, MoonPay, and Worldpay. Mastercard’s recent product rollouts also connect to this strategy. In late February, the company launched the MetaMask Card in the United States in partnership with ConsenSys and Monavate. The card allows users to make payments with USDC, USDT, mUSD, and yield-bearing tokens, such as aUSDC, via Aave. Mastercard said the product is also active in Switzerland, the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom, Canada, Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, and Mexico. Earlier in March, Mastercard also announced that it had secured SoFi Technologies as a stablecoin settlement partner. I asked Grok two questions: 1) Is it accurate to say TCP/IP protocol changes have followed an asymptotic ossification approach? 2) Would asymptotic ossification be beneficial to Bitcoin if you prioritized immutable money? Asymptotic ossification: the progressive slowdown in a protocol's rate of meaningful evolution toward near-zero. Grok said YES to both. Food for thought 1) First question regarding TCP/IP protocol: **Yes, it's reasonably accurate** to describe the evolution of the core TCP/IP protocols as having followed an **asymptotic ossification** approach — though with some nuance on the terminology and exact framing. "**Ossification**" is a well-established term in networking research and IETF discussions. It refers to the progressive **hardening** or **freezing** of protocols like TCP and (to a lesser extent) IP, where they become extremely resistant to meaningful change. This happens primarily because: - Widespread deployment creates a massive installed base (end hosts, OS kernels, applications). - Middleboxes (firewalls, NATs, load balancers, performance proxies) make brittle assumptions about packet formats, options, flags, and behaviors → they drop or mangle anything unfamiliar. - Changes require near-universal coordination and backward compatibility, which grows exponentially harder as adoption scales. The result is that the rate of **significant, in-protocol evolution** (new options, header changes, semantic modifications) has slowed dramatically over time — approaching zero for core TCP fields and behaviors. Why "asymptotic"? The word "asymptotic" captures this dynamic well: - Early days (1970s–1990s): rapid evolution — multiple major TCP versions, new options (timestamps, window scaling, SACK), IP mobility ideas, etc. - 2000s onward: incremental tweaks still occur (e.g., TCP Fast Open, MPTCP), but deployment is slow/painful, designs are heavily constrained by middlebox behavior, and many extensions fail or take years/decades. - Today: core TCP is largely **frozen** in practice. Meaningful changes to the wire image or semantics are avoided because they break too much of the Internet. The curve of "ability to evolve" flattens toward an asymptote near zero. This matches descriptions across sources: - TCP is described as "significantly ossified," making extension/modification difficult. - QUIC was explicitly designed with anti-ossification measures (UDP base, full encryption of transport headers, minimal ossifiable wire image) precisely because TCP had become too rigid. - Measurements show ~1/3 of paths have middleboxes that modify TCP metadata, and ~6.5% cause harmful ossification effects. Caveats / Where it's not a perfect fit - **IP itself** has ossified less severely than TCP (e.g., ECN, flow labels, some extension headers still work), but core IPv4 is very stable. - Some evolution still happens — just slowly and carefully (e.g., TCP congestion control variants in user space or via pluggable modules). - The phrase "asymptotic ossification approach" implies this was a deliberate strategy, but it was more an **emergent consequence** of success + deployment dynamics than an intentional "approach." In summary: the core TCP/IP protocols have indeed exhibited **asymptotic-like ossification** — rapid early change → progressively slower → now very hard to evolve in-place. That's why new transports like QUIC are built on UDP and encrypt everything that middleboxes might ossify. The description is accurate in spirit and commonly accepted in networking literature. 2) Second question regarding Bitcoin protocol: **Yes — if your top priority is truly immutable money** (in the sense of a monetary protocol whose core rules, especially the 21 million supply cap and the prohibition on arbitrary inflation/reissuance, are effectively unchangeable forever), then **asymptotic ossification** of the Bitcoin protocol would be highly beneficial, and arguably essential. This mirrors the TCP/IP analogy we discussed: just as TCP became so widely deployed and brittle (due to middleboxes, OS kernels, applications) that meaningful core changes became nearly impossible, Bitcoin's consensus rules can reach a point where even soft forks become extremely risky or impossible without near-universal agreement. That "asymptotic" flattening — change rate → 0 — is exactly what protects the monetary properties from mutation. Key Benefits for Prioritizing Immutable Money 1. **Preserves the Hard Supply Cap as Sacred** The 21 million BTC limit is enforced by consensus rules. Any change that could enable inflation (e.g., raising the cap, altering halvings, introducing tail emission) would require a **hard fork** (non-backward-compatible). Once the network is large enough (economic weight in nodes, miners, holders, institutions), coordinating such a change becomes politically and practically infeasible — no single group or even majority can force it without splitting the chain and losing the majority hashpower/economic value. Ossification cements this as effectively immutable. 2. **Prevents Feature Creep That Risks Dilution** Bitcoin maximalists (e.g., Jameson Lopp, Michael Saylor in recent debates) argue that every protocol change introduces vectors for: - Centralization pressure (e.g., complex features favor big players) - Unintended consequences (bugs, new attack surfaces) - Political capture (special interests pushing changes) Ossification forces innovation to **layers** (Lightning, sidechains, Ark, covenants via soft forks if consensus allows, but ideally minimal base-layer changes), keeping the base layer simple, boring, and predictable — like "digital gold" rather than a general-purpose smart-contract platform. 3. **Builds Unshakable Trust in Long-Term Properties** Users and institutions (corporates, nation-states) hold Bitcoin precisely because they believe the rules won't be altered to their detriment. Asymptotic ossification signals maturity: "This is no longer experimental; the monetary rules are frozen." This is why figures like Saylor frame protocol mutability as the "greatest risk" to Bitcoin's value proposition — any perception that rules can still be meaningfully changed undermines the immutability premium. 4. **Analogy to TCP/IP Holds Strongly** TCP/IP ossified because it became infrastructure everyone depends on — changes break too much. Bitcoin aspires to the same status as monetary infrastructure. Once it's deeply embedded (wallets, exchanges, custody, nation-state treasuries), ossification protects it from being "upgraded" into something else, just like IPv4 lingered despite IPv6. Trade-Offs (Even If You Prioritize Immutability) - **Innovation Slows** — Privacy, scaling, efficiency improvements move to L2s or require very conservative soft forks (e.g., Taproot was accepted because it was opt-in and non-disruptive). Some desired features may never make it to base layer. - **Bugs or Design Flaws Get Frozen In** — If something is discovered later that's hard to fix without risk (rare, but possible), you're stuck. - **Contentious Soft Forks Still Possible** — Even in an ossified state, narrow, backward-compatible changes can happen if consensus is overwhelming (e.g., past activations like SegWit). True asymptotic ossification would eventually make even those too risky. Bottom Line If "immutable money" means **rules that cannot be credibly altered in any material way once Bitcoin reaches global/monetary scale**, then **yes — pursuing (or at least accepting) asymptotic ossification is one of the strongest safeguards**. It's the path from "sound money experiment" to "unchangeable monetary constitution." Many prominent Bitcoin thinkers (Lopp, Svetski, and others in recent debates) explicitly argue this is desirable or inevitable for long-term success as immutable money. The alternative — keeping the protocol more malleable — suits platforms that prioritize flexibility and features (Ethereum-style), but it trades off precisely the kind of rock-solid immutability that "digital gold" maximalists value most.

InterLink Network and the New Wave of Blockchain Infrastructure: Why Tokenization Could Become the Major Narrative for 2026–2030 The development of blockchain is opening a new major trend in global finance: the tokenization of real-world assets (Real World Assets – RWA). Instead of using crypto purely for speculation, the market is gradually entering a new phase where traditional assets such as stocks, bonds, ETFs, gold, and real estate are brought onto blockchain networks in the form of tokens. This tokenization process introduces several important changes to the financial system. Assets can be traded more transparently, faster, and 24/7, while allowing investors to access global financial markets through a self-custodied blockchain wallet. This opens the door to a new financial model in which blockchain functions as the infrastructure layer for assets and transactions in the real economy. The Participation of Major Financial Institutions The tokenization trend is not driven only by crypto projects but is increasingly supported by traditional financial institutions. For example, Trust Wallet has integrated infrastructure from Ondo Finance, allowing users to manage tokenized stocks and ETFs directly within their wallet, effectively transforming crypto wallets into a type of global financial asset marketplace. Meanwhile, major financial groups such as SBI Group, Ripple, WisdomTree, and the London Stock Exchange are also developing blockchain platforms for issuing, trading, and settling tokenized assets. A clear example of this trend is the tokenized gold market. Within a short period, the market capitalization of this segment has increased significantly, with tokens such as Tether Gold (XAUT) and PAX Gold (PAXG) dominating the market share. In 2025 alone, the tokenized gold market capitalization grew by approximately 177%, with trading volume reaching around $178 billion. This indicates that more investors are choosing to trade gold on blockchain rather than through physical gold or traditional ETFs. Governments and Regulatory Frameworks Begin Supporting Tokenization Not only private companies, but governments and regulators are also starting to participate in the tokenization wave. Robinhood has proposed a national regulatory framework in the United States for RWA. Dubai has introduced regulations allowing the issuance and trading of tokenized assets, while Japan is developing specialized blockchains designed for tokenized financial asset trading. Even in Vietnam, early signals are emerging. Tether has signed a memorandum of understanding with the city of Da Nang to explore the application of blockchain, digital assets, and potential tokenization models in the future. These developments suggest that tokenization is no longer an experimental concept but is gradually becoming part of the global financial infrastructure for the coming decade. The Shift of Crypto: From Trading to the Real Economy This transformation also reflects a maturing stage of the crypto market. In previous cycles, most capital was concentrated on short-term trading opportunities. However, as institutional capital increasingly enters the space, the market is shifting its focus toward assets that generate stable cash flows and are connected to the real economy. Products such as tokenized U.S. Treasury bonds, investment funds, gold, and commodities are attracting attention because they offer more stable yields and lower risk compared to many purely crypto-native assets. Some forecasts suggest that the RWA market could reach $30 trillion by 2034, marking a major transition where traditional finance and blockchain begin to converge. InterLink Network and the Narrative of “Transaction-Backed Digital Assets” Within this context, a new direction in blockchain development is beginning to emerge: Transaction-Backed Digital Assets. According to kv_interlink , Co-founder of inter_link, blockchain is entering a more mature phase in which the value of networks will not come solely from trading activity, but from real economic activity occurring on-chain. The Transaction-Backed Digital Assets model aims to: •Tokenize businesses •Tokenize commercial transactions •Tokenize cash flows generated from real economic activities In other words, instead of only tokenizing assets, this model also tokenizes economic transactions happening in the real world. This makes Transaction-Backed Digital Assets broader than the traditional RWA concept because: •RWA → focuses on tokenizing assets •Transaction-Backed → tokenizes entire economic activities and transactions If implemented effectively, blockchain could evolve into the infrastructure layer for the digital economy, where businesses, users, and global payment systems are all connected on a unified network. Crypto Cycles and the New Narrative of 2026–2030 The history of blockchain shows that each cycle is defined by a new infrastructure layer: •2013–2017 → Bitcoin and decentralized digital assets •2017–2020 → ICOs and smart contracts •2020–2022 → DeFi and NFTs •2023–2025 → Memecoins and trading ecosystems In the next cycle, the narrative will most likely revolve around: The tokenization of the real economy. If this trend continues to develop, blockchains that focus on connecting businesses, assets, and real economic transactions could become the next foundational infrastructure layer of Web3.
