What are the tax changes that affect crypto taxes in 2026? Beginning this year, the IRS Form 1099-DA will be required to report cost basis of crypto sold or disposed of, in addition to the gross proceeds. In 2025, brokers only had to report "gross proceeds" (what you sold it for). You will receive this new form in early 2027 to help you file your 2026 taxes. It mirrors the Form 1099-B used for stocks. In 2025, you had to track cost basis separately for each wallet or exchange. This did not change for 2026. If you sell Bitcoin on Coinbase, you can only use the cost basis of Bitcoin actually held on Coinbase at that time. You cannot "match" it against Bitcoin sitting in a separate hardware wallet to manipulate your gains/losses. Outside the U.S., 48 countries (including the UK and EU members) began implementing the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) on January 1, 2026. Exchanges in these jurisdictions must now collect detailed user data and transaction history to be shared internationally starting in 2027. The European Union's DAC8 directive also officially took effect on January 1, 2026, standardizing crypto reporting across all member states. While not yet law as of early 2026, there is ongoing legislative discussion regarding applying "wash sale" rules to crypto, which would prevent you from claiming a loss if you rebuy the same asset within 30 days. Presently you can still sell crypto at a loss and repurchase the same crypto immediately without having to defer any losses incurred. Other legislation includes having a de minimis exemption on the amount of crypto sales that would be considered to be taxable. States are also looking to change crypto tax laws. Things continue change with crypto tax laws. Make sure to stay on top of the changes.

There seems to be a lot of FUD floating around about how Bitcoin isn't "fast" because it only settles every 10 minutes. What most don't seem to grasp is that the bitcoin block chain is a settlement layer. It shouldn't be compared to say buying something with a Visa Card at the store. If you think paying with your visa card is a settled transaction then you are quite confused about how our current banking system works. The quickest means to settle a transaction in our current system is via wire transfer and even that often takes a few hours, even an ACH transfer typically isn't settled for several days, usually 5 days, and if it is over a threshold it often takes longer. A bitcoin can be settled within as little as 10 minutes and if you want to be completely certain then wait for a few confirmations which could take 20-50 min depending on your level of risk. But understand that most of your day to day transactions are not happening on a settlement layer but on a second or third layer of the current monetary system.

Bitcoin quantum resistance just got a big boost... BTQ Technologies launched testnet v0.3 of Bitcoin Quantum - the first live implementation of BIP 360, a key step toward a quantum-proof upgrade for BTC. Let's break it down: Right now, Bitcoin uses something called elliptic curve cryptography (ECDSA) to lock up your wallet. Think of it like the deadbolt on your front door. It's worked great for 15 years. The problem? Quantum computers are basically a lockpick that doesn't exist yet - but everyone knows someone's building one. A powerful enough quantum computer could reverse-engineer your private key from your public key. That's the nightmare scenario. BIP 360 is part of the fix. It introduces Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR) outputs that hide the public key, paving the way for quantum-proof signatures like Dilithium - built specifically to be quantum-resistant. And this isn't just a whitepaper or a Twitter thread. The testnet is live. Real code. Running. Now before you go full "Bitcoin is saved" mode, a few things: This is BTQ's testnet. Not mainnet. We're still in the "kicking the tires" phase. Oh, and quantum computers that could actually crack Bitcoin? They don't exist yet. The threat is valid, but it's like worrying about a hurricane that's still a thousand miles offshore. Getting this onto mainnet requires a soft fork - which means the whole Bitcoin community has to agree. And if you've ever watched Bitcoin governance... yeah, bring snacks. Either way, forward-thinking Bitcoin developers and teams like BTQ saw a problem on the horizon and started building the fix before it was an emergency. That's how it should work.

The new U.S. 501(c)(3) nonprofit aims to decentralize Bitcoin development by supporting an alternative, consensus-compatible node implementation alongside Bitcoin Core. As Bitcoin secures trillions in value, the group argues the network must reduce reliance on a single dominant client to avoid centralization risks and single points of failure. ProductionReady will fund both developer education and protocol development, with a focus on a more conservative approach to changes, prioritizing long-term stability and sound money principles. The board includes Samson Mow (Excellion), Jimmy Song (jimmysong), Parker Lewis (parkeralewis), and John W. Ratcliff. Jimmy Song will lead developer education efforts. The initiative comes amid growing debate within the Bitcoin community around code quality, governance, and how changes to the protocol should be proposed and implemented. The nonprofit plans to support a Bitcoin client built on Bitcoin Core, designed to act as a counterbalance to more aggressive development paths and reinforce Bitcoin’s monetary properties. The group indicated the client may restore OP_RETURN limits to previous defaults and is unlikely to include BIP-110 at this stage due to lack of broad consensus. ProductionReady says its goal is to foster a more meritocratic and resilient development ecosystem, where multiple implementations coexist and no single codebase dictates Bitcoin’s future. The organization is now inviting developers and donors to participate as it begins building out the project.

Crypto has a funny way of being two things at once - more mature by the day, and still a complete mess. Bitcoin is now held by asset managers in Patagonia vests, discussing basis trades on Bloomberg. At the same time, half the internet still thinks it’s mostly used to buy illegal things on the dark web. Ethereum is being pitched as a future settlement layer for global finance. At the same time, someone is paying $18 in gas to swap $47 worth of a dog token. BlackRock is launching products tied to staking and tokenization. At the same time, crypto Twitter is debating the Ethereum Foundation’s mandate like it’s constitutional law. Regulators are finally writing real guidance instead of press-release nonsense. At the same time, the market loses momentum the moment clarity arrives. Crypto was built to bypass financial intermediaries. At the same time, Mastercard is building rails to plug on-chain payments straight into fiat systems. Tokenization is being framed as the biggest structural evolution in markets in decades. At the same time, most people still associate the industry with cartoon apes and speculative mania. The macro backdrop is increasingly defined by war risk, rising debt, and economic uncertainty. At the same time, crypto’s long-term structural case arguably looks stronger than ever. The list goes on and on... Markets have always had a strange ability to hold opposing realities at the same time. Things can look fragile on the surface while subtly getting stronger underneath. The reality is, short-term chaos and long-term progress rarely move in sync. Investors want clean narratives and tidy timelines. But real change rarely shows up like that. Crypto just happens to live inside that tension more than anything else. One headline makes it look like a speculative circus. The next makes it look like the early foundation of a new financial system. Somehow, both are true. That’s not a flaw in the market. It’s the natural environment. As investors, the game isn’t to resolve the paradox. It’s to survive long enough to benefit from where it leads.

Recent examples of non-finance companies doing something similar: In September 2021, British American Tobacco (BAT) successfully raised €2.0 billion by issuing hybrid perpetual bonds. Because BAT is a massive, blue-chip corporation with an investment-grade credit rating, they were able to secure much lower interest rates than a smaller tech or treasury company would pay. However, the structure of their raise is exactly what makes the perpetual concept so powerful BAT split the €2.0 billion raise into two separate €1.0 billion tranches to appeal to different types of institutional investors: Tranche 1 (€1.0 billion): Issued as a "Non-Call 5.25-Year" perpetual bond. The Interest Rate: 3.000% fixed annually. Tranche 2 (€1.0 billion): Issued as a "Non-Call 8-Year" perpetual bond. The Interest Rate: 3.750% fixed annually. 2. The "Fixed-to-Reset" Mechanism (The Catch) To get those incredibly low 3% and 3.75% interest rates, BAT had to include a "step-up" or reset feature. While the bonds are legally perpetual (meaning they have no maturity date and BAT never has to repay the principal), the terms state that after the initial 5.25 or 8-year periods are up, the interest rate "resets." If BAT chooses not to buy the bonds back at that time, the interest rate automatically switches from the low fixed rate to a floating rate (tied to the 5-year Euro Swap Rate) plus an added penalty percentage that increases over time. What I don't know is the cost of something like this. I expect it would be quite high, so a decent size would probably be needed in the first instance to make it worthwhile. Secondly, I don't know what the liquidity would be like, but it's not clear if that would particularly matter if we can continually issue more of these bonds over time. One of the limiting factors is liquidity in our common stock. We would need to be able to raise enough capital through the ATM or equivalent every month to pay the dividends. If the volume equity dries up, that can create some problems. Gemini broke down an example for us: Here is the maths on a £30 million raise at a 7% yield, assuming the current £51,015 BTC price and 33p share price: The Immediate Jump: Raising £30m buys you ~588 BTC. Without issuing a single new share on Day 1, your Sats per Share instantly rockets from 680 sats to 829 sats, an immediate 21.8% increase. The Year 1 Dilution: A 7% rate costs £2.1m a year in interest. Funding this via the ATM at 33p requires issuing ~6.36 million shares over the year (just 1.6% dilution). The Net Result: At the end of Year 1, even after paying all the monthly interest through equity sales, your fully diluted share base sits at ~402.4 million shares holding 3,283 BTC. Your Sats per Share is now 816 sats. Bottom Line: By dropping the interest rate to 7%, a £30m raise delivers a permanent, net +19.9% increase in Sats per Share after the first full year of dilution. Because your cost of capital (7%) is so much lower than the sheer volume of Bitcoin you just added to the balance sheet (a ~21.8% treasury expansion), the accretion is massive and locked in.

Tokenized gold is not a real threat to Bitcoin’s deepest role. It is a threat to lazy Bitcoin narratives. That is the real answer. If you take gold, wrap it in a token, and move it onto faster rails, you get a more convenient claim on an old hard asset. You do not get a new monetary base. You get custodial gold with better UX. That can absolutely attract capital. It can absolutely appeal to older, more conservative money. It can absolutely outperform Bitcoin in periods where gold is the preferred macro refuge. All of that is real. But it still inherits the old world. Someone has to hold the metal. Someone has to attest the reserves. Someone has to honor redemption. Someone can freeze, censor, rehypothecate, gate, or politically pressure the system. That means tokenized gold solves transport and interface friction. It does not solve trust. Bitcoin solved something deeper. It created a digitally native hard asset with no vault, no issuer, no redemption gate, no national storage node, no auditor class standing between you and the asset. That is a different category of thing. Gold is matter first and money second. Bitcoin is monetary finality first. So when Schiff says tokenized gold is everything Bitcoin was supposed to do, he is still thinking from inside the old frame. He sees store of value plus transferability. He misses the part that actually made Bitcoin dangerous: neutral settlement, self-custody, endogenous scarcity, and the removal of institutional trust from the center of the system. That is why tokenized gold is stronger as a product than as a thesis. As a product, it is compelling. As a thesis, it is weak. It gives people familiar collateral with better rails. That matters. A lot of capital wants exactly that. But the second the world gets adversarial enough, the question comes back hard: who holds it, where is it, under whose law, under whose gun, under whose balance sheet, under whose freeze button? Bitcoin has a much cleaner answer. The deeper truth is that tokenized gold probably helps Bitcoin more than it hurts it. It trains the market to want hard assets on-chain. It teaches institutions and users that old finance wrapped in digital rails is still better than old finance trapped in old rails. Once that door opens, the comparison gets more dangerous for gold, not less. Because then people start asking why they should settle for a tokenized claim on scarce matter when they can hold scarce digital bearer collateral directly. So my actual view is simple. Tokenized gold can win flows. It can win conservative capital. It can win some payments and treasury use cases. It can expose how much demand exists for hard assets with digital mobility. Bitcoin still owns the stronger endgame. Gold tokenization modernizes gold. Bitcoin replaces the need for trusted monetary packaging. That is the difference.

The US tax code was designed for “20th-century money,” while crypto operates in an entirely different way. However, treating crypto purely as “property” means that even the smallest transactions can trigger tax obligations. This will lead to a system where everyday usage is a compliance headache. Coinbase sees 34% jump in tax queries Shirzad mentioned that under the current rules, something as simple as paying a gas fee or using a stablecoin for a routine transaction is technically a taxable event. He added that the users are expected to calculate cost basis, track gains or losses, and report them. This happens even when the amounts involved are negligible. He noted that crypto’s ability to move seamlessly across wallets and platforms makes this even harder. It often leaves gaps in reporting that brokers themselves cannot fully resolve. According to a report, Coinbase has seen a 34% jump in customer service inquiries. All of them were linked to tax reporting compared with the same period last year. Meanwhile, the introduction of new reporting needs is generating what the company describes as a paperwork overload. It added that millions of Form 1099-DAs will be issued for the 2025 tax year. However, many of them are tied to extremely small transactions. A big portion of these forms relates to proceeds under $600, and hundreds of thousands even track activity below $1. The volume of reporting risks is doing the opposite. It is not improving the clarity among users and is burying meaningful info under huge amounts of data. This is purely due to crypto’s move between wallets and exchanges. Because of this, taxpayers either overpay or are forced to manually reconcile transactions, and that too with limited support. De minimis exemption for small transactions might work here. Similar limits already exist in other parts of the tax code. It can be applied to crypto to eliminate the need to report minor payments. Google makes Gemini. Anthropic makes Claude. Direct competitors. Google also owns 14% of Anthropic, sells it billions in custom AI chips, and, per the Financial Times, is now financing the construction of Anthropic's data centers. I went through every deal I could find between these two. The FT report: Google is backing construction loans for a $5 billion+ data center in Texas. A company called Nexus Data Centers is building it. Anthropic already signed the lease. But Nexus can't get great loan rates from banks on its own: it's too small. So Google steps in with its own credit rating and suddenly the borrowing gets a lot cheaper. The site covers 2,800 acres, targets 500 megawatts of power by late 2026 (enough to power about 400,000 homes), and skips the public power grid entirely. Their own gas turbines, fed by nearby pipelines. Dodges the electricity price spikes that have been hammering data center operators all year. That's one deal. Google has been doing this across Anthropic's entire infrastructure network for months, mostly through a company called FluidStack, which builds and runs AI server farms. Google guaranteed $1.8 billion when FluidStack partnered with TeraWulf (a former Bitcoin miner turned data center company) and took an 8% stake in TeraWulf. It guaranteed $1.73 billion for a FluidStack deal with Cipher Mining and took a 5.4% stake. Backed a $7 billion deal between FluidStack and Hut 8 in Louisiana. Total Google guarantees across Anthropic's infrastructure partners: over $13 billion. Zoom out. Google's 14% stake at Anthropic's current $380 billion valuation (from its February funding round, the second-largest private raise in tech history) is worth roughly $53 billion on paper. The chip deal from October 2025, up to a million of Google's custom processors, locks in tens of billions more in cloud revenue. The infrastructure financing adds another layer entirely. And the loan guarantees gave Google ownership stakes in the actual data center companies building the physical sites. To their credit, Anthropic hasn't given anyone a leash. They train AI on Amazon, Google, and Nvidia chips. Sell through Amazon, Google, and Microsoft cloud platforms. No exclusivity with any provider. Revenue hit a $19 billion annual pace in March per Bloomberg, up from $1 billion fifteen months ago. I keep thinking about the structure Google has quietly assembled here. They get paid when Anthropic buys chips. They get paid when Anthropic runs AI on Google's servers. The financing and guarantees add another cut on top. And they own 14% of the upside if Anthropic's valuation keeps climbing. If Gemini wins instead, Google still owns the platform. They're selling the shovels, the land, the permits, and the financing to a prospector digging for gold right next to them.

“That Anja, always pinching her nose and dissolving into laughter at something no one else finds funny,” I imagine God saying, watching me from above. A private joke with the universe, perhaps. Let me tell you a story about little me, born exactly 40 years ago in a small Croatian town called Sisak. A tiny detail that somehow followed me everywhere, largely because the literal translation is… “little titty.” The cities I lived in later, especially in Serbia, were much bigger, but somehow no one had ever heard of Sisak. I changed five primary schools, and every time I had to stand up and introduce myself, it was the same ritual. Name, where I’m from… and then laughter. Not cruel, just surprised, a little too delighted, but enough to make you feel like you’d accidentally told a joke you didn’t mean to. Like you were the punchline without signing up for the role. Comedy found me early, whether I liked it or not. I started school a year ahead of schedule, mostly because I couldn’t wait to follow my big brother out into the world and, if I’m honest, to get out of the house. Even then, I had a will of iron and an independence streak that didn’t always land well at home. My mother and I… let’s just say we tested each other. We left Croatia just before the war in the early 90s, only to return because of my dad’s work, right to the border where the first line of defence was. Our childhood home was overshadowed by weapons of all kinds: hand grenades, Kalashnikovs, rocket launchers, you name it. It wasn’t even our home. It belonged to someone who had the good sense to leave the fight zone. Hyperinflation was rampant, and my parents quietly began plotting our escape from the never-ending madness. In 1997, we arrived in Australia, the promised land of peace, freedom, and stability. Life, as it turns out, has a wicked sense of humour. My teenage years were spent untangling just how abnormal my childhood had been, while feeling suspended between two cultures, belonging fully to neither. So I did what made the most sense. I leaned into humour. My brother had razor sharp wit, the kind that comes with a brilliant mind, and I played my role as the younger sister perfectly, laughing until I couldn’t breathe, getting the zoomies when things got too funny. And then he was gone. That loss reshaped everything. It’s the kind of grief that makes you nostalgic for your old problems, the ones you once thought were unbearable. A brutal reminder that life doesn’t negotiate. Oh no. Not long after, the COVID shenanigans arrived, and when the world reopened, something in me refused to go back to normal. I sold my two small apartments (which were much cheaper only 5 years ago), packed up the life I had so carefully constructed, and moved to Sydney. From safe and secure to fuck this shit, there has to be more than this. Questionable life choices, possibly. Necessary, absolutely. It would still be a few years until I discovered Bitcoin, and honestly, it made perfect sense. A child of a post-communist country, shaped by hyperinflation, constant upheaval, loss, and, ironically, authoritarian overreach (this time in Australia), and the slow realisation that climbing the corporate ladder often leads not to truth, but to politics and performance. Of course I questioned everything. Of course I became disillusioned with a world that never quite added up. So when I discovered the idea of Bitcoin, something shifted. Equal parts hope and terror. I let go of the safety nets I had clung to for so long and chose time over status, freedom over accumulation. Most people grind for decades to get there. I, in true Anja fashion, seem to have just… jumped. Sometimes I still catch myself thinking, what the hell are you doing. You had the job, the mortgage, the investment property, the checklist. And you traded it for uncertainty and significantly less income. Am I evolving, or just slightly unhinged with the risk tolerance of a caffeinated squirrel? But then I imagine going back to concrete boxes, political games, fear driven environments, people surviving instead of living, and the answer becomes clear. No thanks. Now I live simply. I earn enough. I’m surrounded by people I respect, people I can actually talk to without mentally planning my escape mid conversation. A small, grounded village kind of life. And for the first time in my entire life, I feel like I am walking a path I want, not the one sold to me as the one I should. Who knows where this path will lead. But for the first time, that uncertainty feels like freedom, not fear. Happy 40th to me. And to the truest souls who have entered my life since the 2024 halving, thank you. Because of all of you, I feel less alone.

Kaspa is different because many blocks can be created at the same time. Imagine two miners finding blocks at the same time. How does the network know which blocks really matter? That is what the k cluster does. Blocks that are well connected to other blocks are Blue because they strengthen the network. Blocks that are mostly alone are Red because they are valid but do not add to security. Kaspa checks each block’s Anticone, which is like asking how many blocks are not connected to this one. If a block sees most other blocks, it becomes Blue. If it is mostly alone, it becomes Red. The k factor sets the limit for how many unconnected blocks are allowed. On faster networks, k increases to keep the network secure. In short, the k cluster helps Kaspa stay fast, secure and reliable, even when many blocks are created at the same time. He came up with GHOST which even influenced Ethereum’s early direction and later moved into blockDAGs with PHANTOM and eventually GHOSTDAG. The core idea is simple: instead of a single longest chain, you use a DAG where every block connects to recent ones. Miners build on everything, not just one chain. Then you select the largest connected set (the “k-cluster”), and suddenly you get sub-second block times, high throughput, and no real latency bottleneck. Bitcoin ends up as “digital gold” slow, but strong as a store of value. Kaspa is aiming for “silver” fast, practical, actually usable as money. No premine, pure PoW. The tradeoff is a bit more complexity for nodes, but you get speed and low fees in return. The goal? Replace Litecoin as the real “silver to Bitcoin’s gold.” Mistakes along the way are part of it, but the vision is pretty clear: Nakamoto consensus, just pushed to internet speed.

The Physics of Bitcoin: A Rigorous Framework for Understanding Digital Money Giovanni Santostasi’s The Physics of Bitcoin arrives at a pivotal moment in both Bitcoin’s evolution and our understanding of complex systems. Unlike the countless speculative treatises on cryptocurrency markets, this book makes a bold scientific claim: that Bitcoin’s price behavior over its sixteen-year history follows a power law relationship with time—the same mathematical signature found in earthquakes, river networks, metabolic scaling in organisms, and city growth. If substantiated, this claim reframes Bitcoin not as a financial asset following market psychology, but as an emergent complex system operating near criticality. The central equation is deceptively simple: P(t) = A · t^5.69, where P is price and t is time from the Genesis Block. What makes this remarkable is not the equation itself—any dataset can be curve-fitted—but rather the combination of extraordinary statistical fit (R² = 0.951 across seven orders of magnitude), the theoretical mechanism proposed to explain it (Metcalfe’s Law applied to user growth), and the persistence of the relationship through multiple halvings, crashes, and regulatory shocks. A Physicist’s Journey The book’s structure is both personal and pedagogical. Part I recounts Santostasi’s discovery of the pattern in 2012, when he initially expected exponential growth but found instead the telltale curve-that-becomes-a-straight-line-on-a-log-log-plot. This narrative frame works exceptionally well: readers witness the scientific process unfolding through a trained physicist’s eyes, complete with false starts, conceptual breakthroughs (triggered by watching Geoffrey West’s TED talk on city scaling), and the painstaking work of statistical validation. Part II is where the book earns its subtitle. Santostasi provides masterful explanations of self-organized criticality (Per Bak’s sandpile model), power laws, scale invariance, and network dynamics. These are not cursory treatments—the chapter on power laws alone could serve as an undergraduate text. Yet the exposition remains accessible, using the physicist’s trick of explaining concepts through multiple lenses: verbal, visual, mathematical, and through natural examples. A reader who has never encountered Zipf’s law or the metabolic scaling of mammals will finish these chapters with genuine understanding. The Evidence Under Scrutiny Part III presents the empirical case across three domains: price, hash rate (physical infrastructure), and address growth (social network). Here the book’s scientific rigor is most apparent. Santostasi doesn’t merely show that the data fits a power law—he demonstrates: • Temporal stability: The exponent β ≈ 5.69 has remained remarkably constant across Bitcoin’s history • Residual analysis: Deviations from the power law show log-periodic oscillations, not random noise • Multiple scaling regimes: Evidence of power laws across all three fundamental metrics • Theoretical grounding: The exponent 5.69 ≈ 6 can be derived from Metcalfe’s Law (N²) combined with cubic user growth (N ∝ t³) The statistical methods are sound—ordinary least squares on log-transformed data, proper calculation of confidence intervals, discussion of correlation vs. causation. However, the book would benefit from more robust treatment of potential confounds: regulatory changes, the rise of institutional adoption, and the question of whether sixteen years constitutes sufficient data for such confident extrapolation. Beyond Physics: Implications and Predictions Part IV ventures into philosophical territory: what does it mean that Bitcoin exhibits these scaling properties? Santostasi argues that the power law is not merely descriptive but diagnostic—it reveals Bitcoin as a fundamentally different type of monetary system, one that operates according to thermodynamic constraints (proof-of-work energy consumption) rather than institutional discretion. This is where the book will face its sharpest criticism from economists. The claim that Bitcoin is “money reimagined” through physics and complex systems theory may strike traditional monetary economists as category confusion. Money is a social technology, they might argue, whose value derives from collective agreement and institutional backing, not from mathematical elegance. The book engages with Austrian economics and monetary history thoughtfully, but doesn’t fully grapple with institutional economists’ skepticism. The projection chapters are simultaneously the book’s most exciting and most vulnerable element. If the power law holds, Bitcoin should reach $1 million around 2030-2033. Santostasi is admirably careful with caveats—scale invariance can break, external shocks can disrupt emergent patterns, etc.—but the very act of making such projections invites accusations of wishful thinking disguised as science. Technical Depth and Accessibility The mathematical appendices are excellent, providing derivations of the Metcalfe-based value equation, treatments of log-periodic oscillations, and connections to renormalization group theory that will satisfy technical readers. Yet the main text never requires following the mathematics—equations appear as expressions of ideas, not replacements for them. The book’s prose is clear and often elegant, though occasionally veers into repetition (the distinction between exponential and power law growth is explained at least four times). The integration of figures is excellent—every major claim is supported by high-quality data visualization. Critical Assessment Strengths: - Rigorous application of complex systems theory to a novel domain - Exceptional pedagogical clarity in explaining advanced physics concepts - Honest engagement with falsifiability and the limits of prediction - Integration of personal narrative with scientific investigation - Comprehensive treatment across multiple domains (price, hash rate, adoption) Weaknesses: - Limited engagement with alternative explanations for the power law - Insufficient treatment of how institutional adoption might alter scaling dynamics - The mechanism (Metcalfe + cubic growth) is proposed but not rigorously derived from first principles - Sample size concerns: sixteen years may not be enough for confident extrapolation - Some readers may find the cross-disciplinary analogies (Bitcoin as city, as organism) overreached Verdict The Physics of Bitcoin represents serious interdisciplinary scholarship applied to a phenomenon that has largely evaded such treatment. Whether Bitcoin is truly a complex system exhibiting self-organized criticality, or whether Santostasi has found an elegant but ultimately coincidental pattern, remains to be determined by future data. What is certain is that this book establishes a rigorous framework for asking the right questions. For physicists and complex systems researchers, this is required reading—Bitcoin may well be one of the most accessible complex systems for study, with transparent data and clear network topology. For Bitcoin enthusiasts, it provides the most sophisticated scientific defense of long-term value appreciation yet articulated. For skeptics, it offers a testable hypothesis with clear falsification criteria. The ultimate test, as Santostasi repeatedly emphasizes, is not the elegance of the theory but its predictive power. If Bitcoin’s price diverges significantly from the power law trajectory over the next several years, the framework collapses. If it continues to track the projection, we may need to fundamentally rethink how we categorize and understand decentralized monetary networks. The scientific method has arrived in Bitcoin analysis. This book is the opening argument. Rating: 4.5/5 stars The Physics of Bitcoin by Giovanni Santostasi, PhD Scientific Bitcoin Institute Press, 2026 Foreword by Stephen Perrenod, PhD Approximately 400 pages with mathematical appendices Available in Kindle and print formats Recommended for: Physicists, complex systems researchers, econophysics scholars, serious Bitcoin researchers, and readers interested in interdisciplinary approaches to emergent phenomena. Not recommended for: Those seeking investment advice, readers allergic to mathematics, or those looking for a comprehensive Bitcoin primer (the book assumes familiarity with Bitcoin basics).

Privacy in blockchain often sparks heated debate. Some see it as an essential shield for personal freedom, while others worry it only helps criminals hide their tracks. So, which is it? A necessary protection or a clever cover for wrongdoing? The truth lies in understanding how blockchains actually work. Most popular ones - Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron and others are completely public by design. Every transaction, every address, and every amount is visible to anyone forever on a public explorer. This transparency helps verify that the system isn't being cheated, but it also turns your financial life into an open book. Privacy technologies (zero-knowledge proofs in Zcash, ring signatures in Monero, stealth addresses, shielded transactions) were created to fix this flaw. They hide the sender, receiver, and amount while still allowing the network to confirm that the transaction is valid. It's like restoring the level of privacy that cash, face-to-face deals, and closed doors have always provided in the real world. Why privacy is genuinely needed Financial self-defense: On a public chain, once someone links your wallet to your identity (via an exchange, social media, or a single payment), they can see your entire history. This makes you an easy target for hackers, stalkers, or extortionists. Protection from surveillance and abuse: Governments, corporations, or malicious actors can track donations, spending, salaries, or medical payments. In countries facing political tension or conflict, this creates real risks for journalists, activists, and ordinary people. Everyday practicality: Businesses don't want competitors spying on supplier payments. Families don't want neighbors knowing exact balances. Privacy makes blockchain usable for real life instead of broadcasting everything globally. Human rights compatibility: Laws like GDPR emphasize control over personal data. Total transparency on-chain often clashes with these principles. Privacy doesn't create evil - it simply prevents good people from becoming easy victims in a system that would otherwise expose them completely. But what about crime? Yes, privacy can be misused, just like cash, encrypted messaging (Signal, WhatsApp), or VPNs. Criminals have used Monero in some ransomware and darknet cases. However, the data tells a more nuanced story. According to the Chainalysis 2026 Crypto Crime Report, illicit addresses received at least $154 billion in 2025 - a record high, largely driven by a 694% surge in sanctioned entities' activity (state-level sanctions evasion). TRM Labs estimates a similar $158 billion. Yet even these record figures represent less than 1% (Chainalysis) to about 1.2% (TRM) of total crypto transaction volume. The vast majority - over 98–99% remains legitimate. Stablecoins now dominate illicit flows at 84%, not privacy coins. Privacy coins like Monero and Zcash occupy a small niche. Their usage in illicit activity has dwindled in relative terms as criminals prefer liquid stablecoins on public chains, which are easier to move at scale. Darknet markets still process around $2–2.6 billion annually, but this is a tiny slice overall. The hidden cost of absolute transparency Public blockchains don't just help catch criminals - they create new vulnerabilities: Wrench attacks (physical coercion: kidnappings, beatings, or threats with a "wrench" to force wallet access) exploded in 2025. According to CertiK's Skynet Wrench Attacks Report: 72 verified incidents worldwide (+75% from 2024). Confirmed losses: $40.9 million (+44%). Physical assaults rose by 250%. These attacks rely directly on transparency: criminals scan public explorers, identify "rich" addresses, link them to real people, and strike. Without visible on-chain data, targeting specific individuals becomes far harder. zodl_app ⬇

Tadge Dryja, the co-inventor of the Lightning Network, just dropped an update on Utreexo, one of the most underappreciated scaling projects in bitcoin. The problem is straightforward. Every bitcoin node that wants to validate transactions has to store the entire UTXO set, every unspent output on the network. Right now that's 11GB and growing. As more transactions hit the chain, as inscriptions and other data-heavy outputs pile up, every node operator has to store all of it. The UTXO set doesn't get pruned like old blocks can. It just grows. Utreexo eliminates the entire UTXO set from your node. Instead of storing 11GB of data, a Utreexo node stores less than 1KB of hashes and still fully verifies every transaction. It's not a light client. It's not trusting anyone else. It's full validation with radically less storage. The tradeoff has always been bandwidth. Utreexo nodes need to download extra proof data to verify transactions without storing the full set. Until recently, syncing the blockchain with Utreexo took 2-3x the data download of a normal node, pushing into terabytes. That problem is now being solved, new aggregator techniques from SwiftSync have eliminated the extra download overhead. The implementation is still being finalized, but the hard part appears to be behind them. Two things worth noting: First, Utreexo is quantum safe. The accumulator and aggregator are built entirely on hash functions, not elliptic curve cryptography. Whatever quantum computing does to bitcoin's signature scheme, it won't touch Utreexo. At a time when the quantum conversation is heating up, that's a meaningful design advantage. Second, Utreexo directly addresses the tension around "spam" on bitcoin. Inscriptions, BRC-20 tokens, and other data-heavy outputs bloat the UTXO set that every node has to carry. Pruning helps with old block data but doesn't touch the UTXO set. Utreexo makes the entire debate irrelevant, if your node doesn't store the UTXO set at all, the size of it doesn't matter. New releases are out for both utreexod (BTCD-based) and Floresta (rust-based, built with rust-bitcoin). Both are in testing mode, not ready for real funds yet, but ready for developers and node operators to try. This is the kind of quiet, foundational work that actually scales bitcoin at L1. No token. No VC round. No press tour. Just better engineering.

A strong argument can be made that Ether has the strongest properties of any candidate global reserve asset. It beats out fiat currencies like the US dollar because of its monetary discipline. Ether's maximum supply growth is mathematically capped at 1.6% per year, and that's under extreme circumstances. In practice, because network usage burns fees, Ether's actual growth has stayed below 0.5% per year. In contrast, fiat currencies have no cap on supply growth, as numerous hyperinflation events throughout history attest. The typical rate of supply growth is also much higher than Ether's. The USD's M0 supply, for example, has grown by an average of about 6% per year in the modern era. Other cryptocurrencies share many of Ether's strong monetary properties, but Ether is better than all of them. Bitcoin, for example, has a long-term security budget problem: its new issuance drops by half every four years, and its base layer cannot process enough transactions to generate the fees needed to replace that lost security budget. Ether solves this through both scalability (soon 10,000 transactions per second at the base layer alone, which is 1,500x larger than Bitcoin) and perpetual issuance (~0.5% a year), which sacrifices a cap on supply in order to gain a floor on security. As for other cryptocurrencies, they are all vastly less decentralized and credibly neutral than Ether, and they have much smaller market caps, making them far less likely to become the Schelling point for storing value. The other major reserve asset option is gold. Gold is physically cumbersome, slow to move, and non-programmable, in contrast to Ether, which can be moved at the speed of light and can be used as programmable collateral in complex financial contracts. Gold's scarcity also relies entirely on the limits of physical extraction on Earth, a limit that will weaken as the space industry expands and the mining of M-class asteroids begins. That may be far in the future, but for a reserve asset, these kinds of long-horizon implications matter. Ether's scarcity is enforced by protocol, so it is not undermined by the increasingly relevant prospect of technology-induced abundance in physical resources. Mechanically, Ether is the most logical choice for a global reserve asset.

The First Bitcoin Blog Post as Policy: Zooko’s Strategic Omission and the Birth of Neutral Narration On January 26, 2009, Zooko Wilcox-O’Hearn published what is widely regarded as the first blog post about Bitcoin, titled “Decentralized Money.” At first glance, the post appears modest—almost understated. It links to Bitcoin, frames it as an interesting attempt at decentralized currency, and situates it within the broader lineage of cypherpunk thought. But what it does not say is far more revealing than what it does. This was not merely a blog post. It was an early act of narrative policy-setting—one that helped define how Bitcoin would be introduced to the world: not as a project of known individuals, but as an idea standing on its own. I. The Context: A Dense but Invisible Network By the time Zooko wrote his post, the “Bitcoin network” was not an abstract concept—it was a tiny, real, human network. Hal Finney had already run the software and received the first transaction. Satoshi Nakamoto was actively communicating on mailing lists. Zooko himself was deeply embedded in the same cryptography circles, with long-standing relationships across that network. This was not a case of ignorance. It was a case of selective representation. II. The Omission: A Deliberate Silence Zooko’s post notably excluded: Any mention of Hal Finney, despite his active participation Any reference to named cypherpunks already involved His own prior attempts at digital cash His skepticism that Bitcoin would actually work The fact that he himself had not yet run the software This is not accidental minimalism. It is policy through omission. In communications theory, omission is not absence—it is signal. What Zooko constructed was a clean-room narrative: Bitcoin as an idea, not a social graph. III. Neutrality as a Foundational Policy Why does this matter? Because early-stage technologies—especially those attempting to displace monetary systems—face a fundamental risk: If the story begins with people, it inherits their credibility constraints. If it begins with ideas, it inherits conceptual legitimacy. Zooko’s post implicitly chose the latter. By not naming Hal Finney or others, he avoided: Centralization of authority (“this is Hal’s project”) Reputational dependency (tying Bitcoin to known figures) Premature social clustering (turning Bitcoin into a clique rather than a protocol) Instead, he framed Bitcoin as: A proposal, not a movement A system, not a team A possibility, not a commitment This is remarkably aligned with what would later become Bitcoin’s strongest property: credibly neutral infrastructure. IV. Skepticism as Policy Discipline Equally important is what Zooko withheld about himself: his skepticism. He has since said he believed Bitcoin would not work in practice. Yet the blog post does not convey this doubt. This restraint reflects another subtle policy: Do not overfit early narratives to personal conviction. Instead of declaring belief or disbelief, Zooko positioned Bitcoin as: Worth observing Worth understanding Not yet worthy of commitment This created optionality—for both himself and the reader. V. The “No Name-Drop” Principle One of the most striking aspects of the post is the absence of name-dropping in a culture that was otherwise deeply relational. In modern terms, this would be like: Launching a startup blog post without mentioning the founders Introducing a protocol without referencing its contributors Publishing a breakthrough without citing collaborators This was not standard behavior—it was a deliberate break from norm. The implicit rule becomes: Bitcoin should not inherit legitimacy from people. People should derive legitimacy from Bitcoin.

And now, solutions like Lombard’s Bitcoin Smart Accounts are solving that problem, which could open the doors for more institutional capital. DeFi also looks different now. Before, it felt like you had to hand your money over and hope for the best. Now, institutions can stay in control, set their own risk, and still access liquidity. That shift matters more than most people realize. There’s also a lot of talk about “vaults.” At first, it sounds technical, but it’s actually simple, a smarter way to manage assets on-chain without giving up control. It might seem small now, but it’s likely to become standard soon. The yield conversation is also misunderstood. Hearing “2%” sounds small. But 2% on Bitcoin is not the same as 2% on cash. The work to protect Bitcoin is already underway, so it’s something to watch but no need to panic. Even the usual critics don’t have the same arguments as before. Concerns about regulation, scams, and lack of returns are slowly being addressed. The space is maturing. One line from the event summed it up: It’s not that DeFi is coming to Bitcoin, it’s that Bitcoin is coming to DeFi. That flips the perspective. Bitcoin is slowly moving from something you just hold to something you can actually use. And the crazy part? Most people still haven’t caught on yet. The shoulder devil that whispers “if only you had been humble enough, smart enough, brave enough…” So they don’t want it dead. They want it cheaper. They want a crash they can survive emotionally, not one that proves them right. What they’re actually praying for is a do-over. A drawdown ugly enough to reset the math on their opportunity cost, and allow their ego to be simultaneously right (that bitcoin died) and at the same time be a pioneer (you thought it was dead but I actually knew it wouldn’t die all along) Pain without death. There’s a difference between someone who wants you dead and someone who wants you cheaper. One is an enemy. The other is a buyer wearing the costume of one. Bitcoin barely has enemies anymore. Let me tell you a funny story about me and Matthew. Last year I was in Amsterdam to present at the Bitcoin conference. The talk went really well—lots of positive feedback and appreciation (I’ll put the link in the comments). After the conference, I was having duck sandwiches with some friends from Italy, and one of them offered me a brownie. She may have mentioned it was a “special” brownie, but I didn’t really pay attention—I just took a small piece and ate it. A bit later, I was in the VIP area and saw Matthew. He was one of the people I really wanted to meet—I respect him both personally and as an analyst. So I went up to introduce myself (this was our first time meeting in person) and started telling him about my recent work in Italy and Europe—conferences, meetings, even a visit to the Italian parliament where I met one of the few politicians genuinely interested in Bitcoin. At some point I was saying he was specialized in “…”—and then I just froze. Time started to slow down, almost like a power law stretching everything out, and I couldn’t form a coherent sentence. That’s when it hit me. Amsterdam… special brownie… oh no. I immediately realized what was happening and thought, “This is a terrible first impression.” So the only thing I could do was just be honest and tell him what was going on. He laughed it off, was incredibly kind, and told me to relax, let the experience unfold, and even try to enjoy it. I apologized for not being able to have a proper conversation about all the interesting topics we could have discussed, but he was very understanding and supportive. At some point it got so intense that I had to call my son to help me find my way out of the conference—I literally couldn’t navigate anymore. I don’t usually take anything like that, so I probably had a stronger-than-normal reaction. In the end, though, it was a memorable experience—and still a great time with friends.

Bitcoin mining, which relies on SHA-based hashing, remains effectively secure. Upgrades including BIP-360 to remove on-chain public keys, hash-based post-quantum signatures and commit/reveal schemes for mempool transactions are already under discussion. Blockstream CEO Adam Back separately urged developers to give users a decade to migrate to quantum-resistant wallet formats.

It just became a fragility and trust story, and that shift ties Anthropic’s Mythos, the Clarity Act, and Bitcoin together in a way investors are badly underpricing. It forced policymakers to acknowledge, in public, that the core software of the financial system is now one well‑aimed AI exploit away from systemic risk. When Scott Bessent and Jerome Powell are in emergency meetings with the heads of Wall Street banks to discuss AI‑driven cyber threats, the conversation has moved beyond sandbox innovation and into the realm of financial stability. The implicit message is clear: the incumbent architecture is not built for an adversarial, model‑driven world. Bessent’s op‑ed arguing that the Clarity Act must pass as a matter of national security is the political counterpart of that realization. If AI can pierce legacy rails, then the United States needs clear, durable rules for digital assets and blockchain infrastructure, not so it can speculate on tokens, but so it can deliberately integrate cryptographic, verifiable, tamper‑resistant rails into the heart of its financial system. Clarity on custody, stablecoins, and blockchain‑based settlement is no longer a regulatory luxury; it is a defence priority. Put together, Mythos, the Bessent–Powell Wall Street meetings, and the Clarity Act op‑ed point in the same direction: the centre of gravity is shifting from “AI will boost earnings” to “AI will test the integrity of our money pipes.” In that world, open, auditable, cryptographic infrastructure stops being a fringe experiment and starts looking like the logical upgrade path. Public blockchains, and Bitcoin in particular, offer precisely the properties an AI‑exposed system now needs: transparent rules, global replication, adversarial testing at scale, and settlement that does not depend on a single compromised database or trusted intermediary. The connection investors are missing is that the AI shock and the regulatory turn are not separate stories. Mythos revealed how fragile the old code base is; Bessent’s call to pass the Clarity Act is an attempt to give the US a legal framework to adopt stronger, blockchain‑based rails; and the emergency meetings between Fed, Treasury, and Wall Street are the first visible signs that the establishment knows it cannot patch its way through this era with 1980s technology. How much STRC does Strategy have to issue to drive Bitcoin to $1,000,000? Realistically, something like 0.5% to 1.5% of a $300T global debt market is the zone I’d watch, with ~0.6% to 1.2% as a very clean base case. Here’s the logic. Bitcoin is about $71,680 right now, and circulating supply is about 20.01 million BTC, which puts current BTC market cap around $1.43T. At $1,000,000 per BTC, market cap would be about $20.01T. So the gap to close is roughly $18.58T. If you did the dumb, literal accounting version where every fresh dollar of STRC capital only created one extra dollar of BTC market cap, Saylor would need capital equal to about 6.19% of $300T. That is the upper-bound, brute-force answer, and it is way too conservative because markets do not reprice that linearly. The reason the real answer is lower is that Bitcoin has a flow-to-market-cap multiplier. Recent academic work explicitly defines a “crypto multiplier” as the market-cap response to investor inflows and says major cryptocurrencies likely have large multipliers because most coins are held as investments, not used for payments. Separate flow research on spot BTC ETFs also finds that ETF inflows have a persistent positive effect on BTC prices, which reinforces the basic idea that fresh capital can move market value by more than one-for-one. So if you model that $18.58T repricing gap through different multipliers, you get this: 20x multiplier: about $0.93T of net BTC buying, about 0.31% of $300T 10x multiplier: about $1.86T, about 0.62% 5x multiplier: about $3.72T, about 1.24% 3x multiplier: about $6.19T, about 2.06% If STRC-style issuance became a major global fixed-income product, Saylor probably does not need 6% of the debt market. He more likely needs something in the neighborhood of 0.5% to 1.5% captured cumulatively over time, assuming Bitcoin reprices reflexively as float tightens. That range corresponds roughly to a 10x to 5x effective market-cap multiplier, which feels aggressive but not insane for an asset with scarce liquid supply and persistent corporate/ETF demand. There is one more wrinkle. STRC is not a zero-cost funding source. Strategy says STRC currently carries an 11.50% variable annual dividend, payable monthly in cash. If Strategy wanted to reserve, say, roughly 2 years of dividend coverage on new issuance, then only about 77% of gross proceeds would actually go into BTC. Under that assumption, the gross debt-market share needed rises to roughly 0.80% in the 10x case and 1.61% in the 5x case. And just to show how early this still is, Strategy’s site currently shows STRC notional at about $5.355B, which is only about 0.0018% of $300T. So to do this through STRC alone, the machine would need to scale by hundreds of times from here. $1M Bitcoin via STRC alone probably implies capturing around 1% of the global debt market, give or take, not 6%. 6% is the static-accounting answer. ~1% is the reflexive-market answer. StarkWare's Chief Product Officer, Avihu Levy, has released a paper proposing Quantum Safe Bitcoin (QSB), a scheme designed to fortify Bitcoin transactions against future quantum attacks without necessitating any softforks or changes to the core Bitcoin protocol. This initiative seeks to provide a preemptive solution to a long-theorized vulnerability. The proposal directly addresses a significant theoretical concern: Bitcoin's current reliance on Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) signatures. These signatures could eventually be broken by sufficiently powerful quantum computers leveraging Shor's algorithm, potentially compromising the security of funds. QSB aims to mitigate this future risk by operating entirely within Bitcoin's existing framework, avoiding disruptive protocol upgrades. At its core, QSB shifts Bitcoin's transactional security from elliptic curve cryptography to hash-based assumptions, specifically relying on hash pre-image resistance. The scheme is engineered to function within the stringent limitations of Bitcoin's legacy Script, adhering to its 201 opcode cap and maximum script size of 10,000 bytes. This approach builds upon earlier work known as Binohash, which integrated one-time signature schemes into Bitcoin Script. While the technical pathway for QSB within current Bitcoin Script constraints is outlined, the practical challenges of widespread adoption and implementation across the network remain substantial. The timeline and scale of a credible quantum threat also continue to be subjects of ongoing research and debate among cryptographers and physicists, making the urgency and necessity of such a solution a dynamic consideration. These are based on economic models, historical parallels (e.g., past Hormuz tensions), and current analyst forecasts actual outcomes depend on how long the blockade lasts, Iranian responses, and allied involvement. Crude Oil Sharp price spike expected immediately. Brent crude was around $95–97/bbl as of April 10 (pre-announcement). A full or prolonged disruption could push it toward $100–115+/bbl in the near term, or even $150+ in worst-case scenarios if flows stay blocked for weeks. Why? Removing ~15–20 million barrels/day from the market (the largest supply shock since 1973) forces buyers to scramble for alternatives, draw down inventories, and bid up prices. Models show a one-quarter closure could lift WTI to ~$98/bbl and extend higher if it drags on. Gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel prices would rise globally, with ripple effects on transport and heating costs. Even partial reopening wouldn't fully reverse this quickly due to restocking and tanker rerouting. World Economy Inflationary shock + growth slowdown (stagflation risk). Higher energy costs feed directly into transport, manufacturing, and food prices (fertilizer/LNG also transit the strait). One economic model estimates a one-quarter closure could shave ~2.9% off annualized global GDP growth while spiking inflation. Stock markets and risk assets would likely sell off on risk aversion; supply chains (especially Asia-Europe routes) face higher freight/insurance costs. Longer term (months+): Potential recession in energy-import-heavy regions, higher borrowing costs, and strained public finances in vulnerable countries. Developing economies suffer most from the pass-through to food and fuel. Crypto (e.g., Bitcoin and broader market) Short-term negative pressure (risk-off sell-off). Crypto behaves like a high-beta risk asset during geopolitical shocks. Past oil spikes tied to Hormuz/Iran tensions triggered BTC liquidations and drops (e.g., correlating with Nasdaq declines as inflation fears delay rate cuts). Impacts on Africa (Broadly)Mixed but mostly challenging importers hit hardest. Many African nations import refined fuels and fertilizers via global markets. Higher oil prices mean costlier petrol, diesel, and food (agriculture relies on imported fertilizers), worsening inflation and energy poverty. Fuel shortages are already a risk in some spots. Oil exporters (Nigeria, Angola, Algeria) could see revenue gains from higher global crude prices, partially offsetting domestic pain. Broader headwinds: Slower global growth reduces demand for African commodities/exports; currencies may weaken against the USD; debt burdens rise with imported inflation. The country's Bitcoin reserves were estimated at approximately 13,000 BTC in October 2024, but have since experienced a substantial reduction of about 70% from their peak. Arkham data also indicates that significant mining inflows exceeding $100,000 have not been observed for over a year, potentially suggesting a halt in operations around November 2024. As of early April 2026, Bhutan's estimated Bitcoin holdings now range between 3,654 BTC and 3,954 BTC. This reduction includes over $215.7 million in BTC transferred out in 2026 alone, with March seeing movements of more than 1,667 BTC, valued at roughly $120 million. These sales are widely interpreted as strategic liquidations, possibly for portfolio rebalancing, profit-taking, or to fund various state projects. Lightning: from misconceptions to real Infrastructure Lightning is still widely misunderstood. For many people, it is associated with micropayments, retail use cases, or dismissed as “that Bitcoin experiment.” However, this perception is outdated. In reality, Lightning has quietly matured into real infrastructure. It now processes billions in volume, is used by millions of users, and is increasingly integrated into business systems. The Core Idea of Lightning Is Not Speed Most people make a fundamental mistake: they focus on speed. They see instant payments and assume that is the main innovation. But speed is only a byproduct. The real breakthrough is architectural: the separation of execution from final settlement. Payments happen off-chain and instantly Final settlement is recorded later on-chain A familiar model in traditional finance This is not a new concept. It is exactly how large payment systems like Visa operate: Transactions are processed instantly Final settlement happens in batches Fast execution combined with delayed finality is what enables global-scale throughput. Lightning brings this same model to Bitcoin but without banks, payment processors, or intermediaries. A new model of capital usage This fundamentally changes how capital is used. No need to fragment liquidity across multiple chains No need to pre-fund accounts on different platforms Capital can move dynamically through payment channels As a result: Capital is no longer idle - it becomes continuously active. Payments shift from a liquidity problem to a routing problem. Adding stablecoins and privacy layers Now extend this system with stablecoins: USDT can move natively on Bitcoin through Lightning RGB adds privacy and advanced asset capabilities The result is: instant, private, and secure transactions on a single financial rail. The role of utexocom This is where utexo comes in. It abstracts away the complexity of: Lightning RGB channel management node operations This allows payment operators to: integrate once immediately access the infrastructure avoid managing technical complexity

Bitcoin secured settlement is the strongest answer to the trust problem in a world of AI agents. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ WHY THIS MATTERS FOR GOATNETWORK Protocols like x402 and ERC 8004 are open, but the settlement layer matters most. GOAT Network runs an x402 facilitator across ETH, Polygon, Arbitrum, BSC, and Solana. This allows agents to operate across the entire crypto ecosystem while settling to the most secure network in existence. It is the only stack where x402 and ERC 8004 settle directly to Bitcoin. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ FOR BUILDERS If you are building agents that need to transact: 1 Choose your journey. Here’s what you need to know. First, the term "dark web" refers to .onion sites on the Tor network. Tor sends your traffic through three relays (Guard, Middle, and Exit), encrypting it at each step. No single relay knows both your identity and what you’re accessing. For most people, Tor Browser is enough. Download it only from torproject[.]org and verify the cryptographic signature. Supply chain attacks can happen. Your threat model is more important than the tools you use: • For casual privacy, just use Tor Browser. • To avoid ISP surveillance, use a reputabe VPN .e.g Mullvad .e.t.c. before connecting to Tor. (but VPN provider knows you used Tor) • If you face a serious adversary, use Tails OS. • For nation-state threats or high-value targets, use Qubes OS with Whonix. Tails OS is an amnesic operating system. It runs from a USB drive, leaves no trace, and routes all traffic through Tor at the system level. It’s great for temporary use. Even if someone takes your computer, nothing is left to find. Qubes OS works very differently from Tails. It uses the Xen hypervisor to separate tasks. Each one runs in its own isolated virtual machine, called a "qube." Your banking qube can't talk to your dark web qube. Malware in one VM cannot escape to another. This is security by isolation at the OS level. Edward Snowden uses Qubes, which says a lot about its security. Using Qubes with Whonix is considered the gold standard. Whonix is a privacy-focused operating system designed to run inside Qubes as two virtual machines: - Whonix-Gateway: manages all Tor routing - Whonix-Workstation: your main working environment, which never connects to the internet directly Even if the Workstation is compromised, it cannot reveal your real IP address because only the Gateway VM has network access. Tails vs Qubes: what’s the difference? - Tails: best for temporary, mobile sessions where you want to leave no trace (plug in, use, unplug) - Qubes: best for a permanent workstation that offers strong compartmentalization Each solves different problems. Advanced users often use both, depending on the situation. Some OPSEC rules: Never log in to your real accounts over Tor. Never enable JavaScript on untrusted .onion sites. JavaScript has been used to deanonymize users in FBI operations. Never open downloaded files while you’re online. These files could reveal your real IP address. Spoof your MAC address before connecting. Disable WebRTC, since it can leak your real IP address even if you use a VPN. Remove metadata from files, such as EXIF data or document properties, before sharing them. Deanonymization risks people often overlook: - Browser fingerprinting, such as fonts, screen size, and timezone - Behavioral patterns, like your writing style and posting times (stylometry is real) - Buying cryptocurrency on a KYC exchange and then using it on-chain - Reusing usernames on both the clearnet and darknet For payments, Monero (XMR) is better than Bitcoin. Monero uses ring signatures and stealth addresses, making transactions unlinkable by default. TL;DR Casual: use Tor Browser Serious: use Tails OS with Tor Advanced: use Qubes OS, Whonix, Monero, and strict OPSEC Extreme: Use a dedicated air-gapped device along with all of the above

For most of crypto's history, reading institutional demand meant reading proxies. On-chain transfers. Exchange inflows and outflows. Whale wallet movement. Futures open interest. Retail sentiment curves. For more than a decade, that stack was the best we had. Then January 2024 happened. The launch of US spot Bitcoin ETFs, followed by Ethereum ETFs in July of the same year, created the first regulated, transparent channel for traditional finance to allocate directly into BTC and ETH. No futures wrapper. No trust premium. Actual spot exposure, through vehicles that publish flows daily. That changed the structure of this market in a way that doesn't get talked about enough. Pensions. Endowments. RIAs. Hedge funds. Participants who were almost entirely absent from the 2017 and 2021 cycles now have a standing line item for crypto. And every trading day, we get to see exactly how much capital they added or pulled. As of mid-April 2026, US spot BTC ETFs hold north of $96 billion in AUM. Goldman Sachs just filed. Morgan Stanley's MSBT has been one of the strongest ETF debuts of the year. The on-ramp keeps widening. What this means practically: The old signals still work. Funding, OI, liquidations, exchange balances. None of that is obsolete. But there is now a new, high-resolution read on TradFi conviction that wasn't available in any prior cycle. Daily inflows and outflows that mechanically tie to spot demand. Green bars when real institutional money enters. Red bars when it leaves. A price line that tracks the response in near real time. You can ignore it. But you're choosing to ignore the most direct, least noisy signal of institutional positioning we've ever had in this asset class. The real edge isn't the ETF data in isolation. It's ETF flows sitting next to funding, OI, and spot CVD on the same screen. An ETF inflow print hits differently when funding is neutral and OI is building versus when funding is hot and longs are already overextended. Same number. Opposite read. That's the reason this view lives as a widget in the Athenum Terminal rather than as a standalone chart. Context is the whole game. Adapting the framework is the work. Refusing to is the cost.

Rather than treating prediction as something scattered across markets, institutions, or isolated experts, it tries to reframe it as a shared, structured capability that can be continuously refined. At the center of this effort is what it calls “Truth Finality”: the idea that trust in knowledge should not depend on authority, reputation, or institutional gatekeeping, but on transparent rules that anyone can inspect and verify. There is a clear philosophical lineage here, and the project makes it explicit by drawing a parallel to Bitcoin. Bitcoin changed how we think about money by showing that value could move securely between people without banks or intermediaries. That shift is often summarized as “Finality for Value,” where once a transaction is confirmed, it is settled in a way that does not rely on any central party to uphold it. pots_market is attempting to extend that same logic into a different domain entirely, truth itself. Instead of asking how value can be decentralized, it asks how belief and certainty can be decentralized. In practice, this means moving away from systems where truth is decided by institutions or expert consensus alone, and toward systems where claims are resolved through open, rule-based mechanisms that are consistently applied. This is what it refers to as “Finality for Truth.” The ambition is not just to improve prediction markets as tools, but to reshape the underlying structure of how societies decide what is real, what is likely, and what can be trusted. Bitcoin is not what most people think it is. Bitcoin is not primarily “digital money,” “blockchain technology,” or even “a payment system.” It is a self-sustaining protocol—a system of rules—for producing and maintaining decentralized, publicly verifiable truth about ownership and events in an environment where participants have no reason to trust one another. The invention described in the Bitcoin white paper is far greater than merely electronic cash or even “blockchain.” The key innovation is proof-of-work combined with the longest-chain rule. Participants expend real resources (electricity and computation) to compete for the right to extend the record. The white paper ends with characteristic restraint: “We have proposed a system for electronic transactions without relying on trust.” In practice, Satoshi gave the world something far more powerful—a new foundation for trust itself in the digital age. The Bitcoin Network is decentralized truth and coordination, secured by mathematics and economics, that allows strangers across the world to agree on reality without trusting each other or any central power. Money is the first and most obvious application. It will not be the last.

My thoughts on TSLA (Tesla): Despite revenue growth recovery +15.8% YoY, in absolute terms this is far from the largest quarter—revenue was $22.387B, which is lower than three years ago in Q1 2023 ($23.329B). The company missed analyst expectations by 0.4%, and the stock declined by 2.7% after the earnings release. GAAP net income decreased by 22% QoQ, driven by a decline in Bitcoin value and unfavorable FX effects. Gross margin improved across all segments in Q1: Automotive at 21.1% (19.2% excluding regulatory credits), Energy at a record 39.5%, and Services GM also increased to 9.2%. However, management noted that the GM increase included about $230M of one-time warranty write-down benefits and some tariff relief. Global vehicle inventory (days of supply) increased to 27 days, which is close to a record level for Tesla. Growth in energy and storage was -12% YoY, and storage deployments declined by 15.4% YoY, with Megapack 3 production scheduled to start later this year. Tesla shares trade at the highest multiples among the Magnificent 7, with forward P/E at 191.4x, meaning the valuation already reflects significant expectations for future growth. Management guided to more than $25B in CapEx this year, with Tesla investing heavily in future growth, reinforcing investor expectations. Spending will support six factories entering operation, AI infrastructure, Robotaxi scaling, Optimus deployment, a semiconductor fab, solar manufacturing equipment, and related growth systems. Cybercab production has started, and Semi production is expected soon. Global paid FSD customers reached nearly 1.3 million, with FSD version 14.3 released. It has received approval in the Netherlands and China, with broader EU approval potentially later in Q2 and wider China approval expected by Q3. Robotaxi operations are already running in Austin, Dallas, and Houston. Optimus is viewed very optimistically by Elon Musk, who described it as potentially Tesla’s biggest product ever. Optimus V3 is nearly ready for demonstration, with production expected to begin in late July or August. Management remains optimistic about the future and plans to expand production across all vehicle factories, scale the Robotaxi network, launch Optimus production, and roll out Megapack 3. Tesla is clearly investing in its future and, in my view, has strong potential for a positive growth scenario. However, it’s important not to overlook the elevated valuation multiples, as a significant part of the positive scenario is already priced into the stock and still needs to be executed.

On April 23, Tether froze $344 million of USDT on Tron in direct coordination with OFAC and US law enforcement, the largest single enforcement action in the stablecoin’s history. Forty-eight hours. Three posts. One sovereign signal. The sequence is what nobody is saying out loud. Read it slowly. Sun’s decentralization boast was triggered by Arbitrum’s emergency Security Council freezing $71 million of ETH stolen from the Kelp DAO bridge exploit, attributed to North Korea’s Lazarus Group. Sun’s tweet directly mocked Arbitrum’s ability to freeze a hacker’s wallet. His implicit claim was that Tron, with twenty-seven Super Representatives and no protocol-level admin keys, could not be censored that way. Twenty-four hours later Sun filed suit against World Liberty Financial, the Trump-linked crypto venture that froze 545 million of his own WLFI tokens (roughly $100 million) in September 2025. Twenty-four hours after that, two Tron addresses holding $212.9 million and $131.3 million in USDT were blacklisted inside minutes at Tether’s sole discretion, at the USDT smart contract level, on the chain Sun had just branded the most decentralized in the world. Tether’s CEO Paolo Ardoino framed it as compliance. “USDT is not a safe haven for illicit activity.” That is the official reading and is likely true at the level of the specific addresses, which on-chain analysts have traced to layering patterns dating to October 2021. But the narrative geometry is what matters. In one week, three stablecoin and Layer-2 issuers made three different censorship decisions on the same underlying question. Arbitrum froze $71 million from the Lazarus Group via multisig Security Council emergency vote. Tether froze $344 million on Tron at sole issuer discretion in direct OFAC coordination. Circle, which has its own freeze capability, refused to freeze $230 million stolen from the Drift Protocol hack also linked to North Korean hackers, despite the funds moving through its Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol during US business hours. Three issuers, three tempos, three political postures, one demonstration week. The universe-breaking part is what this confirms about the dollar stack. Every dollar-pegged stablecoin on every major chain, whether Ethereum, Tron, Solana, or a Layer 2, runs on admin keys held by the issuer. Those keys are a kill switch. The kill switch can be pulled at the issuer’s sole discretion, in minutes, without user consent, without on-chain governance, without appeal. The kill switch was pulled on Justin Sun’s chain the day after he sued a Trump-linked venture, by the issuer most closely coordinated with OFAC, at a size that sets a new institutional record. The $344 million was almost certainly linked to real illicit conduct. That is not the point. The point is that the capability exists, operates in minutes, and was deployed against a network whose founder had just publicly challenged Trump-adjacent crypto power. Three readings of this week. Routine compliance at unprecedented scale. Priced. Coincidence of timing between Sun’s WLFI lawsuit and the Tether freeze. Likely coincidence. The dollar stack has a visible governor and that governor was demonstrated on the chain whose founder most loudly claimed to have escaped it. The market is pricing the first.
