GROK SAID : Glewme Protocol is a new metaprotocol (launched today, April 24, 2026) built directly on top of Solana. It uses inscriptions to create "sub-chain tokens" that live parasitically inside Solana's existing infrastructure—no separate blockchain, no custom program deployment, and no bridges required for mirroring. Core idea: Inscription via Solana's Memo ProgramSolana has a built-in Memo Program (current ID: MemoSq4gqABAXKb96qnH8TysNcWxMyWCqXgDLGmfcHr). This is an extremely lightweight, no-op program whose only job is to accept a UTF-8 string (the "memo") and log it permanently as part of the transaction record. It costs almost nothing and is already part of every Solana transaction's history.Glewme inscribes token data by embedding specially formatted memos into ordinary Solana transactions. These memos act as the canonical, on-chain record for the token's state (mint rules, ownership, transfers, etc.). Because the data lives directly in Solana's transaction logs, it inherits Solana's security, finality, and low fees without needing its own validators or smart-contract runtime. This is why it's called a "parasitic" or "sub-chain" token— it borrows Solana's compute and ledger but operates as its own protocol layer. Unrecycling How the inscription mechanism works (step-by-step)Create an inscription transaction You (or the Glewme launcher) build a normal Solana transaction that calls the Memo Program and includes a structured payload in the memo field. This payload is typically JSON-like data defining the token operation (e.g., "mint 1,000,000 tokens to address X with supply cap Y"). On-chain verification Solana validators automatically execute the Memo instruction and record the exact string in the transaction log. This is the "on-chain verified" part—no extra trust or oracles needed. The inscription is now immutable and publicly queryable forever on Solana's ledger. Indexers/scanners interpret the data Glewme provides (or will provide) a scanner/launcher that reads these memos and presents them as a coherent token experience. The token exists "parasitically" inside Solana but appears to users as a full sub-chain asset. Bridgeless mirrors & multi-chain expansion The same inscription format can be mirrored to >40 other chains via their equivalent memo/data-embedding mechanisms. Because the canonical record is the inscription itself (not a bridged token), there's no bridge risk or liquidity fragmentation. This is why the project calls it "bridge obsolescence." Unrecycling Key features highlighted in the official graphicInscription Token → The token is created and governed purely through these memo inscriptions. On-Chain Verified → Everything is verified by Solana's consensus itself. Memo-Inscribed → Uses the native Memo Program (the cheapest and most permanent way to store data on Solana). Parasitic sub-chain → Runs "inside" Solana at minimal cost while behaving like its own chain. Why this matters (according to the creator's posts)Maximum infrastructure, minimum cost: You get Solana-level speed/security/fees without deploying anything heavy. Discreet launches: Launch tokens quietly via the Glewme launcher (linked in Unrecycling 's bio). Scanner + launcher included: Tools to view and create these inscribed tokens right away. This is brand-new (literally hours old as of this post), so full technical documentation or open-source code isn't publicly indexed yet. The mechanism is intentionally simple: it's just clever reuse of the Memo Program + a standard inscription format, similar to how Bitcoin Ordinals or earlier Solana SPL-20 inscriptions work, but packaged as a full metaprotocol with bridgeless multi-chain mirroring.

Great inteview by RaoulGMI PeterDiamandis and salimismail Over the last six-plus years, I’ve been obsessed with one question: how do we stay human and evolve inside this coming acceleration? Not just as an informed or productive human, but mature—emotionally, technologically, and economically—while the ground keeps shifting beneath us. We’ve all heard the macro stories by now: Ray Dalio’s changing world order and big cycles, the Fourth Turning, Raoul Pal’s “economic singularity,” Peter Diamandis and Salim Ismail on exponential tech upending every industry. The ideas are simple and terrifying: cycles are converging, institutions are straining, everything is accelerating and we’re heading into a decade where the old order breaks and something new gets forced into being. I don’t disagree with that. Where I want to offer something different is this: the pattern doesn’t have to be a trap. Chaos isn’t just something that happens to us. It’s also the raw material for what we build next. For a long time, I've heard and played inside another familiar story: “to become a billionaire, help a billion people,” or the entrepreneurial motto “find a massive problem and solve it.” It’s a beautiful idea, and it pulled me into years of exploration and building. But it also kept me in a quiet war with reality. To fix the world, you have to keep seeing the world as broken. To save the world, you have to keep seeing it as unsaved. My identity was subtly tethered to what was wrong. A few years ago, that tension leaked into a short post I wrote: “The best investments are anti-inflammatory drugs for inflamed institutions. Religion → Spiritual communities & Psycedelics Big Finance → DeFi Big Government → Network States/Communities Big Tech → Web3, Crowdfunding Venture Capital → Venture Communities Big Pharma → Psychedelics & tech-assisted therapies Education → Homeschooling, Micro-Schools Big Media → Digital Creators The Fed → Bitcoin” At the time, it was mostly a pattern-spotting exercise. Now it feels like a map of where our attention can go instead of getting trapped in fighting the old. Rather than pouring all our energy into trying to repair inflamed institutions from the inside, we can pour more of it into the places where anti-inflammatory experiments are already happening—new ways of doing money, meaning, power, healing, and coordination. President Trump signed an executive order this week asking agencies to accelerate psychedelic and other novel therapies for serious mental illness, and regulators are already responding. Psychedelics are moving from the margins into frontline medicine as tools for healing and rewiring. For me, that matters as much as any AI breakthrough. If our nervous systems can’t adapt—if we stay locked in old fear patterns and stored conditions—no amount of technology will save us. At the same time, decentralization is not just a crypto talking point. Energy, finance, and coordination are all drifting from massive centralized hubs toward more local and networked structures: from national grids toward small modular reactors and microgrids, from big finance toward more permissionless rails, from broadcast media toward creators and niche communities. These shifts don’t automatically fix politics or power, but they do change the terrain we’re playing on. The pattern I see underneath all of this looks something like: - global chaos as background noise, - urgency as a constant state, - outrage and victimhood as default identities, - and brilliant, caring people burning out in isolation instead of building together. I’ve felt that personally—the pull of distraction colliding with the urgency to produce, perform, and insert myself into “the solution.” It’s easy to get caught in a loop where every new crisis is another reason to hustle harder or doom-scroll longer, while the part of you that actually wants to create and connect gets more and more exhausted. This is especially true around AI. The people shaping the loudest narratives—the frontier labs, the big platforms, the talking heads—aren’t neutral observers. Their business models depend on attention, adoption, and urgency. They benefit when we feel like we’re behind, at risk of being left out, or in danger of being replaced. The more rushed and disoriented we feel, the more likely we are to grab for whatever product or story promises safety or an edge. In an attention economy where fear and outrage outperform almost everything else, both AI hype and AI doom run on the same fuel: our amygdala. Pro‑AI content (“you’ll be obsolete if you don’t use this”) and anti‑AI content (“this will wipe out humanity, jobs, and safety”) can end up feeding the same field of chaos. That doesn’t mean risk isn’t real. It means we have to notice when our nervous system is being harvested and choose, consciously, how much of our attention we want to spend there. Lately, I’ve been wondering if there’s another starting point. What if the first move isn’t “find a problem,” but “find out who you are”—the gifts and golden shadow under the fear and performance, the part of you that wants to express, contribute, and collaborate even when no one is watching? Maybe we don’t have to manufacture a desire to serve. Maybe we’re wired for contribution by default, and the work is to uncover that truth and give it real-world form. From that place, we’re not fighting the world as broken so much as fighting for something: for deeper honesty about who we are, for better relationships, for healthier bodies and nervous systems, for communities and infrastructures that reflect that inner shift. As we do that, some of what we set out to “fix” may start to change as a consequence of who we’re becoming, not just because of what we’re attacking. None of this means staying in our heads or on the meditation cushion. It has to land in real arenas: how we treat our bodies and minds, the communities we join or build, the tools and industries we pour ourselves into. For some, that will look like psychedelics and trauma work. For others, decentralized energy or parallel finance. For others, education, humanitarian work, digital creation, or venture communities. The point isn’t which arena you pick; it’s whether you’re acting from fear and performance, or from an honest expression of who you are and what you’re here to contribute. Underneath the macro narratives, I’m convinced the real leverage now is in three places: inner evolution and nervous system work, including psychedelics and other therapies used with care; decentralized infrastructure that brings energy, finance, and governance closer to people; and communities—venture communities, learning groups, neighborhoods—that choose to build together instead of trying to navigate all of this alone. I don’t want to romanticize any of it. People are suffering right now, feel the burden of uncertainty, and systems could fail in ways that cost lives. There will be injustice, shock, and grief. Some of us are called to stand directly in those fires, and that deserves nothing but respect. But inside that, we’ve been handed an opening: a chance to rethink almost everything from a different lens—not from resentment at the old order, but from a deeper relationship with ourselves, each other, and the tools in our hands. To see AI, psychedelics, new energy and money systems, and new forms of community as change agents we can partner with, not just survive. The frontiers are all around us. That kind of rethinking doesn’t start in a boardroom or a video. It starts internally: in how we meet fear, how we manage our own inflammation, and where we place our attention. And then it starts again—outside of us—when we gather with like-hearted, like-minded people who share a direction and a focus, and choose to build together instead of facing this transition alone. If this feels aligned, DM and/or follow for emerging people, projects, and communities I am amplifying! Godspeed.

Betting Too Heavily on the Downside — What Rising OI and Negative Funding Mean for Bitcoin via cryptoquant_com The Bitcoin market is currently showing a strong increase in bearish positioning. This is clearly visible in derivatives data. According to CryptoQuant analyst G a a h (gaah_im), Funding rates, which reflect the balance between long and short positions, have dropped into deeply negative territory. This means more traders are betting on price declines, and importantly, they are paying to maintain those short positions. In other words, the market is not just bearish — it is confidently bearish. At the same time, open interest (OI) is rising. OI represents the total number of outstanding positions that have not yet been closed. When OI increases, it means more capital is being committed to active bets in the market. What matters here is the composition of those bets. Since funding rates are negative, the growing OI is largely driven by short positions. This creates a structure where the market is increasingly positioned for further downside. However, this setup carries a critical implication. Short positions must eventually be closed, and if price begins to rise, these traders are forced to buy back, creating upward pressure. This is known as a short squeeze. Historically, periods of extremely negative funding have often preceded sharp upward moves, not continued declines. That said, this does not guarantee an immediate bullish trend. Rather, it signals a buildup of latent energy that can lead to increased volatility. In essence, the market is in a phase of extreme pessimism while simultaneously accumulating the conditions for a potential rebound.

Back in the day, Chinese gold spot exchanges enforced daily forced liquidation and settlement, with long and short positions paying deferred fees to each other. The exchanges didn't directly collect this money, but when retail investors held a large long position and leveraged highly, the deferred fees became the platform's most stable, hidden source of income—retail investors paid long-term, and the platform indirectly benefited through trading volume and liquidity. The same applies to Bitcoin spot platforms now: They primarily rely on perpetual contracts(not pure spot trading), with long and short positions settling **funding rates** every 8 hours. When long positions are in the majority, they pay short positions; retail investors holding long positions for a long time are constantly paying. The exchange itself doesn't directly collect this money, but it greatly increases trading activity and open interest, indirectly generating transaction fees, liquidity, and user stickiness, indirectly becoming a large and stable source of income for the platform. The only difference is the terminology: back then it was called "deferred fees," now it's called "funding rates," but the essence is exactly the same。

NAT isn't just another token; it's a fundamental shift in how we value the "matter" produced by the Bitcoin network. By the way, there is a deep irony here that most people miss. Gold is rare for a very fundamental reason. In the normal life cycle of a star, elements can only be fused up to iron. Beyond iron, fusion no longer releases energy. It consumes energy. That breaks the delicate balance inside the star between gravity pulling inward and radiation pressure pushing outward. As long as fusion produces energy, the star can sustain itself. But once it builds up iron in its core, that process stops. The star can no longer support itself, gravity takes over, and the core collapses. What follows is a catastrophic event: a supernova. Depending on the original mass, what remains is a neutron star or a black hole. In that violent collapse and explosion, extreme conditions emerge. Temperatures and pressures become so high that heavy elements like gold can finally be formed. It is not a gentle, continuous process. It is explosive, rare, and energetically expensive. Gold is born in a brief, chaotic “soup” of radiation and nuclear reactions during these events. This is, in a very real sense, nature’s proof of work. An enormous amount of energy must be expended to create something that is intrinsically scarce and difficult to produce. That is precisely why gold has value. Its rarity is not arbitrary. It is physically enforced by the laws of nuclear physics and stellar evolution. Bitcoin follows an analogous principle. It forces the expenditure of real-world energy to create new units. This is not waste. It is the mechanism that anchors scarcity in reality. So when PeterSchiff claims that using energy to secure a monetary system is pointless, they are ignoring the fundamental fact that the value of gold itself is rooted in the same principle. The energy cost is not a flaw. It is the foundation.

I read Thinking in Systems when I was 15. At the time I was part of a political experiment here in Italy, and I became very close to the two founders, I'll call them A and D. A very original idea of the group was to organize political proposals using System Dynamics, a method for modeling complex systems through feedback loops, stocks, and flows. Because of this, it was A’s desire that at least those with active roles in the group read Thinking in Systems: a Primer. I read the book, found it very interesting, and decided to translate it from English into Italian to make it more accessible to the group, which I did over the following two months. The different pace imposed by translation meant I paid much closer attention on the second reading. During those two months, Donella Meadows became my mentor: I would spend hours staring into space, digging through my memory and reorganizing everything using a systemic method, and I began picking up every book I could find on the subject. If today I do research on system dynamics and see the world through a system thinking lens that I apply to everything, from the most abstract ideas to understanding the business model of a company as Strategy (MSTR), it is certainly because of A, those two months, and this book. In those same years, I actually became much closer to D than to A, with entire nights spent discussing politics, technology, history, and future. And a couple of years later, after my “platonic” encounter with Meadows, he was the first to tell me about Bitcoin, and the one with whom I made my first transaction on the Bitcoin network, which would become another major obsession of mine. This is why, when in the future people ask me what possessed me to put almost my entire family’s wealth into an imaginary internet Ponzi coin and into a company leveraged to that same internet Ponzi coin (described by its CEO as “the goddess of wisdom”), I will say that I had good friends, read good books, and followed my heart.

Quantum computing isn’t expected to impact crypto anytime soon, but it does challenge one core assumption that blockchain security relies on. Today, private keys cannot realistically be derived from public keys, and that is what makes ownership secure across networks like Bitcoin and Ethereum. But blockchain data is already public. Once a transaction is made, the public key gets exposed. This means the data needed for a future attack is already available and can be stored today and potentially used later. The real risk is not a sudden collapse. It is gradual exposure over time as quantum capabilities improve. Solving this is not simple either. Upgrading cryptography in blockchains requires coordination across developers, wallets, exchanges, and infrastructure, and that process can take years. The industry does not need urgency today, but it does need to start preparing early to avoid problems later. Because in crypto, it always comes down to one rule. Whoever controls the key controls the assets.

Maybe you don’t fully realize how serious quantum attacks on crypto could be. So let me explain it simply, so you can understand what QUIP is trying to protect us from. The biggest danger comes from something called Shor’s algorithm. In simple terms, it allows a powerful quantum computer to solve complex math problems in seconds, problems that would normally take classical computers billions of years. Right now, blockchains like Bitcoin and Ethereum rely on this same math for security. They use something called elliptic curve cryptography to protect wallets. However, here’s the scary part: once your public key is visible onchain, a quantum computer could reverse it and find your private key in minutes. On the other hand, there is Grover’s algorithm, which is less dangerous and can be handled by increasing security strength. It is about a specific zone: a -2% ADP deviation on Bitcoin. ⠀ This is the point where the manipulation aimed at removing excess participants has already been completed, while the next impulse has not yet started. An ideal entry for those who know how to wait and read these signals. ⠀ Over the past month, we saw three clear cases: ⠀ March 30 — ADP touched -2%, after which the asset confidently returned above the zero boundary. The signal played out cleanly. ⠀ April 12 — the same scenario repeated. ADP moved into the -2% zone, excess passengers were removed, and the move continued. ⠀ April 16 — the same story again. Touch, recovery, continuation. ⠀ Why -2%, and not -5% or -10%? ⠀ Because deeper deviations on Bitcoin mean something different. They either point to a structural shift on higher timeframes, or mark the beginning of cascading liquidity grabs, after which a confident recovery does not always happen. ⠀ -2% is a calibrated shakeout. Stops are collected, excess participants are removed, and the market maker is ready to continue the established direction without overloading the position or needing to reverse the structure. ⠀ Context is essential. ⠀ The signal works together with higher timeframes. If 1D and 3D confirm the buyer’s side, then -2% becomes a gift that would be strange to ignore. ⠀ But if higher timeframes show weakness, then -2% may only be an intermediate point before a deeper decline. ⠀ So always check the context: higher timeframes define the direction, while ADP on lower timeframes provides the entry point. ⠀ Trade carefully, without greed. ⠀ Want to understand more? Crypto taxation in India is more detailed than most people realise. It is not just about the 30% tax rule. Every crypto transaction is evaluated separately under the current tax framework. For example, if you buy Bitcoin at ₹1 lakh and sell it at ₹1.4 lakh, the ₹40,000 profit is taxed at 30%. If you buy at ₹1 lakh and sell at ₹70,000, there is no tax payable because there is no profit. However, this loss cannot be adjusted against other crypto gains. Crypto-to-crypto swaps are also treated as taxable transfers, and staking rewards may trigger taxation when received, depending on their nature, with further tax implications if sold later at a profit. The very first ICO in crypto raised over 5,000 BTC worth $391M at today’s prices. And that was before Ethereum even existed. In 2013, Mastercoin conducted what is widely regarded as the first ICO. Participants sent BTC to a designated address and received Mastercoin (MSC) in return. > There were no smart contracts. > No launchpads. > No KYC. > No dashboards showing allocations. Just send BTC and receive tokens later. The idea came from J. R. Willett’s “Second Bitcoin Whitepaper,” which proposed building new layers and assets on top of Bitcoin. Over 5,000 BTC was raised that way (at a time when BTC was around $100). What’s interesting is how much has changed since then. Today, ICO-style launches involve: - structured allocations - vesting schedules - compliance layers - exchange considerations - and heavy expectations around immediate liquidity Yet the core idea is still the same: fund a network before it exists, in exchange for tokens. The structure evolved, but the mechanism didn’t. Would people still trust something as simple as that first ICO today?

Cardano’s governance model is built into the protocol, and that changes how decisions actually get made. At a basic level, governance is about where influence sits and how it moves when there is pressure. In many blockchains, influence ends up concentrated around a small group of visible actors. These are usually tied to funding, infrastructure, or early ownership. Over time, decision making leans on those people rather than the system itself. That creates fragility. Incentives change. External pressure builds. There is also a security angle that often gets ignored. When influence is tied to known individuals, they become targets. That can be financial, legal, political, or more direct forms of coercion. The risk is no longer just technical, it becomes personal. It is far easier to pressure a handful of identifiable people than it is to influence a distributed set of participants. Bitcoin approached this problem in a very specific way. It reduced reliance on identifiable leadership from the beginning and leaned on social consensus and conservative change. The system is simple in that regard. Changes are slow. Assumptions are minimal. “I've moved on to other things.” — Satoshi Nakamoto That absence became part of its strength. It is also something that cannot easily be recreated. Most blockchains do not start from that position. They need a way to distribute influence after launch. Without it, governance exists, but it is informal and exposed, with clear points where pressure can be applied. Cardano handles this at the protocol level. Any holder can delegate their voting power. Any individual can register as a DRep. Those representatives vote on treasury withdrawals, protocol parameter changes, and future direction. What matters is how influence flows. It is not fixed to a name or position. It moves with delegation. If trust changes, voting power moves with it. Representation becomes something that can adjust over time rather than something that stays locked in place. That spreads both influence and risk. You can see the difference when looking across blockchains. Where coordination depends on known figures or informal groups, decision making tends to narrow when it matters most. Where it is built into the system and spread out, it has more room to respond. Cardano makes governance an explicit part of the system, with defined paths for how influence is used and how it can change. Over time, that matters. We’re wrapping up a week in crypto that looks set to close roughly flat. We dipped midweek, then recovered after FOMC and earnings reports came in stronger than expected across many sectors. With that now behind us, we can start looking ahead. I’m fully aware that a 20%+ move in BTC will likely lead to a pullback sooner or later. My expectation was that the extremely negative funding rates would trigger a short squeeze, something we still haven’t seen yet. What I am highly convinced of, however, is that the pessimistic sentiment we’re seeing right now is a very bullish sign for the rest of 2026. Building long-term bottoms takes time. Retail needs to lose interest. Algos need to play out their game. People need to question the rally, “aren’t we supposed to bottom in October like always?” We’ve spent the last three months building a solid base, and from a long-term perspective, things look very constructive. The fact that we’ve stabilized around 78k is probably no coincidence, that’s where the True Market Mean currently sits. So what is the True Market Mean? In simple terms, it’s the average purchase price of Bitcoin, but only for active investors. As most people know, there are many wallets that haven’t moved their BTC in years, Satoshi’s wallets being the most obvious example. This metric filters those out and instead calculates the average price paid by investors who have actually been moving and trading their coins recently. That gives us a fairly accurate estimate of where recent market participants are sitting at breakeven. Right now, that level is around 78k. And as the chart shows, it would be very constructive if we can establish acceptance above it, since historically that has signaled the beginning of long-term bullish trends in BTC. Credit to OnChainMind for the chart. The S&P is currently sitting at all-time highs, with a lot of liquidity resting below current price. That’s really my only concern at the moment. Crypto is, as we know, a risk-on asset, and if equities see a pullback, crypto & Bitcoin will most likely follow. If that happens, I’d view it as a very attractive opportunity to position for a swing long, especially for anyone still underallocated. Overall, I think the market structure looks very healthy, and I’m excited to see how the rest of 2026 unfolds. When we look back at this year, I believe crypto will end up being one of the stronger-performing asset classes, but time will tell.

Japan just announced it's preparing crypto ETFs for 2027. Everyone focused on the ETF headline. Nobody is talking about what actually has to happen first. JPX CEO Hiromi Yamaji told Bloomberg on April 30 that Japan Exchange Group which operates the Tokyo Stock Exchange and Osaka Exchange is ready to list BTC and ETH spot ETFs as early as 2027. Technical infrastructure is already in place. The exchange can move "anytime once the legal framework is in place and the tax treatment is clarified." That second part is the whole story. Japan currently taxes crypto gains as miscellaneous income. Top rate: 55%. That's not a typo. A Japanese investor who made significant returns on BTC last cycle paid more than half of it to the government. By comparison, stocks and investment trusts in Japan are taxed at a flat 20%. The proposed reform cuts crypto gains to that same flat 20% rate. It would also allow investors to offset crypto losses against gains for up to three years something currently unavailable for crypto but standard for equities. That's not a marginal change. That's a structural transformation of the investment case for crypto in the world's fourth largest economy. Here's why this matters more than the ETF announcement itself. Japan has 67 million retail brokerage accounts. A crypto tax rate sitting at 55% meant that even investors who wanted exposure had a rational reason to stay out. At 20% flat, the after-tax return profile of BTC held through a regulated ETF becomes directly comparable to holding Japanese equities. For the first time, a Japanese retail investor can make an apples-to-apples comparison between allocating to a Nikkei index fund and allocating to a BTC ETF and the tax treatment won't punish them for choosing crypto. Nomura Asset Management, SBI Global Asset Management, and Daiwa Asset Management have all already studied or prepared ETF products. They were waiting for exactly this legal window. But there's a complication nobody is covering. JPX is simultaneously running a separate consultation deadline May 7 on whether to exclude companies holding more than 50% of their assets in crypto from the TOPIX index. This would directly affect Metaplanet, Remixpoint, and ANAP Holdings during the October 2026 rebalance. Think about the contradiction that creates. JPX is opening the front door to crypto ETFs while potentially closing the back door on publicly listed companies that adopted Bitcoin treasury strategies. The same institutional framework being built to bring BTC to Japanese retail investors could simultaneously eject the Japanese companies that bet on BTC earliest. MSCI ran the same debate earlier this year and decided not to exclude crypto treasury companies from its Global Investable Market Indexes in February. JPX hasn't decided yet. Now zoom out and look at what this week actually represents. The US has $105B in BTC ETF AUM. Europe has MiCA. Canada just banned crypto ATMs. Belarus built a crypto banking system. And now Japan the fourth largest economy in the world is reclassifying crypto under its Financial Instruments and Exchange Act. cutting the tax rate by 35 percentage points, and giving its largest asset managers a legal path to launch BTC and ETH products. The global institutionalization of crypto isn't a narrative anymore. It's a regulatory pipeline that's active in every major economic bloc simultaneously. Japan's timeline has one real risk. Diet legislative progress. If the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act revision doesn't clear parliament by year-end, the 2027 window slips to 2028. Yamaji acknowledged this explicitly. The exchange is ready. The lawyers are ready. The asset managers are ready. The politicians have to actually vote. That's always the last mile.

A hidden fingerprint inside Bitcoin earliest blocks reveals a single miner quietly accumulated 1.1 million BTC and never spent a coin In 2013, researcher Sergio Demian Lerner uncovered a pattern buried inside the first 50,000 Bitcoin blocks. By analyzing the ExtraNonce field, a small value that changes during mining, he discovered something no one had noticed since launch. When plotted, these values formed distinct slopes, each representing different miners operating in the network early days. A single entity mined roughly 22,000 out of the first 36,000 blocks with perfectly consistent timing, identical behavior, and no overlap. Lerner named this dominant miner Patoshi. The conclusion was striking. One individual mined approximately 1.1 million BTC between 2009 and mid 2010, equal to 5.7 percent of total Bitcoin supply. Despite having the power to dominate nearly the entire network, Patoshi deliberately limited mining activity to around half of capacity. This behavior suggests an intentional effort to allow others to participate, supporting decentralization in its earliest phase. Even more telling, the mining schedule followed human like rhythms. Activity started and stopped at consistent times, resembling one person operating a machine rather than an industrial system. Around April 2010, the pattern vanished completely. No further blocks were mined by this entity. The most astonishing part is what remains untouched. Around 1.1 million BTC still sit across thousands of addresses, unmoved for over 16 years. At current value, this represents over 115 billion dollars, making it the largest dormant fortune in history. If these coins ever move, markets would face the largest liquidity event ever seen. If they remain untouched, a massive portion of supply is effectively removed forever. Either scenario reshapes Bitcoin future. And the decision belongs to a figure who disappeared in 2011 without a trace.

If OnlyGiri was just an Ordinals collection I decided to launch, hoping it would mint out fast, disappear for months, and then come back with another collection, then yes, maybe the conclusion would be simple. It did not mint out, so it failed. But that is not what this is. OnlyGiri is part of a much bigger world I am trying to build. The collection was created with two very clear goals in mind. First, to raise some money so I can pay people to help with the things I cannot do alone. Second, to find the first holders, the first supporters, and the first signs of community around OnlyGiri. And let me be very clear about the money part too. Would I be profitable if the collection minted out at the current price? Yes, slightly. Maybe a few thousand dollars. Is that life changing money? Hell no. Can I still try to build this without the collection minting out? Yes. I will try my best. It will just take more time. But there is something interesting I have noticed in this space. When the price is low, people sometimes question it more. When a founder raises millions, there are somehow fewer questions. But when someone is trying to raise 10 to 30k to actually build something, people look at it with more doubt. I understand that too. This market has made people cautious, and for good reasons. But for me, the goal was never to extract as much money as possible. The goal was to make the collection accessible, raise enough to move faster, and start building a small early community around something I truly believe in. Now, let’s talk about the collection size and price. Do I think OnlyGiri is not performing well because of the price? Absolutely not. The mint price is $7. I do not believe that is expensive for what is being created. Quite the opposite. I honestly think it is priced way, way lower than what it should be, but I chose that price because I wanted it to be accessible. History has shown us many times that price alone is not what makes a collection succeed or fail. What matters far more is product market fit and marketing. Supply goes hand in hand with that conversation. OnlyGiri has a total supply of 4,444. Is that too big? I do not think so. The number 4 plays an important role in the lore and the story I am building, so the realistic options were 444, 4,444, or 44,444. To be honest, I was more inclined toward a much bigger supply, because a bigger supply gives you a better chance to onboard more people and create a larger community. But I chose 4,444 because I wanted it to feel reasonable and not scare people away. Again, I do not believe supply and price are the main issue here. What matters most is product market fit and strong marketing. Another thing I want to address is market conditions. Some people might say the mint is struggling because the market is bad. I personally do not agree with that. I have been in crypto long enough to know that everyone experiences the market differently depending on what they hold. To me, when Bitcoin is above $70,000, I cannot seriously call that a crypto winter. If someone bought an asset at $50,000 and today that asset is worth $50, and they are still waiting for it to return to their entry, then yes, for them it probably feels like a brutal bear market. But that is a personal bear market. That is not automatically the whole market. There are people holding assets that are performing well. There are people holding Bitcoin. There are people holding things that are outperforming yours. Those people do not experience the same market you do. So I do not fully buy the idea that the overall market is simply bad. Market sentiment is relative. It depends on your position, your timing, your assets, and your expectations. And personally, as long as Bitcoin is above $10,000, I will probably forever feel like we are in a bull market. That is just how I see it. Even when Ordinals were at their highest attention, Bitcoin was not at $100,000 either. So again, I do not think market conditions are the main reason. So, is there product market fit for OnlyGiri right now? Probably not yet. And that is the challenging part. I am trying to introduce something new and original into the Ordinals and NFT space. Would OnlyGiri have performed better if it was a derivative? Honestly, yes. Most likely. We have seen it in recent times. Derivatives of Shrooms, Pizza Ninjas, Puppets, Punks, and many others get attention faster because people already understand them. They already feel familiar. They already speak the language of an existing audience. And that is not a bad thing. Derivatives can be fun, powerful, and culturally relevant. They often have a higher chance of success because the audience already has an emotional connection with the original thing they reference. But that is not what I wanted to build. OnlyGiri is not a derivative because it belongs to a different story, an original story I am crafting. So by nature, it cannot be a derivative. At the same time, I have embedded traits, references, and small pieces of influence from many collections I have grown to love and respect into the OnlyGiri world. That balance matters to me. Original, but still connected to the culture that inspired it. Creating something original is risky. People are not familiar with it yet. They do not instantly know how to place it, how to value it, or how to connect with it. That is part of the risk I chose. Maybe the Ordinals space is not ready yet for what I am trying to do. Maybe something like this needs more time, more context, and a wider audience before it can be fully embraced. And that is completely fine. Because the Ordinals audience is not the only audience I am building for. The goal is much bigger than that. OnlyGiri is meant to be part of a wider world, a story, a game, and a brand that can reach far beyond the current Ordinals market. That is why I do not accept the idea that OnlyGiri has failed just because the mint has not gone well so far. What I see right now is not failure. I see feedback. I see a starting point. I see proof that building something original is harder, slower, and riskier. But I also see the exact reason why it is worth doing. OnlyGiri was never supposed to be a quick mint and disappear. It was always supposed to be the beginning of something much bigger. All these points, and more, I will cover during the Space today. I would genuinely love to hear your point of view on this. Your feedback, your disagreement, your questions, your support, all of it. If you have been watching the OnlyGiri mint from the side, if you minted, if you considered minting, or even if you think I am wrong about some of this, I would love you to join the Space tonight. Let’s talk about it openly

While somewhat hidden for non-technical users, local/private sounds GREAT but it comes with heavy technical tradeoffs. Long post (for X) but as simple as I can make it, to explain. Typically, when you work with AI you log in to some sort of system or you're working with a mirror, i.e. you log in to X site but it's really just a Claude/etc wrapper sold to you at 20% token-markup. Good business, this is pretty much all AI you see today, I'm guilty of it too. When you are running local, the main issue is package/session fetching. So, you have to load WebGPU in the background (in the case of Greater) or you have to understand enough about the system with which you're integrating to either 1) trust it to work automagically, or 2) furnish client apps with cross-app/parental permissions, which is extremely challenging in a mobile environment. Within Greater, I can stash the Bitcoin+ repo(s) anywhere, I can host them as an extremely verbose and likely abusive NOSTR profile, but then this becomes a relay-dependent frustration most users won't want. You CAN create navigational style innovation to paginate this stuff and make it referential, but in that case, the WebGPU/etc instance needs to remain constant (centralized) whilst the reference KB/corpus needs to remain agnostic and JIT. It is a challenging problem to solve. Further, for someone on a mobile data plan with download/upload speeds and limits, downloading a 350mb "lightweight" in-browser LLM is simply too freakin expensive. I get it. Especially if you're researching Bitcoin/crypto/et al, you can easily chew through 1-3 gigs like... instantly. The tradeoff then comes from what is locally available or "harness engineered" or whatever term matters now, haha, to what is cached and referenceable. You wind up managing a knowledge base that is lifting database-level weight, and as an eng team, you are trying to minimize processing costs that can't keep up with user demands. I don't have a solution to this, but I wish I did. I think the cleanest solution is a device-auth processor agent that is single-download and then works across apps without auth, and the apps themselves provide the knowledge tree/graph, rock and roll. That's the best. But this is hard to explain to users, and is similar to the challenges I think Alby has with auth/sig tech in NOSTR. People claim stuff all the time, I definitely am guilty of this. If it's not abundantly clear, I am selling nothing here, I am just trying to explain how the world works, y'know, that world into which we've all been thrust and for which we're finding ourselves ill-prepared. As short as I could make it, unrevised.

The Realized Profit/Loss Ratio is rising again, but this may be more common than it seems during a bear market. Historically, every time Bitcoin entered a bear market, the Realized Profit/Loss Ratio started to decline before the cycle’s all-time highs, signaling imminent risk. Profit-taking is also observed throughout bear markets, as the network may perceive certain rallies as opportunities to exit due to broader market conditions. In the current scenario, the Realized Profit/Loss Ratio has not yet reached the minimum levels seen in some past cycles, where realized losses were truly elevated and pushed the index much lower. Many already believe this cycle is different, and it may indeed be different. Even some on-chain analysts are starting to change their views. We could be in a different regime, but it is very hard to justify the risk vs. reward when going against on-chain metrics. The smartest thing to do is to wait a few days or a few weeks for better confirmation. That is intelligent. About the chart: The Realized Profit/Loss Ratio compares the USD value of coins spent in profit against the USD value of coins spent in loss. Formula: Realized Profit / Realized Loss. How to use it: values above 1 show that profit-taking dominates loss realization, which is common in strong uptrends. Values below 1 show that loss realization dominates, often during stress, capitulation, or weak demand.

~ hey, ever heard of an 𝑬𝑻𝑭? ~ An ETF lets you invest in an asset without directly buying or holding it yourself. 𝐌𝐞𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 ETF stands for Exchange-Traded Fund. It’s a fund that tracks the price of something, like a stock, gold, or even Bitcoin, and is traded on regular stock markets. So instead of buying Bitcoin directly, you can buy a Bitcoin ETF and still get exposure to its price. 𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐈𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 ETFs make crypto more accessible to a different type of investor. For example: > People can invest through apps they already use for stocks > Big institutions can enter more easily > No need to manage wallets or private keys It brings more attention and money into the space, but through traditional systems. 𝐑𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 Think of it like investing in oil without owning barrels of oil. You’re not holding the actual asset, you’re just investing in something that follows its price. That’s what an ETF does. 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐨𝐧 𝐌𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞 Thinking buying a crypto ETF is the same as owning crypto. It’s not. ~ You don’t control the asset ~ You can’t use it on-chain ~ You’re relying on a company to manage it You’re getting price exposure, not ownership. 𝐐𝐮𝐢𝐜𝐤 𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 When you hear “ETF,” think: “This is crypto through the stock market.” It’s useful for exposure, but if you want full control or to actually use crypto, you’ll need to hold it yourself. _ Stay learned :)

Developers provide workloads, node operators offer infrastructure, and the network's activity itself becomes the basis for value distribution. The security model and the economic model are interconnected through the same workflow. The activity on the testnet indicates early momentum, with thousands of wallets and nodes engaged; however, the more critical indicator will be whether this abstraction layer can maintain its seamlessness as it scales and as real assets are subjected to stress tests. Bitcoin mining ≠ Ai datacenters While many similarities exist between the two, there’s a massive difference worth noting. The bitcoin network is the king of curtailment, the Führer of flexibility, the Don of dynamic load. Ai datacenters are irrational consumers of power (at least in the short/mid-term) chasing an unknown “general/super artificial intelligence, worth infinity b/c it’ll solve all health/consumer problems” and be like a god. They’re willing to spend anything to take some of Google’s market share on information search & delivery. Literally in their deal with Microsoft OpenAi defined general Ai as when “OpenAi/ChatGPT generates >$100B in profit from Ai product.” Pretty telling, I think. Because of this, they want electricity/power, and they’re willing to burn endless cash to get it to be the first to create superintelligence, because even if you burn $250B, the supposed return is gonna be 100x+ that. So Ai datacenters directly compete with residential power consumers. They compete with YOU when you want to turn on your oven or air conditioning. Ai datacenters aren’t flexible. They’re chasing the mother of all technological investments, they’re not willing to turn off. They demand tier 3 or 4 infrastructure (99.995% uptime guarantees, redundancy everywhere, fiber internet, HEPA clean air quality throughout entire facility, bazillions of dollars). Bitcoin miners are very very different. They only want to buy power **when nobody else wants to consume that power** You want to turn on your oven, dryer, or AC? No problem, bitcoin miners will not dare to compete with you for that power, they’ll curtail and turn computers off, and when you no longer want electricity, they’ll turn em back on. The bitcoin network is an infinitely flexible electricity buyer ⭐ of last resort⭐ Power producers love this — when little-to-nobody on the grid needs power, the electricity producer doesn’t need to turn off gigantic massive natgas turbines, or waste a bunch of hydroelectric power, they push it to the bitcoin miner. This lowers their operating costs while improving their base load, creating value that then ripples throughout the entire stack including to other ratepayers, saving power customers money. Bunch of Ai datacenters coming to your town/city? Different story. Multinational faceless corporations coming to compete for the kWh’s that make your life comfortable. They’re not interested in curtailing. If there’s a big winter storm or something, they MIGHT curtail to avoid liability/scrutiny, but they don’t have any rational incentive to curtail, whereas bitcoin miners have direct economic incentive to turn off. The rational behavior of bitcoin miners is synergistic/harmonious to electricity markets. Anyone who equates bitcoin mining to training & running LLM’s & Ai is likely ignorant of both topics. Of course many overlaps and similarities exist, but vastly different microeconomic incentives + operational nuances highlight how differently they incorporate into power markets. Nothing acts like bitcoin miners on the grid. The closest parallel is batteries, as they’re a power consumer of last resort, but batteries aren’t nearly as flexible or capital-efficient of a consumer as bitcoin miners, from a power capacity standpoint. So be careful when grouping “datacenters” as a single thing operating a single way as the truth is far far more nuanced.

Still have room to run. As we can see from these two metrics, even with Bitcoin's $20,000 rise, we could still have quite a way to go. The first image, the Bitcoin Value Days Destroyed Multiple (VDDM), identifies market tops and bottoms by tracking when long-term holders sell their coins. How it works: Coin Days Destroyed: When a coin held for a long time is finally sold, it "destroys" the days it sat idle. The Multiple: VDDM compares the dollar value of this selling activity over the last 30 days against the 1-year average. Market Signals: High VDDM: Long-term holders are selling heavily into a rally. This typically signals a cycle top as the smart money exits. Low VDDM: Long-term holders are sitting tight. This suggests a cycle bottom or period of accumulation. So, high values mean old money is leaving and low values mean old money is staying put. The second image is the UTXO Block P&L Count, this metric measures the percentage of Bitcoin "chunks" currently in profit versus loss. It identifies market extremes by tracking the financial health of every holder. How it works: It compares the price of Bitcoin when a coin last moved to its price today. In Profit: The current price is higher than the purchase price. In Loss: Current price is lower than the purchase price. Market Signals: High Profit: Almost everyone is in the green. This suggests euphoria and a high probability of a market top as people begin taking profits. High Loss: A large portion of the network is underwater. This typically indicates capitulation and proximity to a market bottom. Basically, it tracks investor pain vs. gain to signal when the market is overextended or undervalued. As we can see, these are both moving out of extremely low levels, suggesting that this recent move could be the beginning of a much larger run. Beginning of something bigger, or nah? Crypto Bitcoin

Bitcoin vs A-Network: A Simple Side by Side Look... Most people know Bitcoin as the original crypto, the one that started everything. A-Network is still very new and small. But the team keeps comparing their design to Bitcoin on purpose. So let’s break it down in plain English, no jargon, just the facts. What they have in common (the similarities): Both have a strict limit of exactly, 21 million coins that will ever exist. Once that number is reached, no more new coins can be created, ...EVER Both use a halving system where the reward for work gets smaller over time. Both started from absolute zero, just an idea, a whitepaper and a few early believers building the first blocks. Both are designed to run without any company or boss in control. And both treat the smallest unit of their coin like a “Satoshi”, tiny, divisible pieces that make everyday use possible. Where they are very different: Bitcoin mining needs powerful computers and lots of electricity. It’s a hardware race. A-Network mining needs only your phone and 6 hours of verified time each session. Anyone can do it. Bitcoin’s main job is to be digital money, a store of value that people hold or send. A-Network’s main job is to be a full network where your daily time gives you real ownership....decentralized identity, voting power in decisions, and eventually your own personal AI that belongs only to you. Bitcoin has no built in governance or extra features. A-Network ties your voice and your tools directly to how much you actually participate. In short: Bitcoin proved that scarcity and decentralization work. A-Network is trying to prove that time and consistent effort can be turned into the same kind of scarce, decentralized value, but in a way normal people can actually join. My analytical view... This is an interesting experiment. Bitcoin showed the world that a fixed supply, no central boss system can survive for 17 years and become worth trillions. A-Network is borrowing that same scarcity model but replacing the expensive hardware barrier with simple daily time. If it works, it could open the door for millions of regular people (not just those who can afford mining rigs) to own part of a real blockchain ecosystem. The risk is obvious...time based mining is easier to join, but it still needs enough honest participants to make the network strong and useful over the long run. Right now A-Network is still early, private mainnet, empty DEX pools, and everything being built step by step. But the design choice is clear...they want contribution, not capital, to be the main signal of value. It’s not trying to copy Bitcoin. It’s trying to take Bitcoin’s strongest idea (fixed supply + true decentralization) and make it more human and accessible. Whether that becomes the next big evolution or just stays a small experiment will depend on one thing...do enough people show up every day and do the work? What do you think, is “time as the new proof of work” a smart evolution of Bitcoin’s idea, or too different to succeed? ANetwork

Reflexivity is a term coined by George Soros to describe events in markets where the cognitive and manipulative functions of thinking cannot fully be separated, due to the inherent bias of the participants’ directional strategies. causing extended distortions in market behavior. While it is true that cryptos are almost purely reflexive assets, it’s worth bearing in mind that reflexive as the term is defined by George Soros contains the implication that there is massive mispricing. After a thorough investigation, TrinityMultiSig ruled in Sally’s favor and released 0.03824262 BTC to her. Harry received the remaining balance of 0.06175738 BTC, which he was free to keep or sell. Pleased to announce that another 25 Bitcoin have been added to The Smarter Web Company treasury today. This takes our total Bitcoin holdings to 2,830 BTC. I have seen some comments asking specific questions, and what I would ask people to do is trust the management team and judge us over months and quarters rather than individual transactions. You can always view our treasury data in real time via our Bitcoin treasury analytics page. As both the operating business and treasury grow, it will become impossible for us to demonstrate that every single transaction is immediately accretive. However, my view is that every transaction should contribute towards our medium to long term goal of increasing value for shareholders. My primary metric is Bitcoin per share. After that, I focus on total Bitcoin holdings. I also want to achieve this using a simple structure that can scale effectively. To drill down further, there are many variables involved, but here are a few useful points to consider: 1) If we raise capital through equity issuance, it will not necessarily be accretive immediately. It becomes accretive if the equity is issued at a premium to enterprise value and, after all costs, including retaining capital for working capital purposes, that capital is deployed into Bitcoin at the right level. 2) We can increase Bitcoin per share by adding debt. While we believe this is the right approach at this moment in time, investors also need to monitor the leverage (amplification) ratio, as increasing leverage also increases risk. It is also important to remember that debt - whether through our Coinbase facility or through preference shares used by other companies - has a cost, and that cost must be factored into the equation. 3) A Bitcoin treasury company also has operating costs. These costs must be funded using company resources. In our case, they are funded through a combination of operating cash flow and equity sale proceeds. This is one of the reasons why growing our operating business over the coming years remains an important objective. As a public company in the UK we announce our cash position twice a year, and must hold an appropriate amount of working capital as cash, so this cash position is invisible to investors when looking at the treasury day to day. 4) A Bitcoin treasury company can also improve the denominator: i.e. improve Bitcoin per share by reducing the fully diluted share count. Year-to-date, we have bought back and cancelled 42 million pre-IPO warrants, funded through our Coinbase facility. The company then needs to either service or reduce that debt over time. In simple terms, buying back those warrants was similar to purchasing heavily discounted Bitcoin. The most analytical way to evaluate that transaction is to consider the original transaction, the cost of the capital over time, and the long-term impact on the treasury and Bitcoin per share. Note that the share price will also change over that time period along with the Bitcoin price. 5) Please note that there are numerous other aspects of managing a treasury and in this post I am just highlighting a few things we consider. I believe it is critical for investors to understand that treasury management will naturally become more complex as the business scales. Even though our starting strategy is to keep the capital toolkit as simple and fair as possible. Please judge us by our results over months and quarters, rather than individual transactions. Ironically, the guy who first told me to buy Bitcoin was just some random internet influencer selling paid group memberships and courses, with no real trading track record at all. But he did tell me one important thing: “Use cold storage. Keep your Bitcoin on a Trezor.” So I started searching what Bitcoin actually was. I found the Chinese translation of Satoshi Nakamoto’s whitepaper. I couldn’t understand any of it. As someone who mainly studied history, geography, and politics, the entire paper looked like incomprehensible scripture to me. So instead of trying to understand the technical details, I decided to study the community around Bitcoin instead. I read forums, discussions, debates, and what other people thought about it. Luckily, back then the Chinese Bitcoin community still had many true believers passionately explaining Bitcoin and trying to communicate what it actually meant. I learned a lot during that era. And then one day, something suddenly clicked. In a country like China, under an authoritarian government, the ability for an individual to freely hold and transfer value — without government permission, surveillance, or even awareness — is unbelievably rare. Actually, not rare. Unique. My family had already experienced political persecution under the Chinese Communist system, and our family wealth was wiped out because of it. So deep down, I always understood how dangerous unchecked political power could be. Life in China revolves around power. Everything revolves around political authority. There’s a famous saying in Chinese society: “If they say you can, then you can — even if you can’t. If they say you can’t, then you can’t — even if you can.” And then I realized: Bitcoin solved this problem. My first impression of Bitcoin wasn’t “digital gold” or “fixed supply.” It was the realization that human beings could finally own a form of value transfer that nobody could control. And once I realized that, another thought shocked me: “How is this thing not completely banned in China already?” (Or at least — not successfully banned, despite many attempts.) Because any form of freedom is incredibly precious for people living in China, even if many Chinese people themselves don’t care. So honestly, I barely even researched the price. Compared to ownership beyond political power, valuation felt insignificant. I bought as much Bitcoin as I possibly could during the early 2018 bear market, around an average price of $10,000. Only after moving it into my Trezor did I continue researching more deeply. That’s when I discovered Austrian economics. I started reading Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, and The Denationalization of Money. And then I arrived at another conclusion: Bitcoin has no valuation ceiling. Whatever wealth humanity ultimately stores economically, divided by 21 million. Of course, that sounds too extreme. So let’s use a smaller assumption. If Bitcoin absorbs just 1% of total global wealth, then by 2026 standards, Bitcoin already justifies prices around $150,000. Back then I never built complicated valuation models. I simply felt, instinctively, that this thing had no ceiling.

Bitcoin Wasn’t Born in a Vacuum People are asking if Bitcoin came from the PayPal mafia, intelligence agencies, or even someone like Jeffrey Epstein. The honest answer is: we’ll probably never know who created Bitcoin and that’s not the most important question anyway. Epstein clearly wasn’t Satoshi. He wasn’t technical. But the emails suggest he was aware of Bitcoin very early and connected to people in the space like Gavin Andresen and Adam Back. He likely knew the kinds of people who could build something like Bitcoin. More broadly, the idea that Bitcoin started as a completely pure, outsider project isn’t really true. Powerful networks, especially people tied to PayPal and early tech finance, were involved early, mining, investing, and experimenting with digital money long before Bitcoin took off. That matters, because those early players may still hold a significant share of the supply today. If Bitcoin becomes a global reserve asset, that concentration could translate into enormous wealth and influence. But it also doesn’t matter in one key way: owning Bitcoin doesn’t give you control over the network. You can’t change the rules, inflate the supply, or censor transactions just because you hold a lot of it. The bigger point is that Bitcoin didn’t emerge in a vacuum. It came out of years of experimentation with digital economies, online currencies, and attempts to build money native to the internet. People like Epstein weren’t necessarily creators but they were connectors, investors, and early observers of this shift. So focusing too much on “who created Bitcoin” misses the real issue. The real question is what Bitcoin becomes. Does it actually deliver on the promise of open, neutral, global money? The sun is setting on BTC’s pump-and-dumpers. Vitalik’s idealism is exactly what crypto needs most right now. That is my strongest takeaway after reading his latest long post on where the Ethereum Foundation is going. VitalikButerin makes it clear that the ethereumfndn is deliberately becoming smaller, more focused, and more principled — not because it is retreating, but because it is choosing longevity over breadth. The EF is not the “center” of Ethereum. It is one node in a much larger ecosystem, with a specific role: to protect and advance the values that make Ethereum meaningfully different. Those values are what he frames as CROPS: censorship/capture resistance, openness, privacy, and security. Unsurprisingly, the post sent shockwaves through the crypto community. Some people pointed to the wave of talent leaving the EF and questioned its leadership. Others accused the Foundation of shrinking away from responsibility. Bankless co-founder David Hoffman selling all his ETH was widely interpreted as a loss of conviction from a long-time supporter. Many also criticized Vitalik for being too idealistic — too focused on formal verification, intermediary minimization, privacy, and long-term anti-censorship goals, while supposedly ignoring short-term execution, narratives, and price performance. These reactions are understandable. With core contributors leaving, ETH’s recent price action, and growing anxiety around Ethereum’s direction, people naturally want stronger leadership, clearer execution, and more immediate confidence. But I think these criticisms miss the deeper point. Vitalik is not saying Ethereum should stop scaling, stop competing, or stop being useful. He is saying Ethereum should not become just another chain chasing speed, hype, and short-term market narratives. The original crypto spirit was never simply about who has the lowest latency, the highest TPS, or the loudest marketing machine. It was about decentralization as a real shield against censorship and capture. It was about financial sovereignty. It was about building systems that cannot be easily controlled by any single company, government, foundation, or personality. When Vitalik says “Ethereum must be impressive,” he does not mean Ethereum should chase 250ms latency and 1M TPS at the cost of everything else. He means Ethereum should be impressive in the dimensions that actually matter in the AI age: verifiable security, minimized intermediaries, privacy, resilient consensus, and credible neutrality. These goals might sound unreasonable. That is exactly why Ethereum still feels different. The most important part of his post, is the idea that the EF should become “one node” rather than the center. That is not weakness. That is maturity. It pushes Ethereum closer to a genuinely permissionless future. In a way, it brings Ethereum closer to the spirit of Bitcoin: no single foundation as the savior, no central treasury as the source of truth, no one organization everyone depends on. Just a protocol, a community, and thousands of voluntary builders and users maintaining it together. This feels like a profound social experiment. In a world increasingly shaped by AI, capital, surveillance, and concentrated power, can one major project still hold onto its cypherpunk soul? Can it resist becoming fully captured by short-term incentives? Can it remain idealistic enough to protect the very values that made crypto meaningful in the first place? I strongly support this direction. What has always made crypto cool is not who lists first, who pumps hardest, or who tells the best story. It is the promise of sovereignty, censorship resistance, and the possibility of building systems that are not fully controlled by any single power. If even Ethereum gives that up and becomes just another execution-and-marketing machine, then something essential in crypto will be lost. Vitalik’s idealism is one of the rarest and most valuable things in this space right now. Short-term noise is loud. Long-term direction matters more. Respect to everyone still building for real decentralization, censorship resistance, and long-term resilience. Ethereum is still walking the hardest path — and that is precisely why it remains valuable. VitalikButerin, you are still the idealistic kid with that shy smile in my mind. Respect.

CONSOLIDATION IN BLOCKCHAIN — WHEN CHAOS STARTS BECOMING STRUCTURE In blockchain, consolidation is not simply about “merging things together.” It’s the process where fragmented systems begin evolving into something more unified, efficient, and sustainable. As the industry matures, ecosystems naturally move from experimentation → coordination. And this happens across multiple layers. --- 1. Liquidity Consolidation Early crypto ecosystems often scatter liquidity everywhere: different DEXs multiple bridges isolated chains fragmented pools The result? higher slippage inefficient routing poor user experience Over time, protocols begin connecting liquidity sources together. This creates: deeper markets smoother trading better capital efficiency Because in the end: > liquidity becomes stronger when it flows together, not separately. 2. Infrastructure Consolidation Not every blockchain needs to rebuild everything from zero. Today, many ecosystems are beginning to share the same foundations: OP Stack shared security shared sequencers Ethereum settlement layers Instead of competing through isolated infrastructure, projects begin coordinating through common standards. This creates: faster development better interoperability stronger ecosystem compatibility It’s similar to modern cities sharing the same highways, internet protocols, and energy systems. Different destinations. Shared foundations. --- 3. Asset Consolidation In some blockchains, consolidation also happens at the asset level. For example: combining small UTXOs in Bitcoin reorganizing staking rewards merging liquidity positions simplifying wallet balances This helps networks become cleaner and more efficient. Sometimes consolidation isn’t visible to users directly… …but it quietly improves scalability and transaction management behind the scenes. --- 4. Ecosystem & Community Consolidation The strongest ecosystems are not always the loudest. Over time, mature projects begin focusing on: governance clarity aligned vision sustainable collaboration stronger community coordination Because long-term ecosystems cannot survive on hype alone. They need structure. Direction. Shared purpose. --- The Bigger Picture Most industries begin in chaos. Blockchain is no different. At first: everyone builds separately liquidity fragments infrastructures duplicate communities divide But eventually… the market starts rewarding ecosystems that are: connected efficient interoperable sustainable That is where consolidation begins. And honestly? Consolidation is often a sign that an ecosystem is no longer just experimenting… …it’s starting to mature

A lot of people still don’t understand the difference between buying Bitcoin… and actually possessing Bitcoin. Bitcoin was created as peer-to-peer electronic cash. The entire idea was reducing dependency on centralized intermediaries. But today, many people “buy Bitcoin” on exchanges and still can’t actually move it for days because banks, ACH systems, settlement delays, fraud controls, and custodial restrictions are sitting in the middle. So the question becomes: Do you really own something if another institution ultimately controls when you can access it? To me, sovereignty is one of the most important ideas behind Bitcoin. Sovereignty means: • control • possession • self-custody • direct ownership • the ability to transfer value without asking permission That’s one reason cash became so important to our business model. If Bitcoin is supposed to be an alternative to traditional banking systems, then people need ways to access Bitcoin that don’t fully depend on the same systems Bitcoin was originally designed to route around. There’s a huge difference between: “An exchange owes me Bitcoin” and “I actually possess Bitcoin myself.” More people are starting to understand that difference.

Network usage does not automatically equal token value. Ask yourself: Does increased usage FORCE buying pressure on the token itself? Directly. Not indirectly. Gas fees. Staking. Validator security. Governance. Most of that is baseline Layer 1 utility. The real question is: Can institutions use the network while abstracting the token away from holders? Because if they can, the network can grow while the token itself bleeds value through: • inflation • unlocks • emissions • validator sell pressure • treasury selling That means the VALUE is being extracted from the network while holders absorb the dilution. Direct value capture is when the token itself becomes unavoidable: • the network requires the token • security depends on the token • users must acquire the token to participate/ strict amount • demand rises as network usage rises • supply gets locked or removed from circulation/ hard locks, not a 14 hour window That’s the difference between a token being part of the product… and the token BEING the product. Most tokens in this space are just apart of the product… not the actual product itself. A few examples of “direct” value capture mechanics than the average crypto indirect value capture: •Bitcoin The asset itself IS the network reserve asset. Security, scarcity, settlement, and demand all revolve around BTC itself. •Tellor Reporters, disputes, and network security revolve around TRB. Participation directly affects token demand and available supply. •Maker Historically one of the stronger value capture models because protocol activity and stability mechanisms were tied into MKR burn/governance dynamics. •Aave The token is tied into protocol security, governance, and ecosystem participation. Not perfect forced value, but stronger than many generic Layer 1s. •Binance Coin Exchange activity, fee reductions, burns, ecosystem utility, and Binance growth historically fed directly back into BNB demand. Usage increases token relevance instead of… usage happens while the token becomes optional…

And that's what's important to understand next.: The more supply goes into such "hard hands", the more strongly any new large influx of demand will affect the price. When most of the coins stop participating in regular trading, even relatively small amounts of sales or purchases can cause more dramatic movements. Liquidity is becoming more fragile. 2013 was the year. I wasn't quite sold yet on quitting my job to dive into Ripple. It was a tiny startup, and they were hosting a side event at Money20/20 in Las Vegas. Stefan Thomas, the CTO, was presenting his vision for smart contracts on Ripple and the plan to build programmable money directly into the Ripple ledger so you could run all kinds of applications. The minds behind 'Colored Coins' were there too, some of whom ended up at the Omni Protocol and, later, Tether. Can't forget a certain editor from Bitcoin Magazine back then, Vitalik Buterin, who was exploring smart contracts with Stefan and David Schwartz. We went to Google headquarters in Mountain View a few times to meet with their secure compute team. They had a product called NaCl, a secure sandbox for executing untrusted code safely inside Chrome. We were working with them to figure out how to leverage that technology to execute code in a trustless way on the Ripple system. But the organization was growing rapidly, and the decision was made to pivot to a pure payments model. Our primary customers would be banks, which meant we needed to freeze the Ripple protocol. To ensure the absolute security and stability of the platform, arbitrary code execution and smart contracts were taken off the table. In other words, the business side didn’t really buy into the vision for programmable money. They asked us to spin smart contracts out into a separate R&D project and just merge them back into the main Ripple code later. Right around that point, Vitalik launched Ethereum. Ethereum exploded because programmable money and trustless execution were the real paradigm shift. At the time, XRP was the number two coin by market cap, but Ethereum quickly surpassed it by an order of magnitude. The lesson we learned later at Ripple was just how massive of an opportunity we had missed. The value of public, auditable code that is guaranteed to execute exactly the same way every time is immense. It virtually eliminates counterparty risk. Certain categories of human friction are entirely wiped out when you can place your trust in code.

Bitcoin currently has the biggest network effect and has that because it was the first "cryptocurrency", but there is nothing about being the first that guarantees an enduring network effect. Moreover, the only reason any cryptocurrency at all has any network effect or value is, ultimately (not necessarily in the minds of every speculator), because people expect them to become money at some point (of course any increase in value in the meantime comes as an expected consequence of this same expectation, see Mises's regression theory). What this all means is that if Bitcoin stops making moves towards becoming money what we should absolutely expect is that its value will decrease, and so the price, its network effect will diminish and some other cryptocurrency (hopefully) will take its place and hopefully do a better job. LEARN WITH MUJAHIDDEEN — DAY 2 THE HISTORY OF MONEY Money did not appear overnight. It evolved over thousands of years. And understanding this evolution helps you understand why cryptocurrency was eventually created. Let’s start from the beginning. - BARTER TRADE Before money existed, people exchanged goods directly. Example: • Rice for fish • Goat for clothes • Milk for grains This was called barter trade. But barter had major problems: • What if the other person doesn’t want what you have? • What if the value isn’t equal? • What if the item cannot be divided? Trade became stressful. Humans needed a better system. - COMMODITY MONEY People began using items everyone considered valuable. Things like: • Salt • Cowries • Gold • Silver These became early forms of money simply because people trusted their value. But there was still a problem: Carrying heavy metals or goods around wasn’t convenient. - METAL COINS Governments later introduced coins made from metals like: • Gold • Silver • Bronze Coins made trade easier and more organized. People now had: • standard value • portable money • easier exchange - PAPER MONEY Later, paper currency was introduced. Instead of carrying gold everywhere, people could carry notes representing value. This eventually became modern currencies like: • Naira • Dollar • Pound • Euro And governments became responsible for controlling money supply. - DIGITAL MONEY As technology advanced, money became digital. Today: • bank transfers • debit cards • mobile banking • online payments …are all forms of digital money. Most money today exists only as numbers in databases. THE NEXT EVOLUTION: CRYPTO Then came a new idea. “What if money could exist online without banks controlling it?” That idea led to: • Bitcoin • Blockchain • Cryptocurrency Crypto became another step in the evolution of money. From: Barter → Gold → Paper → Digital → Crypto And that evolution is still continuing today. Next lesson: “Problems With Traditional Money Systems”
