Time-Enhancing Assets: Rare Sats as an Example At its core, every investment comes down to a single question: Which side is time on? Some assets lose value as time passes. Some remain largely unchanged. And a rare few become stronger simply because time continues to pass. I classify them into three categories: time-decaying, time-neutral, and time-enhancing assets. Stablecoins are a typical example of time-neutral assets. Holding USDC for one day or ten years makes little difference. Their value comes from utility and circulation, not from the accumulation of time. Many technology-driven companies, on the other hand, are time-decaying assets. Their competitive advantages gradually erode as rivals catch up and innovations become commoditized. Bitcoin and Rare Sats belong to a different category altogether: time-enhancing assets. Their greatest moat is not technology, but history. Every additional day Bitcoin operates strengthens its credibility, expands its consensus network, and deepens its irreplaceable historical record. Any competitor can copy Bitcoin’s code, but no one can replicate its seventeen years of uninterrupted existence. Rare Sats amplify this phenomenon even further. Their rarity is rooted in the mathematical structure of the Bitcoin protocol itself, not in marketing, narratives, or human decisions. As time passes, more Rare Sats are discovered, identified, cataloged, and collected. Awareness spreads, and once someone understands the concept of protocol-level scarcity, that knowledge rarely disappears. Discovery is irreversible. Recognition is cumulative. Conviction-based holders gradually replace short-term speculators, reducing available supply and strengthening the asset's long-term foundation. In this sense, time does not weaken Rare Sats—it continuously reinforces them. The unique characteristic of a time-enhancing asset is that you are not merely waiting for value to emerge; you are participating in the process by which value is formed. Time itself becomes a productive force. For such assets, time is not a cost. It is a source of compounding. It is not something consumed, but something accumulated. Ultimately, what is truly scarce is not the asset itself, but a structure in which time consistently works in your favor.

As much as I agree with the argument that just because bitcoin:native is oversold on the daily RSI doesn't mean it can't go lower, I'd like to offer some context to that discussion. Since the bear market lows of 2022, every time Bitcoin has reached an oversold reading on the daily RSI, it has presented an excellent buying opportunity. On average, buying or dollar cost averaging into those oversold conditions has led to roughly 74% returns by the time Bitcoin reached its next significant local high. Now, I'm not claiming that an oversold RSI marks the exact bottom. In fact, if you look at June 2024, Bitcoin dipped below the initial oversold low several times before eventually moving to new local highs. My analysis isn't based on buying the exact low. Instead, I've measured the returns from each oversold reading to the next local high. The point is that while oversold conditions don't guarantee an immediate reversal, they have consistently offered strong risk to reward opportunities. We're currently back in one of those oversold zones. Even during the bearish period following the October 2025 highs, every oversold daily RSI reading has produced a meaningful relief rally. The weakest of those rallies was still around 21% from low to high, while the most recent oversold reading led to a move of approximately 40%. So while I completely agree that an oversold RSI does not prevent Bitcoin from moving lower, history suggests that these conditions have generally been very attractive areas to accumulate. That's why there's so much debate right now. Both sides have a valid point. Bears are correct that oversold does not equal bottom, but bulls are equally justified in pointing out that oversold daily RSI readings have repeatedly provided some of the best buying opportunities of this cycle.

IBIT shed about $2 billion over a nine session streak, a $440 million single day, as rate cut odds faded and Middle East tension bid traditional havens into a thin summer tape. That is borrowed money and hot money leaving through the most liquid door in the market. It is just positioning. It is not a verdict on the asset, so calm down. Now the two headlines doing the biggest psychological damage amongst plebs, against the actual filings. Saylor did not break. Strategy sold 32 coins. Thirty two, for $2.5 million, at $77,135, above their $75,699 cost basis and above spot that day. That is 0.004 percent of an 843,706 coin position. The proceeds fund the STRC preferred dividend, it was pre announced on the Q1 call, and Saylor has said on record they buy 10 to 20 coins for every one they sell. They raised $128 million through the ATM the same week and hold a $900 million cash reserve. This is plumbing, not capitulation. Anyone trading the headline never opened the 8-K. The convenience that made it the easiest on ramp makes it the easiest off ramp, so it moves first and largest in both directions. First out is not gone. So much for the noise. Now the one structural fear worth actually respecting, and the metric most people quote wrong with MSTR. Basic mNAV, market cap over Bitcoin NAV, is sitting around 1.2x. A 21 percent premium. Looks like cushion. It is not. Common equity is roughly $54 billion. Senior to it sits about $8 billion of convertible notes and north of $13 billion of preferred across four series, STRK at 8, STRF at 10, STRD at 10, STRC variable near 11.5. Put the whole enterprise over the Bitcoin and the premium nearly vanishes, an enterprise value mNAV closer to 1.0x than 1.2x, and it already printed 0.97x once in November. The common is not a 21 percent cushion. It is the thin equity slice on top of $21 billion of senior capital, all backed by one volatile asset. Basic mNAV flatters it. EV mNAV tells the true view. That stack carries roughly $1.4 billion a year in cash dividends, and the software business turns over about $124 million a quarter. So coupons get funded by issuing common, issuing more preferred, or selling Bitcoin. Above 1x mNAV they issue at a premium and the dividend is covered by accretive raises. Forward flywheel. Below 1x, issuing common is dilutive, the cleanest lever breaks, and the quiet option left is selling Bitcoin. Reverse flywheel. The 32 BTC sale was the first time in company history that Bitcoin funded a coupon. That is the lever going live. But it is not a death spiral, and saying so is how you get the call wrong. A death spiral needs a creditor who can force you under. Strategy does not have one. Preferreds are equity, not debt you idiot. No acceleration, no margin call, no liquidation trigger. STRD is non cumulative, they can defer it. They have been retiring actual debt, $1.5 billion of converts bought back. Nobody can force a sale of the stack. The risk is not collapse, it is a slow grind where a 10x proxy quietly becomes a 1x proxy with a coupon problem. And that risk lives in the vehicle, not the asset. Bitcoin has no dividend. This is a Strategy problem, not a Bitcoin problem. So what does Bitcoin actually have to do for this to win. Three lines, not one. Below about 2.5 percent a year you lose, the stack does not grow enough to cover the coupons. Above about 7 percent you win, that is the blended cost of the senior stack, and once Bitcoin compounds past it the asset out-earns the capital used to buy it. Above 10.5 percent it rips, every dollar of preferred ever issued was accretive and the flywheel runs at full power. The target is not a moonshot. It is Bitcoin north of 7 percent, ideally north of 10. And here is why that is not bleak. The hurdle is near the floor of what Bitcoin should do, not the ceiling. Global fiat supply grows 6 to 8 percent a year by design. Gold has compounded around 8 percent over decades just sitting there as the debasement hedge. Bitcoin is the harder version of that trade. Debasement alone, with zero new adoption, roughly clears the 7 percent line. Then add the demand against a capped supply. Issuance is 450 coins a day and halving. Four million are lost forever. Against that float sit buyers who did not exist at this scale in any prior cycle. You cannot run structural buyers of that size against a shrinking float without the clearing price re-rating by multiples. That does not deliver 7 percent. It delivers multiples of it. Strategy bleeds if Bitcoin goes flat to down for years, mNAV stays pinned below 1, the reserve empties, and they are forced to sell coins into weakness to service a stack they refused to throttle. Not impossible. But it requires Bitcoin to do something for years it has never done for years, while management does nothing, which is the opposite of how they run the book. Every lever to avoid it, throttle STRC, defend the premium, manage the liabilities, is in their own hands. So put the whole thing together. Last night was a leverage flush and panic mode. The one real risk is the leverage in the vehicle, not the asset, and it only triggers in a multi-year winter the demand stack is built to prevent. Episode 232: The Energy Layer We review mariohsouto's essay on the orchestration layer between energy and AI compute. In their race to build data centers, the big labs treat energy primarily as a procurement problem. This misses a bigger picture. (Yeah I'm gonna hand this one to ChatGPT. Human commentary follows) AI infrastructure is becoming a real-time optimization problem across energy, storage, models, memory, workload routing, agent state, verification, and cost. It is not just deciding which GPU runs which prompt. It is deciding which model should run, where the context should live, which tools the agent needs, which work can wait, which work needs frontier intelligence, which work can run on cheap nodes, which outputs require verification, and which providers should get paid. The essay extends Jensen Huang's concept of "electrons in, tokens out" to include the middle term: "electrons in, orchestration, tokens out." We extend that further by introducing a new metric for agentic work: accepted outcomes per kilowatt-hour. So our version is: "electrons in, orchestration, accepted outcomes out." Bitcoin miners are the obvious players to pay attention to here. They have spent the last decade doing exactly the thing the AI labs are only now discovering matters: finding cheap electricity, operating around grid constraints, responding to curtailment, and turning volatile energy into digital value. That does not mean Bitcoin miners automatically become AI labs. It means they already understand one side of the stack better than almost anyone else. They understand power markets. They understand stranded energy. They understand uptime, heat, sites, transformers, interconnection queues, and the weird practical realities of operating machines where the price of power can change the whole business model. The missing piece is the workload layer. Bitcoin mining is simple in one important way: every hash is the same. AI work is not like that. Some jobs need to run immediately. Some can wait. Some need GPUs. Some can run on CPUs. Some need high memory. Some need verification. Some are only valuable if the output is accepted by the user. That is where agentic inference changes the picture. Agentic work is not just a chat response. It is tasks. It is code. It is research. It is data cleaning. It is benchmark runs. It is verification. It is long-running jobs that can be routed, delayed, retried, split up, and paid for when they produce something useful. So the opportunity is not just: miners add GPUs. The opportunity is: miners become part of an agentic compute market. They bring cheap electrons and operational discipline. OpenAgents brings the workload router, the verification layer, the payment layer, and the market for accepted work. This is the bridge from Bitcoin mining to AI. Not abandoning Bitcoin. Not pretending every mining site becomes a hyperscaler. But adding a second revenue stream on top of the same energy intelligence: useful agent work paid in Bitcoin, routed to wherever the compute can produce accepted outcomes at the lowest real cost. That is the energy layer as a market. 1. Cheap power in. 2. Energy-aware routing. 3. Verified agent work out. --- "Hey Car do you know any soon to be major AI labs that are based in Texas?"
